{:db/id 17592186130226}} {:db/id 17592186130225 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130460 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $\\mathbf{T}: U \\to \\mathbb{R}^2$ is a transformation given by\n\n![](images/f9/f9a1c3375eed570284c4e001f119f21901f4493a0b851919b92b678a74187444.svg) \n\nWe'll assume that $\\mathbf T$ is a $\\boldsymbol{C}^1$ **transformation**, which means that  $x$ and $y$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives on an open set $U$ contained in $\\Bbb R^2.$ \n\nThe **Jacobian determinant** of $\\mathbf T,$ denoted $\\dfrac{\\partial (x, y)}{\\partial (u, v)} ,$ is defined as\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \\frac{∂x}{∂v} \\\\ \\frac{∂y}{∂u} & \\frac{∂y}{∂v}\\end{aligned}|=\\frac{∂x}{∂u}\\cdot \\frac{∂y}{∂v}-\\frac{∂x}{∂v}\\cdot \\frac{∂y}{∂u}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n  \n\nWe sometimes refer to the Jacobian determinant simply as the **Jacobian.**\n\nLet's compute the Jacobian determinant of the following transformation:\n\n![](images/b4/b433bcafea1c84c67f2fb65ac8343a4d8401ce6d4e745f6d464b010a4258164a.svg) \n\nTo compute the Jacobian determinant of this function, we first calculate the required partial derivatives:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =\\operatorname{cos}⁡v & \\,\\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-u\\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\\\ \\frac{∂y}{∂u} & =\\operatorname{sin}⁡v & \\,\\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =u\\operatorname{cos}⁡v\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\\begin{aligned}\\operatorname{cos}⁡v & -u\\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\\\ \\operatorname{sin}⁡v & u\\operatorname{cos}⁡v\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =\\operatorname{cos}⁡v\\cdot (u\\operatorname{cos}⁡v)-(-u\\operatorname{sin}⁡v)\\cdot \\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\\\  & =u{cos}^{2}⁡v+u{sin}^{2}⁡v \\\\  & =u({cos}^{2}⁡v+{sin}^{2}⁡v) \\\\  & =u.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n \n\nWe'll spend some time discussing the meaning behind the Jacobian shortly. But for now, let's get some practice at computing it." :tutorial/id #uuid "f0ea7366-d3d6-5645-99d8-72f7febb8d19" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7668 :tutorial/title "The Jacobian Determinant"} :step/id #uuid "eadcf9f2-f662-5ba3-8bbc-b9166dfa1142" :step/math-academy-id 44550 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130065}} {:db/id 17592186130226 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130461 :tutorial/content "To understand what the Jacobian describes, we recall our knowledge of affine transformations.\n\nConsider the affine transformation $\\mathbf T:\\Bbb R^2 \\to \\Bbb R^2,$ defined by the matrix equation \n\n$$\n\\mathbf x = T\\mathbf u + \\mathbf b,\n$$\n\nwhere $\\mathbf u, \\mathbf b,$ and $\\mathbf x$ are vectors from $\\mathbb R^2,$ and $T$ is a $2\\times 2$ matrix. \n\nFor an affine transformation, the determinant of $T$ gives us the following information:\n\n- The *area scale factor* of the transformation:\n\nIf a rectangle in the $uv$-plane has area $A,$ its image in the $xy$-plane is a parallelogram of area $|\\det(T)|\\cdot A.$\n\n![](images/04/04f36d98bf7589d1faadeffee0812590337fd36d8bb44f5abe1920948dee5bb0.png)\n\n- Whether the transformation is *orientation-preserving* or *orientation-reversing:*\n\nIf $\\textrm{det}(T) > 0,$ the transformation is orientation-preserving.\n\n![](images/49/496a49ee541eab31f69f9c571e450547b0c6942b100bc8e24fbd927dd43e4d33.png)\n\nIf $\\textrm{det}(T) < 0,$ the transformation is orientation-reversing.\n\n![](images/21/211369d6f3fc70bcf7cf40f3270c24c245d306247efc429cb85589e42c19ee07.png)\n\n- Whether the transformation is *invertible* or *non-invertible:*\n\nIf $\\textrm{det}(T) \\neq 0,$ the transformation is invertible.\n\n![](images/e4/e4b840ad5a3efa082ac4056d1d9b7c03d2e3e11e016e053df055dbb2b39f0d1f.png)\n\nIf $\\textrm{det}(T) = 0,$ the transformation is non-invertible. In such cases, a rectangle in the $uv$-plane collapses to either a line segment or point in the $xy$-plane.\n\n![](images/9a/9a038c5de0e9f3205194fd7941a4b371c695c51c294f2ad5ac0b8fc1015811d1.png)\n\n![](images/98/9813ba294a0242abbfb885ebd3e82505d05a2f8a1cfa3975c7859f9530cac8b1.png)\n\nAffine transformations are special because these properties are *global*. In other words, they apply *everywhere* in the plane. So, for example, if $\\textrm{det}(T) = 2$, then the image of *every* rectangle in the $uv$-plane is a parallelogram with double the area of its preimage." :tutorial/id #uuid "4dcb1ce1-bfad-524c-a89a-a589532a1067" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7672 :tutorial/title "A Review of Affine Transformations"} :step/id #uuid "c956f456-bd29-5cf7-83bd-de9b757b718f" :step/math-academy-id 44557 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130227}} {:db/id 17592186130227 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130462 :tutorial/content "The Jacobian determinant gives information about nonlinear transformations similar to that described by the determinant properties of affine transformations.\n\nThe critical difference is that, in general, the Jacobian describes *local* effects, not global ones. \n\nTo understand what this means, suppose that $\\mathbf{T}: U \\to \\mathbb{R}^2$ is a transformation, where\n![](images/d0/d0149013f12e5cdad31611d4c64489c0aaf6049707e9eed22202ae70d2d8a38a.svg) \n\nand we assume that $x(u,v)$ and $y(u,v)$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives on $U.$\n\nFor ease of notation, let's introduce $J(u_0,v_0)$ to denote the Jacobian determinant of $\\mathbf T$ evaluated at $(u_0, v_0){:}$\n\n$$\nJ(u_0,v_0) = \\left.\\dfrac{\\partial(x,y)}{\\partial(u,v)}\\right|_{(u_0,v_0)}\n$$\n\nLet's describe $\\mathbf T$'s effect on a *tiny* rectangle in the $uv$-plane whose bottom-left corner is the point $(u_0,v_0).$\n\n![](images/dc/dc084ec02cd0c4fac71379590e8dc4973354cacc898e267a0eb15a6e8500f31f.png)\n\nIt's important to note that the image of our rectangle in the $xy$-plane is typically *not* a parallelogram! However, provided that our rectangle is very small, its image can be *approximated* by a parallelogram (we'll justify this in a future lesson). \n\nThe Jacobian determinant of $\\mathbf T$ evaluated at $(u_0,v_0)$ describes the following key features between our tiny rectangle and its (approximate) image:\n\n- The *local* area scale factor of $\\mathbf T$. \n\nSuppose the length and width of our rectangle are $\\delta u$ and $\\delta v,$ so its area is $\\delta A = \\delta u\\delta v.$ Then, it can be shown that the parallelogram in the $xy$-plane has an area equal to $\\left|J(u_0,v_0)\\right| \\cdot \\delta A.$\n\n![](images/be/be1771ebb041c418c58d7d5615510e2fcacfeaf3677fbace739498ef1998ef11.png)\n\nNote the similarity of this formula with that of affine transformations described earlier (we've simply replaced $\\det(T)$ with the Jacobian).\n\n- Whether the transformation is *locally* orientation-preserving or *locally* orientation-reversing.\n\nIf $J(u_0,v_0)> 0,$ the transformation is (locally) orientation-preserving.\n\n![](images/8c/8c649fdd526a831fb990393b292fb4582dad14c2391d129e9ed59792ebb8ac31.png)\n\nIf $J(u_0,v_0)<  0,$ the transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing.\n\n![](images/ae/ae5a3d0a42e1c4b9f692994b89815382a30cdf3e676bbd9844258ad2a6961608.png)\n\n- Whether the transformation is *locally* invertible or *locally* non-invertible.\n\nIf $J(u_0,v_0)\\neq 0,$ the transformation is (locally) invertible.\n\n![](images/33/33ca98206a347e13aa8ec179a52dd755008d9a7d74882391e0c3f2344f6f6641.png)\n\nIf $J(u_0,v_0)= 0,$ the transformation is (locally) non-invertible.\n\n![](images/3d/3d4534c263a9a5bb26ba35ce8f879cf01db741441d948c023acaa9407d58e6e0.png)\n\n![](images/65/659f26ac6aba808d66a760d5683f265fd7c54431d894b2eabdc255b46368fc24.png)\n\nPoints $(u_0,v_0)$ such that $J(u_0,v_0)=0$ are called **critical points.** Critical points are very important. We'll discuss these in more detail in future lessons.\n\nWe again stress that the Jacobian describes *local* properties, that is, local to the point $(u_0,v_0).$ The effect of a nonlinear transformation on an object varies as we move around the $uv$-plane, so its local properties also vary. So, for example, if a transformation is orientation-preserving at one point, it does *not* mean it's orientation-preserving everywhere!" :tutorial/id #uuid "3f6a2c63-d9fc-533c-8c4b-fd822216f0f1" But for now, let's get some practice at computing it." :tutorial/id #uuid "f0ea7366-d3d6-5645-99d8-72f7febb8d19" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7668 :tutorial/title "The Jacobian Determinant"} {:db/id 17592186130461 :tutorial/content "To understand what the Jacobian describes, we recall our knowledge of affine transformations.\n\nConsider the affine transformation $\\mathbf T:\\Bbb R^2 \\to \\Bbb R^2,$ defined by the matrix equation \n\n$$\n\\mathbf x = T\\mathbf u + \\mathbf b,\n$$\n\nwhere $\\mathbf u, \\mathbf b,$ and $\\mathbf x$ are vectors from $\\mathbb R^2,$ and $T$ is a $2\\times 2$ matrix. \n\nFor an affine transformation, the determinant of $T$ gives us the following information:\n\n- The *area scale factor* of the transformation:\n\nIf a rectangle in the $uv$-plane has area $A,$ its image in the $xy$-plane is a parallelogram of area $|\\det(T)|\\cdot A.$\n\n![](images/04/04f36d98bf7589d1faadeffee0812590337fd36d8bb44f5abe1920948dee5bb0.png)\n\n- Whether the transformation is *orientation-preserving* or *orientation-reversing:*\n\nIf $\\textrm{det}(T) > 0,$ the transformation is orientation-preserving.\n\n![](images/49/496a49ee541eab31f69f9c571e450547b0c6942b100bc8e24fbd927dd43e4d33.png)\n\nIf $\\textrm{det}(T) < 0,$ the transformation is orientation-reversing.\n\n![](images/21/211369d6f3fc70bcf7cf40f3270c24c245d306247efc429cb85589e42c19ee07.png)\n\n- Whether the transformation is *invertible* or *non-invertible:*\n\nIf $\\textrm{det}(T) \\neq 0,$ the transformation is invertible.\n\n![](images/e4/e4b840ad5a3efa082ac4056d1d9b7c03d2e3e11e016e053df055dbb2b39f0d1f.png)\n\nIf $\\textrm{det}(T) = 0,$ the transformation is non-invertible. In such cases, a rectangle in the $uv$-plane collapses to either a line segment or point in the $xy$-plane.\n\n![](images/9a/9a038c5de0e9f3205194fd7941a4b371c695c51c294f2ad5ac0b8fc1015811d1.png)\n\n![](images/98/9813ba294a0242abbfb885ebd3e82505d05a2f8a1cfa3975c7859f9530cac8b1.png)\n\nAffine transformations are special because these properties are *global*. In other words, they apply *everywhere* in the plane. So, for example, if $\\textrm{det}(T) = 2$, then the image of *every* rectangle in the $uv$-plane is a parallelogram with double the area of its preimage." :tutorial/id #uuid "4dcb1ce1-bfad-524c-a89a-a589532a1067" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7672 :tutorial/title "A Review of Affine Transformations"} {:db/id 17592186130227 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130462 :tutorial/content "The Jacobian determinant gives information about nonlinear transformations similar to that described by the determinant properties of affine transformations.\n\nThe critical difference is that, in general, the Jacobian describes *local* effects, not global ones. \n\nTo understand what this means, suppose that $\\mathbf{T}: U \\to \\mathbb{R}^2$ is a transformation, where\n![](images/d0/d0149013f12e5cdad31611d4c64489c0aaf6049707e9eed22202ae70d2d8a38a.svg) \n\nand we assume that $x(u,v)$ and $y(u,v)$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives on $U.$\n\nFor ease of notation, let's introduce $J(u_0,v_0)$ to denote the Jacobian determinant of $\\mathbf T$ evaluated at $(u_0, v_0){:}$\n\n$$\nJ(u_0,v_0) = \\left.\\dfrac{\\partial(x,y)}{\\partial(u,v)}\\right|_{(u_0,v_0)}\n$$\n\nLet's describe $\\mathbf T$'s effect on a *tiny* rectangle in the $uv$-plane whose bottom-left corner is the point $(u_0,v_0).$\n\n![](images/dc/dc084ec02cd0c4fac71379590e8dc4973354cacc898e267a0eb15a6e8500f31f.png)\n\nIt's important to note that the image of our rectangle in the $xy$-plane is typically *not* a parallelogram! However, provided that our rectangle is very small, its image can be *approximated* by a parallelogram (we'll justify this in a future lesson). \n\nThe Jacobian determinant of $\\mathbf T$ evaluated at $(u_0,v_0)$ describes the following key features between our tiny rectangle and its (approximate) image:\n\n- The *local* area scale factor of $\\mathbf T$. \n\nSuppose the length and width of our rectangle are $\\delta u$ and $\\delta v,$ so its area is $\\delta A = \\delta u\\delta v.$ Then, it can be shown that the parallelogram in the $xy$-plane has an area equal to $\\left|J(u_0,v_0)\\right| \\cdot \\delta A.$\n\n![](images/be/be1771ebb041c418c58d7d5615510e2fcacfeaf3677fbace739498ef1998ef11.png)\n\nNote the similarity of this formula with that of affine transformations described earlier (we've simply replaced $\\det(T)$ with the Jacobian).\n\n- Whether the transformation is *locally* orientation-preserving or *locally* orientation-reversing.\n\nIf $J(u_0,v_0)> 0,$ the transformation is (locally) orientation-preserving.\n\n![](images/8c/8c649fdd526a831fb990393b292fb4582dad14c2391d129e9ed59792ebb8ac31.png)\n\nIf $J(u_0,v_0)<  0,$ the transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing.\n\n![](images/ae/ae5a3d0a42e1c4b9f692994b89815382a30cdf3e676bbd9844258ad2a6961608.png)\n\n- Whether the transformation is *locally* invertible or *locally* non-invertible.\n\nIf $J(u_0,v_0)\\neq 0,$ the transformation is (locally) invertible.\n\n![](images/33/33ca98206a347e13aa8ec179a52dd755008d9a7d74882391e0c3f2344f6f6641.png)\n\nIf $J(u_0,v_0)= 0,$ the transformation is (locally) non-invertible.\n\n![](images/3d/3d4534c263a9a5bb26ba35ce8f879cf01db741441d948c023acaa9407d58e6e0.png)\n\n![](images/65/659f26ac6aba808d66a760d5683f265fd7c54431d894b2eabdc255b46368fc24.png)\n\nPoints $(u_0,v_0)$ such that $J(u_0,v_0)=0$ are called **critical points.** Critical points are very important. We'll discuss these in more detail in future lessons.\n\nWe again stress that the Jacobian describes *local* properties, that is, local to the point $(u_0,v_0).$ The effect of a nonlinear transformation on an object varies as we move around the $uv$-plane, so its local properties also vary. So, for example, if a transformation is orientation-preserving at one point, it does *not* mean it's orientation-preserving everywhere!" :tutorial/id #uuid "3f6a2c63-d9fc-533c-8c4b-fd822216f0f1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7673 :tutorial/title "Intuition Behind the Jacobian"} :step/id #uuid "0e6a94d3-c32f-5582-98ea-69a8605ef653" :step/math-academy-id 44558 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130230}} {:db/id 17592186130462 :tutorial/content "The Jacobian determinant gives information about nonlinear transformations similar to that described by the determinant properties of affine transformations.\n\nThe critical difference is that, in general, the Jacobian describes *local* effects, not global ones. \n\nTo understand what this means, suppose that $\\mathbf{T}: U \\to \\mathbb{R}^2$ is a transformation, where\n![](images/d0/d0149013f12e5cdad31611d4c64489c0aaf6049707e9eed22202ae70d2d8a38a.svg) \n\nand we assume that $x(u,v)$ and $y(u,v)$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives on $U.$\n\nFor ease of notation, let's introduce $J(u_0,v_0)$ to denote the Jacobian determinant of $\\mathbf T$ evaluated at $(u_0, v_0){:}$\n\n$$\nJ(u_0,v_0) = \\left.\\dfrac{\\partial(x,y)}{\\partial(u,v)}\\right|_{(u_0,v_0)}\n$$\n\nLet's describe $\\mathbf T$'s effect on a *tiny* rectangle in the $uv$-plane whose bottom-left corner is the point $(u_0,v_0).$\n\n![](images/dc/dc084ec02cd0c4fac71379590e8dc4973354cacc898e267a0eb15a6e8500f31f.png)\n\nIt's important to note that the image of our rectangle in the $xy$-plane is typically *not* a parallelogram! following:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \\frac{∂x}{∂v} \\\\ \\frac{∂y}{∂u} & \\frac{∂y}{∂v}\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =|\\begin{aligned}-\\operatorname{sin}⁡u & -2v \\\\ 1 & 1\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =(-\\operatorname{sin}⁡u)\\cdot 1-1\\cdot (-2v) \\\\  & =-\\operatorname{sin}⁡u+2v \\\\ \\\\ \\frac{∂y}{∂u} & \\frac{∂y}{∂v}\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =|\\begin{aligned}-2\\operatorname{sin}⁡u & 0 \\\\ 0 & -3\\operatorname{cos}⁡v\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =(-2\\operatorname{sin}⁡u)\\cdot (-3\\operatorname{cos}⁡v)-0\\cdot 0 \\\\  & =6\\operatorname{sin}⁡u\\operatorname{cos}⁡v.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, when $[\\begin{aligned}u \\\\ v\\end{aligned}]=[\\begin{aligned}\\pi /4 \\\\ \\pi /4\\end{aligned}],$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is\n\n$$\n{\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(\\frac{\\pi }{4},\\frac{\\pi }{4})}=6\\operatorname{sin}⁡(\\frac{\\pi }{4})\\operatorname{cos}⁡(\\frac{\\pi }{4})=3.\n$$"} :step/id #uuid "fba89b3b-6b30-58fc-958c-99b3a9d49bb0" :step/next {:db/id 17592186406805}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid \n\nComputing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain the following:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \\frac{∂x}{∂v} \\\\ \\frac{∂y}{∂u} & \\frac{∂y}{∂v}\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =|\\begin{aligned}1 & 2v \\\\ \\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v) & \\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =1\\cdot \\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)-\\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)\\cdot 2v \\\\  & =(1-2v)\\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v) \\\\ {\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(-3,3)} & =(1-2v)\\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)\\,{|}_{u=-3\\,v=3} \\\\  & =(1-2(3))\\operatorname{cos}⁡(-3+3) \\\\  & =-5\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\text{Area}(T(Δ)) & ≈|-5|\\cdot \\delta A \\\\  & =5\\,\\delta A.\\end{aligned}\n$$"} :question/worked-solution "Given a transformation \n\n$$\nT:[\\begin{aligned}u \\\\ v\\end{aligned}]\\to [\\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\\\ y(u,v)\\end{aligned}],\n$$\n\nthe Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \\frac{∂x}{∂v} \\\\ \\frac{∂y}{∂u} & \\frac{∂y}{∂v}\\end{aligned}|.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nHere, we have $x(u,v)={e}^{u+v}$ and $y(u,v)={e}^{u-v}.$\n\nFirst, we find the partial derivatives:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂x}{∂u} & ={e}^{u+v} & \\,\\frac{∂x}{∂v} & ={e}^{u+v} \\\\ \\frac{∂y}{∂u} & ={e}^{u-v} & \\,\\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =-{e}^{u-v}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \\frac{∂x}{∂v} \\\\ \\frac{∂y}{∂u} & \\frac{∂y}{∂v}\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =|\\begin{aligned}{e}^{u+v} & {e}^{u+v} \\\\ {e}^{u-v} & -{e}^{u-v}\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & ={e}^{u+v}\\cdot (-{e}^{u-v})-{e}^{u+v}\\cdot {e}^{u-v} \\\\  & =-{e}^{2u}-{e}^{2u} \\\\  & =-2{e}^{2u}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, when $[\\begin{aligned}u \\\\ v\\end{aligned}]=[\\begin{aligned}0 \\\\ -5\\end{aligned}],$ the value of our Jacobian determinant is\n\n$$\n{\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(0,-5)}=-2{e}^{2(0)}=-2.\n$$"} :step/id Jacobian determinant gives the local area scale factor of the transformation at that point:\n\n$$\n\\text{Area}(T(Δ))≈|\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\\cdot {{\\text{Area}(Δ)}_{⏟}}_{\\delta A}\n$$\n\n \n\nComputing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain the following:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \\frac{∂x}{∂v} \\\\ \\frac{∂y}{∂u} & \\frac{∂y}{∂v}\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =|\\begin{aligned}1 & 2v \\\\ \\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v) & \\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =1\\cdot \\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)-\\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)\\cdot 2v \\\\  & =(1-2v)\\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v) \\\\ {\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(-3,3)} & =(1-2v)\\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)\\,{|}_{u=-3\\,v=3} \\\\  & =(1-2(3))\\operatorname{cos}⁡(-3+3) \\\\  & =-5\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\text{Area}(T(Δ)) & ≈|-5|\\cdot \\delta A \\\\  & =5\\,\\delta A.\\end{aligned}\n$$"} derivatives:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂x}{∂u} & ={e}^{u-v} & \\,\\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-{e}^{u-v} \\\\ \\frac{∂y}{∂u} & =\\frac{1}{u} & \\,\\frac{∂y}{∂v} & \\frac{∂y}{∂u} & \\frac{∂y}{∂v}\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =|\\begin{aligned}{e}^{u-v} & -{e}^{u-v} \\\\ \\frac{1}{u} & \\frac{1}{v}\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & ={e}^{u-v}\\cdot (\\frac{1}{v})-(-{e}^{u-v})\\cdot \\frac{1}{u} \\\\  & =\\frac{{e}^{u-v}}{v}+\\frac{{e}^{u-v}}{u}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, when $[\\begin{aligned}u \\\\ v\\end{aligned}]=[\\begin{aligned}1 \\\\ If\n\n$$\n\\dfrac 35\n$$\n\nof it is paved with asphalt, how long is the paved part?\n\nTo find out the length of the paved part of the road, we need to calculate\n\n$$\n5 \\, \\dfrac{1}{2} \\times \\dfrac{3}{5}\n$$\n\nFirst, we write\n\n$$\n5 \\,\\dfrac{1}{2}\n$$\n\nas an improper fraction:\n\n$$\n5 \\,\\dfrac{1}{2} = \\dfrac{(5 \\times 2) + 1}{2} = \\dfrac{11}{2}\n$$\n\nNow, we can multiply the two numbers. We multiply the numerators, and we multiply the denominators:\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{11}{2} \\times \\dfrac{3}{5} = \\dfrac{11 \\times 3}{2 \\times 5} = \\dfrac{33}{10}\n$$\n\nFinally, by converting this fraction to a mixed number, we get\n\n$$\n33 \\div 10 = 3\\,\\textrm{R}\\,3 = 3\\,\\dfrac{3}{10}\n$$\n\nSo, the paved part of the road is\n\n$$\n3\\,\\dfrac{3}{10}\\,\\textrm{km}\n$$\n\nlong." Confidence Intervals From Normal Populations"}] :question/problem "Consider a sample of size $n=9$ from a normal population. Given that the sample mean is $50$ and the sample standard deviation is $1.5$, find a $99\\%$ confidence interval for the population mean $\\mu$ of the distribution.\n\n*Hint: Use the fact that $P(T > 3.355) = 0.005$, where $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $8$ degrees of freedom.*" :question/worked-solution "We are told that the population is normally distributed, but we do not know the population variance $\\sigma^2$.\n\nIn cases like this, the random variable\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{\\overline{X} - \\mu}{S/\\sqrt n}\n$$\n\nfollows a student's $t$-distribution $T_{n-1}$ with $n-1$ degrees of freedom, where\n\n- $\\overline{X}$ is the sample mean,\n- $\\mu$ is the population mean,\n- $S^2$ is the sample variance, and\n- $n$ is the sample size.\n\nGiven a value $\\alpha$ between $0$ and $1$, the corresponding $[100(1-\\alpha)]\\%$ confidence interval for the population mean $\\mu$ is given by\n\n$$\n\\overline{x} \\pm t_{n-1,\\alpha/2} \\cdot \\dfrac{s}{\\sqrt{n}}\n$$\n\nwhere\n\n$$\nP(T > t_{n-1,\\alpha/2}) = \\dfrac{\\alpha}{2}\n$$\n\nand $T$ has a student's $t$-distribution with $n-1$ degrees of freedom.\n\nIn our case,\n\n$$\n\\overline{x}=50, \\qquad n = 9, \\qquad s = 1.5\n$$\n\nWe are interested in finding a $99\\%$ confidence interval. So, we have\n\n$$\n\\alpha=1-0.99=0.01 \\qquad\\Longrightarrow\\qquad \\dfrac{\\alpha}{2}=0.005\n$$\n\nWe are given that\n\n$$\nP(T > 3.355) = 0.005\n$$\n\nAs a result,\n\n$$\nt_{n-1,\\alpha/2} = t_{8,0.005} = 3.355\n$$\n\n![](images/84/84f060ec1a5e8a8b3db0c0866ebef9db1c242e944717a5abfd28447e0eddb9be.png)\n\nTherefore, a $99\\%$ confidence interval for the population mean $\\mu$ is the following:\n\n$$\n\\begin{bmatrix}50 & ± 3.355 \\cdot \\frac{1.5}{\\sqrt{9}} \\\\ 50 & ± 1.678\\end{bmatrix}\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186048491} {:db/id 17592186050921} {:db/id 17592186188555 :question/id "83fbb490-e605-5aaf-8930-059c037e6897" :step/math-academy-id 37866 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189157}} {:db/id 17592186189092 :step/content {:db/id 17592186189369 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ drawn from a normal population with unknown population mean $\\mu$ and *known* population variance $\\sigma^2$. Recall that a $[100(1-\\alpha)]\\%$ confidence interval for the population mean $\\mu$ is given by\n\n$$\n\\left(\\overline{x} - z_{\\alpha/2} \\cdot \\dfrac{\\sigma}{\\sqrt{n}}, \\: \\overline{x} + z_{\\alpha/2} \\cdot \\dfrac{\\sigma}{\\sqrt{n}}\\right)\n$$\n\nwhere $\\overline{x}$ is the sample mean,\n\n$$\nP(Z > z_{\\alpha/2}) = \\dfrac{\\alpha}{2}\n$$\n\nand $Z \\sim N(0,1)$.\n\nOne thing to realize is that this situation is unrealistic: it's doubtful that we'll not know the population mean yet know the population variance.\n\nA more realistic situation is that $\\sigma^2$ is *unknown*, and we must estimate it using the sample data. To estimate the population variance $\\sigma^2$, we use the sample variance $S^2$, given by\n\n$$\nS^2 = \\dfrac{1}{n-1} \\sum_{i=1}^n \\left(X_i - \\overline{X} \\right)^2\n$$\n\nIt can be shown that\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{\\overline{X} - \\mu}{S/\\sqrt n} \\sim T_{n-1}\n$$\n\nwhere $T_{n-1}$ is a student's $t$-distribution with $n-1$ degrees of freedom.\n\nLet's take a look at a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "98d4374a-d448-5d6a-852b-d1d260b9c6bd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6241 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "68294170-b618-5346-a481-90c4873ac94a" :step/math-academy-id 37870 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189158}} {:db/id 17592186189093 :step/content {:db/id 17592186189370 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a normal population with the unknown population mean $\\mu$ and sample variance $s^2$. Then, for a given value $\\alpha$ between $0$ and $1$, a $[100(1-\\alpha)]\\%$ confidence interval for the population mean $\\mu$ is given by\n\n$$\n\\left(\\overline{x} - t_{n-1,\\alpha/2} \\cdot \\dfrac{s}{\\sqrt{n}}, \\: \\overline{x} +t_{n-1,\\alpha/2} \\cdot \\dfrac{s}{\\sqrt{n}}\\right)\n$$\n\nwhere\n\n$$\nP(T > t_{n-1, \\alpha/2}) = \\dfrac{\\alpha}{2}\n$$\n\nand $T \\sim T_{n-1}$.\n\nThe endpoints of our confidence interval are called **confidence limits** and are given by\n\n$$\n\\overline{x} \\pm t_{n-1, \\alpha/2} \\cdot \\dfrac{s}{\\sqrt{n}}\n$$\n\nEach part of the formula above has a name:\n\n- $\\overline{x}$ is an estimate of the population mean\n- $\\dfrac{s}{\\sqrt{n}}$ is the standard error of the mean\n- $t_{n-1,\\alpha/2}$ is the corresponding $t$-score\n- $E = t_{n-1, \\alpha/2} \\cdot \\dfrac{s}{\\sqrt{n}}$ is the margin of error\n\n$$\nt\n$$\n\nSo, our confidence interval can be written as follows:\n\n$$\n(x^(―) - [margin of error],\\begin{vmatrix}x^(―) + [margin of error]) \\\\ (x^(―) - [[math]t[/math]-score] \\cdot [standard error], \\mid x^(―) + [[math]t[/math]-score] \\cdot [standard error]) \\\\ (x^(―) - t_{n - 1, α/2} \\cdot \\frac{s}{\\sqrt{n}},\\end{vmatrix}x^(―) + t_{n - 1, α/2} \\cdot \\frac{s}{\\sqrt{n}})\n$$\n\nNotice that the expression for the confidence interval is very similar to when the population variance was known. The only difference is that we now use the $t$-scores instead of $z$-scores and the sample standard deviation $s$ instead of the population standard deviation $\\sigma$.\n\nFinally, since computing a confidence interval amounts to finding the corresponding confidence limits, we will use the two terms interchangeably." :tutorial/id #uuid "b3eaa60c-8a64-508a-a094-245270047e8a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6242 :tutorial/title "Summarizing Confidence Intervals for Normal Populations With Unknown Population Variance"} :step/id #uuid "991795bc-9250-5f2f-96cb-2fb57f170b38" :step/math-academy-id 37871 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189091}} {:db/id 17592186189094 :step/content {:db/id 17592186188284 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186187988 :question/id #uuid "c2e2bcbc-ab4b-5a0a-a803-cb98326017ec" :question/math-academy-id "e-10040"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "778f1426-e8a0-597f-84f6-337359a553c8" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186188554} {:db/id 17592186188557}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding Confidence Intervals: Applications"} :step/id #uuid "f1d32a2f-ba24-5d90-9872-8adddcce8f50" :step/math-academy-id 37893} {:db/id 17592186189096 :step/content {:db/id 17592186188285 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186187989 :question/id #uuid "7446f45b-6d41-5a11-8006-853b38fa5142" :question/math-academy-id "e-10047"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "81c8b2bc-d215-5bae-b81f-05870dd39163" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049014}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186188553} {:db/id 17592186188558}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding Confidence Intervals From Large Samples"} :step/id #uuid "c148a2a5-30ac-549d-a5fc-b8016b9a5d06" :step/math-academy-id 37914 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189094}} {:db/id 17592186189157 :step/content {:db/id 17592186189394 :tutorial/content "Up to now, we've assumed that the underlying population is normally distributed. However, if we have a *sufficiently large* sample, then according to the central limit theorem, we have the approximation\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{\\overline{X} - \\mu}{\\sigma/\\sqrt n} \\approx N(0,1)\n$$\n\nMoreover, since $n$ is sufficiently large, $\\sigma^2$ can be approximated as $S^2$. Therefore, we have that\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{\\overline{X} - \\mu}{S/\\sqrt n} \\approx T_{n-1}\n$$\n\n**Watch out!** If the population is *not* normally distributed, then the sample size $n$ must be sufficiently large for this approximation to apply. Typically,\n\n$$\nn\\geq 30\n$$\n\nis sufficient.\n\nIn such situations, we can use our formula for the confidence limits of the population mean $\\mu$:\n\n$$\n\\overline{x} \\pm t_{n-1,\\alpha/2} \\cdot \\dfrac{s}{\\sqrt{n}}\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "cad33eaf-4573-5886-837e-5a914b347274" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6409 :tutorial/title "Large Samples"} :step/id #uuid "1c95af0f-9fb6-5e0c-89fc-852ce2b16b56" :step/math-academy-id 38729 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189096}} {:db/id 17592186189158 :step/content {:db/id 17592186189395 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a random sample of size $n=9$ drawn from a normal population. The sample mean is\n\n$$\n\\overline{x}=30\n$$\n\nand the sample standard deviation is $s=3.3$.\nWe wish to compute a $95\\%$ confidence interval for the population mean $\\mu$.\n\nRecall that a confidence interval is an interval of the form\n\n$$\n(\\overline{x}-E, \\: \\overline{x}+E)\n$$\n\nwhere\n\n- $\\overline{x}$ is an estimate of the population mean, and\n- $E$ is the margin of error.\n\nIn our example, the population is normally distributed. Therefore, the sample mean $\\overline{X}$ is also normally distributed, where\n\n$$\n\\overline{X}\\sim N\\left(\\mu,\\dfrac{\\sigma^2}{n}\\right)\n$$\n\nBy transforming $\\overline{X}$ in the manner described earlier, we have that the random variable $T$, defined as\n\n$$\nT = \\dfrac{\\overline{X} - \\mu}{S/\\sqrt n}\n$$\n\nfollows a student's $t$-distribution $T_{n-1}$ with $n-1$ degrees of freedom.\n\nWe wish to find a $t$-interval that we're $95\\%$ confident that the random variable $T$ lies within. This interval is indicated in the diagram below:\n\n![](images/63/63973d7f59a993d42b7b8145f3354e9e7d7dba3c0393c756b6a95754eb4ead2e.png)\n\nSince we wish to find a $95\\%$ confidence interval, we define our parameter $\\alpha$ as\n\n$$\n\\alpha=1-0.95=0.05\\quad\\Longrightarrow\\quad \\dfrac{\\alpha}{2}=0.025\n$$\n\nNotice that\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{\\alpha}{2}\n$$\n\nis precisely the area bounded by each \"tail\" that we're excluding from our confidence interval. Let's label the critical values at the endpoints of our interval as $\\pm t_{n-1, \\alpha/2}$:\n\n![](images/b5/b557afdbd649aa159addd9fe01021a7c3561f94b0168fd874876980d8bb7c3f4.png)\n\nAccording to our diagram,\n\n$$\nP(T > t_{8,0.025}) = P(T < -t_{8,0.025}) = 0.025\n$$\n\nUsing a table of values for the $t$-distribution, we find that\n\n$$\nt_{8,0.025} \\approx 2.306\n$$\n\nTherefore,\n\n$$\nP(T > 2.306) = P(T < -2.306) = 0.025\n$$\n\nIn other words,\n\n$$\nP(-2.306 < T < 2.306) = 0.95\n$$\n\nTherefore, there is a $95\\%$ probability that our random variable $T$ will lie in the interval $(-2.306, 2.306)$.\n\nSimilar to the case where $\\sigma^2$ was known, we find the appropriate confidence interval by solving the inequality inside the parentheses of the last probability statement for the population mean $\\mu$:\n\n$$\n\\begin{bmatrix}-2.306 & < T < 2.306 \\\\ -2.306 & < (x^(―) - μ)/(s/\\sqrt{n}) < 2.306 \\\\ -2.306 \\cdot \\frac{s}{\\sqrt{n}} & < x^(―) - μ < 2.306 \\cdot \\frac{s}{\\sqrt{n}} \\\\ -x^(―) - 2.306 \\cdot \\frac{s}{\\sqrt{n}} & < - μ < - x^(―) + 2.306 \\cdot \\frac{s}{\\sqrt{n}} \\\\ x^(―) + 2.306 \\cdot \\frac{s}{\\sqrt{n}} & > μ > x^(―) - 2.306 \\cdot \\frac{s}{\\sqrt{n}} \\\\ x^(―) - 2.306 \\cdot \\frac{s}{\\sqrt{n}} & < μ < x^(―) + 2.306 \\cdot \\frac{s}{\\sqrt{n}}\\end{bmatrix}\n$$\n\nTherefore, a $95\\%$ confidence interval for the population mean $\\mu$ is given by\n\n$$\n\\left(\\overline{x}-2.306 \\cdot\\dfrac{s}{\\sqrt{n}}, \\: \\overline{x}+2.306 \\cdot\\dfrac{s}{\\sqrt{n}} \\right)\n$$\n\nFinally, substituting our values\n\n$$\nn=9, \\qquad \\overline{x}=30, \\qquad s=3.3\n$$\n\nwe obtain that our $95\\%$ confidence interval for $\\mu$ is\n\n$$\n\\big(30- 2.537, \\: 30 + 2.537 \\big)\n$$\n\nDescribing this confidence interval using confidence limits, we have\n\n$$\n30 \\pm 2.537\n$$\n\nLet's now describe the general procedure." :tutorial/id #uuid "3941a0da-320f-5a13-b99f-f3556ba560ba" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6410 :tutorial/title "Constructing Confidence Intervals"} :step/id #uuid "a7e1e894-dda6-51e5-9fc8-542ca1fec109" :step/math-academy-id 38730 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189093}}] :activity/title "Confidence Intervals for One Mean: Unknown Population Variance" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186188450} {:db/id 17592186189092 :step/content {:db/id 17592186189369 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ drawn from a normal population with unknown population mean $\\mu$ and *known* population variance $\\sigma^2$. Let's label the critical values at the endpoints of our interval as $\\pm t_{n-1, \\alpha/2}$:\n\n![](images/b5/b557afdbd649aa159addd9fe01021a7c3561f94b0168fd874876980d8bb7c3f4.png)\n\nAccording to our diagram,\n\n$$\nP(T > t_{8,0.025}) = P(T < -t_{8,0.025}) = 0.025\n$$\n\nUsing a table of values for the $t$-distribution, we find that\n\n$$\nt_{8,0.025} \\approx 2.306\n$$\n\nTherefore,\n\n$$\nP(T > 2.306) = P(T < -2.306) = 0.025\n$$\n\nIn other words,\n\n$$\nP(-2.306 < T < 2.306) = 0.95\n$$\n\nTherefore, there is a $95\\%$ probability that our random variable $T$ will lie in the interval $(-2.306, 2.306)$.\n\nSimilar to the case where $\\sigma^2$ was known, we find the appropriate confidence interval by solving the inequality inside the parentheses of the last probability statement for the population mean $\\mu$:\n\n$$\n\\begin{bmatrix}-2.306 & < T < 2.306 \\\\ -2.306 & < (x^(―) - 17592186101886 :step/content {:db/id 17592186102020 :tutorial/content "The **slope-intercept** form of the equation of a line is\n\n$$\ny = {\\color{red}{m}}x+{\\color{blue}{b}},\n$$\n\nwhere ${\\color{red}{m}}$ is the **slope** of the line and ${\\color{blue}{b}}$ is the **$y$-intercept.**\n\nTo illustrate, consider the line $y={\\color{red}{2}}x+{\\color{blue}{1}},$ shown below.\n\n![](images/a4/a4c1f53335d7637a0b08f51e93e760d533986e53a4c8896712262688b156bc70.png)\n\nLooking at the line, we notice that:\n\n- The *slope* of the line is $m={\\color{red}{2}},$ because a change of $1$ in the $x$-direction results in a change of $2$ in the $y$-direction.\n\n- The $y$*-intercept* of the line, denoted $b$, is $b={\\color{blue}{1}},$ because the line hits the $y$-axis at the point $(0,{\\color{blue}{1}}).$\n\n**Note**: The coordinates of the $y$-intercept are always $(0,{\\color{blue}{b}}).$\n\nFinally, if the slope $m = 0$ (i.e., we have a horizontal line), the slope-intercept form must be $y=0x+{\\color{blue}b},$ which reduces to $y={\\color{blue}b}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "7ef443ae-c1bd-551c-9f3b-11a386a427b0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8049 :tutorial/title get\n\n$$\nQ(x)={x}^{T}\\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\\,(Py)={y}^{T}\\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).\n$$\n\n \n\nAs a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is :step/math-academy-id 45757 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199404}} {:db/id 17592186199396 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199516 :tutorial/content "Suppose we're given that the maximum value of the quadratic form \n\n$$\nQ(\\mathbf{x})=x_1^2-2x_1x_2+x_2^2,\n$$\n\n over the ellipse $4x_1^2+x_2^2=4$ equals $5.$ How can we find a vector $\\mathbf{x}$ at which this maximum is attained?\n\nWe can find this vector by applying a suitable change of variable. This change of variable should transform our problem into one where we need to maximize a related quadratic form $Q'$ on the unit circle. Let's see how this is done.\n\nFirst, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:\n\n![](images/7b/7b1fd813963e16887c57d6c10be1bfe288e3209fd3a02ca6e6236b7261feb7b1.svg)\n\nNotice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:\n\n$$\n{x_1^2}+ \\dfrac{x_2^2}{2^2}=1\n$$\n\nwhich  represents an ellipse with semiaxes $a=1$ (along the $x_1$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the $x_2$-axis). \n\nIf we introduce new variables\n\n$$\ny_1={x_1}, \\qquad y_2 = \\dfrac{x_2}{2},\n$$\n\nthe equation of the ellipse will transform into $y_1^2+y_2^2 = 1,$ or $\\|\\mathbf{y}\\|=1.$\n\nSo, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix \n\n![](images/80/80f8e821a60b63dde0f314460adfd31faca5d82315243fb2a3ebdec75bc61538.svg) \n\nwe obtain that $\\mathbf{x} = P \\mathbf{y}.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get\n\n$$\nQ(\\mathbf{x}) = \\mathbf{x}^T \\! A \\mathbf{x} = (P\\mathbf{y})^T A \\, (P\\mathbf{y}) = \\mathbf{y}^T \\! (P^TAP) \\mathbf{y}=Q'(\\mathbf{y}).\n$$\n\nAs a result, since $P^T=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in the new coordinates is \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\\,AP \\\\  & =PAP \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 2\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\\\ -1 & 1\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 2\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\\\ -2 & 2\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 2\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\\\ -2 & 4\\end{aligned}].\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n \n\nNow, the goal is to maximize $Q'(\\mathbf{y})$ when $\\| \\mathbf{y} \\|=1,$ which we do using our usual methods.  \n\nSince we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $5,$ we have\n\n$$\n\\max \\{ Q'(\\mathbf{y}) \\: | \\: \\| \\mathbf{y} \\|=1 \\} = \\lambda_{\\max} = 5.\n$$\n\nNext, we find the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\\lambda_{\\textrm{max}}=5{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}B-5I & =[\\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\\\ -2 & 4\\end{aligned}]-5[\\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 1\\end{aligned}]=[\\begin{aligned}-4 & -2 \\\\ -2 & -1\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSeeking a non-zero solution of $(B-5I)\\mathbf{y}=\\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](images/4b/4b51afece6e21c2fe073a5346557f42f9f03ae3400407d18ed6af3af8f32e310.svg) Dividing $\\mathbf{v}$ by its norm $\\| \\mathbf{v} \\| = \\sqrt{5},$ we get \n\n![](images/ce/ce571338fc1d83f0b0892a356bca56073c096a1f5191a21a4baef56b6d5a399f.svg) \n\nFinally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{x}_{\\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\\text{max}} \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 2\\end{aligned}]\\cdot \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{5}}[\\begin{aligned}-1 \\\\ 2\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{5}}[\\begin{aligned}-1 \\\\ 4\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid this lesson:\n\n*The maximum value of a quadratic form $Q(\\mathbf{x})=\\mathbf{x}^T A \\mathbf{x},$ when $\\| \\mathbf{x} \\|=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A{:}$* \n\n$$\n\\max \\{ Q(\\mathbf{x}) \\: | \\:  \\| \\mathbf{x} \\| = 1 \\} = \\lambda_{\\textrm{max}}\n$$\n\n*The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector $\\mathbf{u}_{\\textrm{max}}.$*\n\n**Note:** We'll show only the first part (about the maximum value) since a similar argument can be used to prove the second part (about the minimum value).\n\nLet $A$ be a real $n \\times n$ symmetric matrix corresponding to a quadratic form $Q(\\mathbf x)\\mathbin.$ As a result, there must be an *orthonormal* matrix $P$ such that \n\n- $D=P^{-1}AP=P^TAP,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.\n\n- The diagonal entries of $D$ are the eigenvalues of $A$. Without loss of generality, we can assume that the eigenvalues are $\\lambda_1 \\geq \\lambda_2 \\geq \\ldots \\geq \\lambda_n,$ where $\\lambda_{\\textrm{max}} = \\lambda_1.$\n\n- The columns $\\mathbf{u}_1,\\mathbf{u}_2, \\ldots, \\mathbf{u}_n$ of $P$ form an orthonormal set of unit eigenvectors of $A.$ So, $\\mathbf{u}_{\\textrm{max}} = \\mathbf{u}_1.$\n\nTake $\\mathbf x=P\\mathbf y.$ Since, $P$ is orthonormal, we have\n\n$$\n\\|\\mathbf x\\| = \\|P \\mathbf y \\| = \\|\\mathbf y\\|\n$$\n\nand\n\n$$\nQ(\\mathbf x) = \\mathbf x^T\\!A\\mathbf x = (P\\mathbf y)^T\\!A(P\\mathbf y) = \\mathbf{y}^T (P^T\\!AP) \\mathbf{y} = \\mathbf{y}^T D \\mathbf{y}\n$$\n\nfor all $\\mathbf{y} \\in \\mathbb{R}^n.$\n\nTherefore, we can conclude the following:\n\n- $\\|\\mathbf x\\| =1 \\Longleftrightarrow \\|\\mathbf y\\| =1$ for all $\\mathbf y$ such that $\\mathbf x=P\\mathbf y$\n\n- Restricted to the unit sphere of $\\Bbb R^n,$ the images of the quadratic forms $Q(\\mathbf x)$  and $Q'(\\mathbf y)= \\mathbf y^T D\\mathbf y$ coincide: \n\n$$\n\\{\\mathbf x^TA\\mathbf x: \\: \\: \\|\\mathbf x\\|=1\\}= \\{\\mathbf y^TD\\mathbf y: \\: \\: \\|\\mathbf y\\|=1\\}  \\subset \\mathbb R\n$$\n\nNow, for any unit vector $\\mathbf{y} \\in \\mathbb{R}^n,$ we obtain\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={Q}^{′}(y) \\\\  & ={\\lambda }_{1}{y}_{1}^{2}+{\\lambda }_{2}{y}_{2}^{2}+⋯+{\\lambda }_{n}{y}_{n}^{2} \\\\  & \\le {\\lambda }_{\\text{max}}\\,{y}_{1}^{2}+{\\lambda }_{\\text{max}}\\,{y}_{2}^{2}+⋯+{\\lambda }_{\\text{max}}\\,{y}_{n}^{2} \\\\  & ={\\lambda }_{\\text{max}}({y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}+⋯+{y}_{n}^{2}) \\\\  & ={\\lambda }_{\\text{max}}\\,‖y{‖}^{2} \\\\  & ={\\lambda }_{\\text{max}}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, we have that  that \n\n$$\nM = \\max \\{ Q(\\mathbf{x}) \\: | \\:  \\| \\mathbf{x} \\| = 1 \\} = \\max \\{ Q'(\\mathbf{y}) \\: | \\:  \\| \\mathbf{y} \\| = 1 \\} \\le \\lambda_{\\textrm{max}}.\n$$\n\n \n\nOn the other hand, if we take ![](images/53/53a051ea36059c9222e717c65adc6531bc313c9807d44a39b262433acfdcbc5c.svg) then $Q(P\\mathbf{e}_1) = Q'(\\mathbf{e}_1) = \\lambda_{\\textrm{max}}.$ So, we conclude that $M = \\lambda_{\\textrm{max}}.$\n\nFinally, since $\\mathbf{u}_1 = P\\mathbf{e}_1$ we have that \n$Q(\\mathbf u_1) =  \\mathbf e_1^T D \\mathbf e_1 = \\lambda_{\\textrm{max}}.$ \nTherefore, the maximum value is attained at $\\mathbf u_{\\textrm{max}}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "364005f5-f0fc-5d17-9d6b-288d52abe715" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8176 :tutorial/title "Proof of the Main Theorem"} :step/id #uuid 17592186199547 :tutorial/content "To complete the picture, let's prove the main theorem of this lesson:\n\n*The maximum value of a quadratic form $Q(\\mathbf{x})=\\mathbf{x}^T A \\mathbf{x},$ when $\\| \\mathbf{x} \\|=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A{:}$* \n\n$$\n\\max \\{ Q(\\mathbf{x}) \\: | \\:  \\| \\mathbf{x} \\| = 1 \\} = \\lambda_{\\textrm{max}}\n$$\n\n*The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector $\\mathbf{u}_{\\textrm{max}}.$*\n\n**Note:** We'll show only the first part (about the maximum value) since a similar argument can be used to prove the second part (about the minimum value).\n\nLet $A$ be a real $n \\times n$ symmetric matrix corresponding to a quadratic form $Q(\\mathbf x)\\mathbin.$ As a result, there must be an *orthonormal* matrix $P$ such that \n\n- $D=P^{-1}AP=P^TAP,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.\n\n- The diagonal entries of $D$ are the eigenvalues of $A$. Without loss of generality, we can assume that the eigenvalues are $\\lambda_1 \\geq \\lambda_2 \\geq \\ldots \\geq \\lambda_n,$ where $\\lambda_{\\textrm{max}} = \\lambda_1.$\n\n- The columns $\\mathbf{u}_1,\\mathbf{u}_2, \\ldots, \\mathbf{u}_n$ of $P$ form an orthonormal set of unit eigenvectors of $A.$ So, $\\mathbf{u}_{\\textrm{max}} = \\mathbf{u}_1.$\n\nTake $\\mathbf x=P\\mathbf y.$ Since, $P$ is orthonormal, we have\n\n$$\n\\|\\mathbf x\\| = \\|P \\mathbf y \\| = \\|\\mathbf y\\|\n$$\n\nand\n\n$$\nQ(\\mathbf x) = \\mathbf x^T\\!A\\mathbf x = (P\\mathbf y)^T\\!A(P\\mathbf y) = \\mathbf{y}^T (P^T\\!AP) \\mathbf{y} = \\mathbf{y}^T D \\mathbf{y}\n$$\n\nfor all $\\mathbf{y} \\in \\mathbb{R}^n.$\n\nTherefore, we can conclude the following:\n\n- $\\|\\mathbf x\\| =1 \\Longleftrightarrow \\|\\mathbf y\\| =1$ for all $\\mathbf y$ such that $\\mathbf x=P\\mathbf y$\n\n- Restricted to the unit sphere of $\\Bbb R^n,$ the images of the quadratic forms $Q(\\mathbf x)$  and $Q'(\\mathbf y)= \\mathbf y^T D\\mathbf y$ coincide: \n\n$$\n\\{\\mathbf x^TA\\mathbf x: \\: \\: \\|\\mathbf x\\|=1\\}= \\{\\mathbf y^TD\\mathbf y: \\: \\: \\|\\mathbf y\\|=1\\}  \\subset \\mathbb R\n$$\n\nNow, for any unit vector $\\mathbf{y} \\in \\mathbb{R}^n,$ we obtain\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={Q}^{′}(y) \\\\  & ={\\lambda }_{1}{y}_{1}^{2}+{\\lambda }_{2}{y}_{2}^{2}+⋯+{\\lambda }_{n}{y}_{n}^{2} \\\\  & \\le {\\lambda }_{\\text{max}}\\,{y}_{1}^{2}+{\\lambda }_{\\text{max}}\\,{y}_{2}^{2}+⋯+{\\lambda }_{\\text{max}}\\,{y}_{n}^{2} \\\\  & ={\\lambda }_{\\text{max}}({y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}+⋯+{y}_{n}^{2}) \\\\  & ={\\lambda }_{\\text{max}}\\,‖y{‖}^{2} \\\\  & ={\\lambda }_{\\text{max}}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, we have that  that \n\n$$\nM = \\max \\{ Q(\\mathbf{x}) \\: | \\:  \\| \\mathbf{x} \\| = 1 \\} = \\max \\{ Q'(\\mathbf{y}) \\: | \\:  \\| \\mathbf{y} \\| = 1 \\} \\le \\lambda_{\\textrm{max}}.\n$$\n\n \n\nOn the other hand, if we take ![](images/53/53a051ea36059c9222e717c65adc6531bc313c9807d44a39b262433acfdcbc5c.svg) then $Q(P\\mathbf{e}_1) = Q'(\\mathbf{e}_1) = \\lambda_{\\textrm{max}}.$ So, we conclude that $M = \\lambda_{\\textrm{max}}.$\n\nFinally, since $\\mathbf{u}_1 = P\\mathbf{e}_1$ we have that \n$Q(\\mathbf u_1) =  \\mathbf e_1^T D \\mathbf e_1 = \\lambda_{\\textrm{max}}.$ \nTherefore, the maximum value is attained at $\\mathbf u_{\\textrm{max}}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "364005f5-f0fc-5d17-9d6b-288d52abe715" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8176 :tutorial/title "Proof of the Main Theorem"} :step/id #uuid "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:\n\n$$\nA=[\\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\\\ 2 & 1\\end{aligned}]\n$$\n\nNotice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:\n\n$$\n\\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1\n$$\n\nThis is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=3$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables\n\n$\\,$ ${y}_{1}=\\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\\,$ and $\\,{y}_{2}=\\frac{{x}_{2}}{3},$\n\nthe equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$\n\nSo, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix \n\n$$\nP=[\\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 3\\end{aligned}],\n$$\n\n \n\nwe obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get\n\n$$\nQ(x)={x}^{T}\\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\\,(Py)={y}^{T}\\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).\n$$\n\nAs a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\\,AP \\\\  & =PAP \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 3\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\\\ 2 & 1\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 3\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}8 & 4 \\\\ 6 & 3\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 3\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}16 & 12 \\\\ 12 & 9\\end{aligned}].\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n \n\nNow, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.\n\nSince we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $25,$ we have\n\n$$\nmax\\{{Q}^{′}(y)\\,|\\,‖y‖=1\\}={\\lambda }_{max}=25.\n$$\n\nNext, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\\lambda }_{\\text{max}}=25:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}B-25I & =[\\begin{aligned}16 & 12 \\\\ 12 & 9\\end{aligned}]-25[\\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 1\\end{aligned}]=[\\begin{aligned}-9 & 12 \\\\ 12 & -16\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSeeking a non-zero solution of $(B-25I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\\begin{aligned}4 \\\\ 3\\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=5,$ we get \n\n$$\n{u}_{\\text{max}}=\\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\\frac{1}{5}[\\begin{aligned}4 \\\\ 3\\end{aligned}].\n$$\n\n \n\nFinally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{x}_{\\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\\text{max}} \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 3\\end{aligned}]\\cdot \\frac{1}{5}[\\begin{aligned}4 \\\\ 3\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{5}[\\begin{aligned}8 \\\\ 9\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$"} :step/id #uuid "3781c4aa-7e7b-5b51-9af4-d354711b0091"} {:db/id 17592186410201 :step/content {:db/id :question/problem "The maximum value of $Q(x)=4{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $9{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=36,$ is $25.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:\n\n$$\nA=[\\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\\\ 2 & 1\\end{aligned}]\n$$\n\nNotice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:\n\n$$\n\\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1\n$$\n\nThis is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=3$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables\n\n$\\,$ ${y}_{1}=\\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\\,$ and $\\,{y}_{2}=\\frac{{x}_{2}}{3},$\n\nthe equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$\n\nSo, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix \n\n$$\nP=[\\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 3\\end{aligned}],\n$$\n\n \n\nwe obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get\n\n$$\nQ(x)={x}^{T}\\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\\,(Py)={y}^{T}\\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).\n$$\n\nAs a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\\,AP \\\\  & =PAP \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 3\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\\\ 2 & 1\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 3\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}8 & 4 \\\\ 6 & 3\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 3\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}16 & 12 \\\\ 12 & 9\\end{aligned}].\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n \n\nNow, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.\n\nSince we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $25,$ we have\n\n$$\nmax\\{{Q}^{′}(y)\\,|\\,‖y‖=1\\}={\\lambda }_{max}=25.\n$$\n\nNext, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\\lambda }_{\\text{max}}=25:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}B-25I & =[\\begin{aligned}16 & 12 \\\\ 12 & 9\\end{aligned}]-25[\\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 1\\end{aligned}]=[\\begin{aligned}-9 & 12 \\\\ 12 & -16\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSeeking a non-zero solution of $(B-25I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\\begin{aligned}4 \\\\ 3\\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=5,$ we get \n\n$$\n{u}_{\\text{max}}=\\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\\frac{1}{5}[\\begin{aligned}4 \\\\ 3\\end{aligned}].\n$$\n\n \n\nFinally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{x}_{\\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\\text{max}} \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 3\\end{aligned}]\\cdot \\frac{1}{5}[\\begin{aligned}4 \\\\ 3\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{5}[\\begin{aligned}8 \\\\ 9\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$"} :step/id #uuid "3781c4aa-7e7b-5b51-9af4-d354711b0091"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\\,AP \\\\  & =PAP \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 3\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\\\ 2 & 1\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\\\ 0 & -16\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSeeking a non-zero solution of $(B-25I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\\begin{aligned}4 \\\\ 3\\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=5,$ we get $‖y‖=1.$\n\nSo, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix \n\n$$\nP=[\\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 2\\end{aligned}],\n$$\n\n \n\nwe obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get\n\n$$\nQ(x)={x}^{T}\\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\\,(Py)={y}^{T}\\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).\n$$\n\nAs a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\\,AP \\\\  & =PAP \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 2\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}8 & -15 \\\\ -15 & -50\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\\\ 0 & -200\\end{aligned}].\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n \n\nNow, we minimize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.\n\nSince we are told that the minimum value of the quadratic form is $-250,$ we have\n\n$$\nmin\\{{Q}^{′}(y)\\,|\\,‖y‖=1\\}={\\lambda }_{min}=-250.\n$$\n\nNext, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\\lambda }_{\\text{min}}=-250:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}B-(-250I) & =[\\begin{aligned}200 & -150 \\\\ -150 & -200\\end{aligned}]+250[\\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 1\\end{aligned}]=[\\begin{aligned}450 & -150 \\\\ -150 & 50\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSeeking a non-zero solution of $(B-(-250I))y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\\begin{aligned}1 \\\\ 3\\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\\sqrt{10},$ we get \n\n$$\n{u}_{\\text{min}}=\\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{10}}[\\begin{aligned}1 \\\\ 3\\end{aligned}].\n$$\n\n \n\nFinally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{x}_{\\text{min}} & =P{u}_{\\text{min}} \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 2\\end{aligned}]\\cdot :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:\n\n$$\nA=[\\begin{aligned}8 & -15 \\\\ -15 & -50\\end{aligned}]\n$$\n\nNotice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:\n\n$$\n\\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{5}^{2}}+\\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1\n$$\n\nThis is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=5$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables\n\n$\\,$ ${y}_{1}=\\frac{{x}_{1}}{5}\\,$ and $\\,{y}_{2}=\\frac{{x}_{2}}{2},$\n\nthe equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$\n\nSo, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix \n\n$$\nP=[\\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 2\\end{aligned}],\n$$\n\n \n\nwe obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get\n\n$$\nQ(x)={x}^{T}\\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\\,(Py)={y}^{T}\\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).\n$$\n\nAs a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\\,AP \\\\  & =PAP \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 2\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}8 & -15 \\\\ -15 & -50\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 2\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}40 & -75 \\\\ -30 & -100\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 2\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}200 & -150 \\\\ -150 & -200\\end{aligned}].\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n \n\nNow, we minimize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.\n\nSince we are told that the minimum value of the quadratic form is $-250,$ we have\n\n$$\nmin\\{{Q}^{′}(y)\\,|\\,‖y‖=1\\}={\\lambda }_{min}=-250.\n$$\n\nNext, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\\lambda }_{\\text{min}}=-250:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}B-(-250I) & =[\\begin{aligned}200 & -150 \\\\ -150 & -200\\end{aligned}]+250[\\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 1\\end{aligned}]=[\\begin{aligned}450 & -150 \\\\ -150 & 50\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSeeking a non-zero solution of $(B-(-250I))y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\\begin{aligned}1 \\\\ 3\\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\\sqrt{10},$ we get \n\n$$\n{u}_{\\text{min}}=\\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{10}}[\\begin{aligned}1 \\\\ 3\\end{aligned}].\n$$\n\n \n\nFinally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{x}_{\\text{min}} & =P{u}_{\\text{min}} \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 2\\end{aligned}]\\cdot \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{10}}[\\begin{aligned}1 \\\\ 3\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{10}}[\\begin{aligned}5 \\\\ 6\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$"} :step/id #uuid "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:\n\n$$\nA=[\\begin{aligned}1 & 8 \\\\ 8 & 4\\end{aligned}]\n$$\n\nNotice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:\n\n$$\n\\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1\n$$\n\nThis is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables\n\n$\\,$ ${y}_{1}=\\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\\,$ and $\\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$\n\nthe equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$\n\nSo, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix \n\n$$\nP=[\\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 1\\end{aligned}],\n$$\n\n \n\nwe obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get\n\n$$\nQ(x)={x}^{T}\\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\\,(Py)={y}^{T}\\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).\n$$\n\n \n\nAs a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\\,AP \\\\  & =PAP \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 1\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}1 & 8 \\\\ 8 & 4\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 1\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}2 & 16 \\\\ 8 & 4\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 1\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}4 & 16 \\\\ 16 & 4\\end{aligned}].\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n \n\nNow, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.\n\nSince we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $20,$ we have\n\n$$\nmax\\{{Q}^{′}(y)\\,|\\,‖y‖=1\\}={\\lambda }_{max}=20.\n$$\n\nNext, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\\lambda }_{\\text{max}}=20:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}B-20I & =[\\begin{aligned}4 & 16 \\\\ 16 & 4\\end{aligned}]-20[\\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 1\\end{aligned}]=[\\begin{aligned}-16 & 16 \\\\ 16 & -16\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSeeking a non-zero solution of $(B-20I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\\begin{aligned}1 \\\\ 1\\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\\sqrt{2},$ we get  \n\n$$\n{u}_{\\text{max}}=\\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}[\\begin{aligned}1 \\\\ 1\\end{aligned}].\n$$\n\n \n\nFinally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{x}_{\\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\\text{max}} \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 1\\end{aligned}]\\cdot \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}[\\begin{aligned}1 \\\\ the amount of reactant in the reactor at time $t.$ Then, the derivative \n\n$$\n\\dfrac{\\mathrm{d}Q}{\\mathrm{d}t}\n$$\n\ndescribes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which reactant enters the reactor minus the rate at which reactant leaves the reactor.\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{\\mathrm{d}Q}{\\mathrm{d}t} = Q'_{\\textrm{in}} - Q'_{\\textrm{out}}\n$$\n\nNote that the units of $\\dfrac{\\mathrm{d}Q}{\\mathrm{d}t}, Q'_{\\textrm{in}}$ and $Q'_{\\textrm{out}}$ are $\\textrm{lb}/\\textrm{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.\n\n**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which reactant enters the reactor.\n\nNote that pure solvent (i.e., a solution containing $0\\,\\textrm{lb/gal}$ of reactant) enters the reactor at a rate of $14\\,\\textrm{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *reactant* enters the reactor is \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\\text{in}}^{′} & =(0\\,\\frac{\\text{lb}}{\\text{gal}})\\cdot (14\\,\\frac{\\text{gal}}{\\text{min}}) \\\\  & =(0\\,\\frac{\\text{lb}}{\\cancel{\\text{gal}}})\\cdot (14\\,\\frac{\\cancel{\\text{gal}}}{\\text{min}}) \\\\  & =0\\,\\frac{\\text{lb}}{\\text{min}}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which reactant exits the reactor.\n\nTo find the rate at which reactant leaves the reactor, we first determine the volume of solution in the reactor at time $t.$\n\nThe reactor initially contains $300\\,\\textrm{gal}$ of chemical solution; solvent enters at $14\\,\\textrm{gal/min}$ and drains out at $14\\,\\textrm{gal/min}.$\nAs a result, the amount of chemical solution in the reactor after $t$ minutes is \n\n$$\n300 + 14t - 14t = 300\\,\\textrm{gal}.\n$$\n\nSince $Q$ is the amount of reactant in the reactor, the *concentration* of the solution at time $t$ is\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{Q}{300}\\,\\dfrac{\\textrm{lb}}{\\textrm{gal}}.\n$$\n\nTherefore, as the completely mixed chemical solution leaves at a rate of $14\\,\\textrm{gal/min},$ *reactant* leaves at a rate of\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\\text{out}}^{′} & =(14\\,\\frac{\\text{gal}}{\\text{min}})\\cdot (\\frac{Q}{300}\\,\\frac{\\text{lb}}{\\text{gal}}) \\\\  & =(14\\,\\frac{\\cancel{\\text{gal}}}{\\text{min}})\\cdot (\\frac{Q}{300}\\,\\frac{\\text{lb}}{\\cancel{\\text{gal}}}) \\\\  & =\\frac{14Q}{300}\\,\\frac{\\text{lb}}{\\text{min}} \\\\  & =\\frac{7Q}{150}\\,\\frac{\\text{lb}}{\\text{min}}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.\n\nThe rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\\text{out}}^{′} \\\\  & =0-\\frac{7Q}{150}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwhich gives the equation\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{\\mathrm{d}Q}{\\mathrm{d}t} = -\\dfrac{7}{150}\\,Q.\n$$\n\n**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.\n\nSeparating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{1}{Q}\\cdot \\frac{dQ}{dt} & =-\\frac{7}{150} \\\\ \\int \\frac{1}{Q}\\cdot \\frac{dQ}{dt}dt & =\\int (-\\frac{7}{150})\\,dt \\\\ \\int \\frac{1}{Q}\\cdot \\,dQ & =-\\frac{7}{150}\\int 1\\,dt \\\\ \\operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =-\\frac{7t}{150}+C \\\\ |Q| & ={e}^{-\\frac{7t}{150}+C} \\\\ Q(t) & =A{e}^{-7t/150},\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwhere $A = \\pm e^C$ is a constant of integration.\n\nWe're told that the reactor initially contains $18\\,\\textrm{lb}$ of reactant. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0) = 18,$ and solve for $A{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =18 \\\\ A{e}^{-7\\cdot 0/150} & =18 \\\\ A & =18\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t){:}$\n\n$$\nQ(t) = 18e^{-7t/150}\n$$\n\nFinally, the amount of reactant in the reactor $25$ minutes after the solvent is first pumped in is\n\n$$\nQ(25) = 18e^{-175/150} \\approx 5.61\\,\\textrm{lb},\n$$\n\nrounded to two decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186050905} {:db/id 17592186115791 :question/id #uuid "64193270-c02d-55f7-b1b5-b71007015ee2" :question/math-academy-id at which salt exits the tank.\n\nNow, to find the rate at which salt leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of brine in the tank at time $t.$\n\n- The tank initially contains of dissolved contaminants.\nClean water is pumped into the basin at a rate of $24\\,\\text{gal/min},$ while the completely mixed liquid leaves the basin at a rate of $18\\,\\text{gal/min}.$\nFind, rounded to two decimal places, the amount of contaminants in the basin $10$ minutes after the clean water pumping begins." :question/worked-solution "Let $Q$ be the amount of contaminants in the basin at time $t.$ Then, the derivative \n\n$$\n\\frac{dQ}{dt}\n$$\n\ndescribes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which contaminants enter the basin minus the rate at which contaminants leave the basin.\n\n$$\n\\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\\text{out}}^{′}\n$$\n\nNote that the units of $\\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\\text{lb}/\\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.\n\n**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which contaminants enter the basin.\n\nNote that clean water (i.e., water containing $0\\,\\text{lb/gal}$ of contaminants) enters the basin at a rate of $24\\,\\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *contaminants* enter the basin is \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\\text{in}}^{′} & =(0\\,\\frac{\\text{lb}}{\\text{gal}})\\cdot (24\\,\\frac{\\text{gal}}{\\text{min}}) \\\\  & =(0\\,\\frac{\\text{lb}}{\\cancel{\\text{gal}}})\\cdot (24\\,\\frac{\\cancel{\\text{gal}}}{\\text{min}}) \\\\  & =0\\,\\frac{\\text{lb}}{\\text{min}}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which contaminants exit the basin.\n\nTo find the rate at which contaminants leave the basin, we first determine the volume of wastewater in the basin at time $t.$\n\nThe basin initially contains $480\\,\\text{gal}$ of wastewater; water enters at $24\\,\\text{gal/min}$ and drains out at $18\\,\\text{gal/min}.$\nAs a result, the amount of wastewater in the basin after $t$ minutes is \n\n$$\n480+24t-18t=(480+6t)\\,\\text{gal}.\n$$\n\nSince $Q$ is the amount of contaminants in the basin, the *concentration* of the wastewater at time $t$ is\n\n$$\n\\frac{Q}{480+6t}\\,\\frac{\\text{lb}}{\\text{gal}}.\n$$\n\nTherefore, as the completely mixed liquid leaves at a rate of $18\\,\\text{gal/min},$ *contaminants* leave at a rate of\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\\text{out}}^{′} & =(18\\,\\frac{\\text{gal}}{\\text{min}})\\cdot (\\frac{Q}{480+6t}\\,\\frac{\\text{lb}}{\\text{gal}}) \\\\  & =(18\\,\\frac{\\cancel{\\text{gal}}}{\\text{min}})\\cdot (\\frac{Q}{480+6t}\\,\\frac{\\text{lb}}{\\cancel{\\text{gal}}}) \\\\  & =\\frac{18Q}{480+6t}\\,\\frac{\\text{lb}}{\\text{min}} \\\\  & =\\frac{3Q}{80+t}\\,\\frac{\\text{lb}}{\\text{min}}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.\n\nThe rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\\text{out}}^{′} \\\\  & =0-\\frac{3Q}{80+t}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwhich gives the equation\n\n$$\n\\frac{dQ}{dt}=-\\frac{3}{80+t}\\,Q.\n$$\n\n**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.\n\nSeparating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{1}{Q}\\cdot \\frac{dQ}{dt} & =-\\frac{3}{80+t} \\\\ \\int \\frac{1}{Q}\\cdot \\frac{dQ}{dt}dt & =\\int (-\\frac{3}{80+t})\\,dt \\\\ \\int \\frac{1}{Q}\\cdot \\,dQ & =-3\\int \\frac{1}{80+t}\\,dt \\\\ \\operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =-3\\operatorname{ln}⁡|80+t|+C \\\\ |Q| & ={e}^{-3\\operatorname{ln}⁡|80+t|+C} \\\\ Q(t) & =\\frac{A}{(80+t)^{3}},\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwhere $A=\\pm {e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration.\n\nWe're told that the basin initially contains $12\\,\\text{lb}$ of contaminants. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=12,$ and solve for $A:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =12 \\\\ \\frac{A}{(80+0)^{3}} & =12 \\\\ A & =12\\cdot {80}^{3}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$\n\n$$\nQ(t)=12{(\\frac{80}{80+t})}^{3}\n$$\n\nFinally, the amount of contaminants in the basin $10$ minutes after the clean water is first pumped in is\n\n$$\nQ(12)=12{(\\frac{80}{90})}^{3}≈8.43\\,\\text{lb},\n$$\n\nrounded to two decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186115375 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186114963 :question/id #uuid This is equal to the rate at which contaminant enters the tank minus the rate at which contaminant leaves the tank.\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{\\mathrm{d}Q}{\\mathrm{d}t} = Q'_{\\textrm{in}} - Q'_{\\textrm{out}}\n$$\n\nNote that the units of $\\dfrac{\\mathrm{d}Q}{\\mathrm{d}t}, Q'_{\\textrm{in}}$ and $Q'_{\\textrm{out}}$ are $\\textrm{g}/\\textrm{s}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.\n\n**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which contaminant enters the tank.\n\nFirst, note that clean water (i.e., water containing $0\\,\\textrm{g/mL}$ of contaminant) enters the tank at a rate of $100\\,\\textrm{mL/s}.$ So, the rate at which the *contaminant* enters the tank is \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\\text{in}}^{′} & =(0\\,\\frac{\\text{g}}{\\text{mL}})\\cdot (100\\,\\frac{\\text{mL}}{\\text{s}}) \\\\  & =(0\\,\\frac{\\text{g}}{\\cancel{\\text{mL}}})\\cdot (100\\,\\frac{\\cancel{\\text{mL}}}{\\text{s}}) \\\\  & =0\\,\\frac{\\text{g}}{\\text{s}}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which contaminant exits the tank.\n\nTo find the rate at which contaminant leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of water in the tank at time $t.$\n\nThe tank initially contains $8\\,000\\,\\textrm{mL}$ of water; clean water enters at $100\\,\\textrm{mL/s},$ and mixed water leaves at $60\\,\\textrm{mL/s}.$\nAs a result, the amount of water in the tank after $t$ seconds is \n\n$$\nV(t) = 8\\,000 + 100t - 60t = 40(200+t)\\,\\textrm{mL}.\n$$\n\nNote that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the tank is filling.\n\nSince $Q$ is the amount of contaminant in the tank, the concentration of the water at time $t$ is\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{Q}{40(200 + t)}\\,\\dfrac{\\textrm{g}}{\\textrm{mL}}.\n$$\n\nTherefore, as the completely mixed water leaves at a rate of $60\\,\\textrm{mL/s},$ *contaminant* leaves at a rate of\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\\text{out}}^{′} & =(60\\,\\frac{\\text{mL}}{\\text{s}})\\cdot (\\frac{Q}{40(200+t)}\\,\\frac{\\text{g}}{\\text{mL}}) \\\\  & =(60\\,\\frac{\\cancel{\\text{mL}}}{\\text{s}})\\cdot (\\frac{Q}{40(200+t)}\\,\\frac{\\text{g}}{\\cancel{\\text{mL}}}) \\\\  & =\\frac{3Q}{2(200+t)}\\,\\frac{\\text{g}}{\\text{s}}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.\n\nThe rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\\text{out}}^{′} \\\\  & =0-\\frac{3Q}{2(200+t)}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwhich gives the equation\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{\\mathrm{d}Q}{\\mathrm{d}t} = -\\dfrac{3}{2(200 + t)}\\,Q.\n$$\n\n**Step 4**: Integrate the equation\n\nSeparating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{1}{Q}\\cdot \\frac{dQ}{dt} & =-\\frac{3}{2(200+t)} \\\\ \\int \\frac{1}{Q}\\cdot \\frac{dQ}{dt}dt & =\\int (-\\frac{3}{2(200+t)})\\,dt \\\\ \\int \\frac{1}{Q}\\cdot \\,dQ & =-\\frac{3}{2}\\int \\frac{1}{200+t}\\,dt \\\\ \\operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =-\\frac{3}{2}(\\operatorname{ln}⁡|200+t|)+C \\\\ \\operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =\\operatorname{ln}⁡|(200+t)^{-3/2}|+C \\\\ |Q| & ={e}^{\\operatorname{ln}⁡|(200+t)^{-3/2}|+C} \\\\ Q(t) & =\\frac{A}{(200+t)^{3/2}},\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwhere $A = \\pm e^C$ is a constant of integration.\n\nWe're told that the tank initially contains $320\\,\\textrm{g}$ of contaminant. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0) = 320,$ and solve for $A{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =320 \\\\ \\frac{A}{(200+0)^{3/2}} & =320 \\\\ A & =320(200)^{3/2}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t){:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =\\frac{320(200)^{3/2}}{(200+t)^{3/2}} \\\\  & =320{(\\frac{200}{200+t})}^{3/2}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, let $t_o$ be the time when the tank begins to overflow. The tank has a capacity of $12\\,000\\,\\textrm{mL},$ so we can use the condition $V(t_o) = 12\\,000$ to solve for $t_o{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =12\\,000 \\\\ 40(200+{t}_{o}) & =12\\,000 \\\\ 200+{t}_{o} & =300 \\\\ {t}_{o} & =100\\,\\text{s}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, the amount of contaminant in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}Q(100) & =320{(\\frac{200}{200+100})}^{3/2} \\\\  & =320{(\\frac{2}{3})}^{3/2} \\\\  & ≈174.19\\,\\text{g}.\\end{aligned}\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186115793 :question/id #uuid pure solvent enters at $90\\,\\text{mL/s},$ and mixed solution leaves at $60\\,\\text{mL/s}.$\nAs a result, the amount of solution in the reactor after $t$ seconds is \n\n$$\nV(t)=7\\,500+90t-60t=30(250+t)\\,\\text{mL}.\n$$\n\nNote that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the reactor is filling.\n\nSince $Q$ is the amount of reactant in the reactor, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is\n\n$$\n\\frac{Q}{30(250+t)}\\,\\frac{\\text{g}}{\\text{mL}}.\n$$\n\nTherefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $60\\,\\text{mL/s},$ *reactant* leaves at a rate of\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\\text{out}}^{′} & =(60\\,\\frac{\\text{mL}}{\\text{s}})\\cdot (\\frac{Q}{30(250+t)}\\,\\frac{\\text{g}}{\\text{mL}}) \\\\  & =(60\\,\\frac{\\cancel{\\text{mL}}}{\\text{s}})\\cdot (\\frac{Q}{30(250+t)}\\,\\frac{\\text{g}}{\\cancel{\\text{mL}}}) \\\\  & =\\frac{2Q}{250+t}\\,\\frac{\\text{g}}{\\text{s}}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.\n\nThe rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\\text{out}}^{′} \\\\  & =0-\\frac{2Q}{250+t}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwhich gives the equation\n\n$$\n\\frac{dQ}{dt}=-\\frac{2}{250+t}\\,Q.\n$$\n\n**Step 4**: Integrate the equation\n\nSeparating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{1}{Q}\\cdot \\frac{dQ}{dt} & =-\\frac{2}{250+t} \\\\ \\int \\frac{1}{Q}\\cdot \\frac{dQ}{dt}dt & =\\int (-\\frac{2}{250+t})\\,dt \\\\ \\int \\frac{1}{Q}\\cdot \\,dQ & =-2\\int \\frac{1}{250+t}\\,dt \\\\ \\operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =-2(\\operatorname{ln}⁡|250+t|)+C \\\\ \\operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =\\operatorname{ln}⁡|(250+t)^{-2}|+C \\\\ |Q| & ={e}^{\\operatorname{ln}⁡|(250+t)^{-2}|+C} \\\\ Q(t) & =\\frac{A}{(250+t)^{2}},\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwhere $A=\\pm {e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration.\n\nWe're told that the reactor initially contains $98\\,\\text{g}$ of reactant. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=98,$ and solve for $A:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =98 \\\\ \\frac{A}{(250+0)^{2}} & =98 \\\\ A & =98(250)^{2}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =\\frac{98(250)^{2}}{(250+t)^{2}} \\\\  & =98{(\\frac{250}{250+t})}^{2}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the reactor begins to overflow. The reactor has a capacity of $10\\,500\\,\\text{mL},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=10\\,500$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =10\\,500 \\\\ 30(250+{t}_{o}) & The vat has a capacity of $9\\,500\\,\\text{mL},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=9\\,500$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =9\\,500 \\\\ 20(325+{t}_{o}) & =9\\,500 \\\\ 325+{t}_{o} & =475 \\\\ {t}_{o} & =150\\,\\text{s}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, the amount of sugar in the vat at the moment it begins to overflow is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}Q(150) & :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186116336 :step/content {:db/id 17592186116425 :tutorial/content "Consider a container which initially holds $V_0\\,\\textrm{gal}$ of solution containing $a\\,\\textrm{lb}$ of a substance.\n\n- Another solution, containing $b\\,\\textrm{lb}$ of the substance per gallon, flows *into* the container at the rate $e\\,\\textrm{gal}/\\textrm{min}.$\n- At the same time, the completely mixed solution flows *out* of the container at the rate $f\\,\\textrm{gal}/\\text{min}.$\n\n![](images/31/312d11bb0a00f6f668b653b00a7eecda55cdb23c5a7c09076734774b7c05a50b.png)\n\nHow can we model the amount $Q$ (in pounds) of substance in the container at time $t?$\n\nTo model $Q(t),$ we can analyze how it changes over time. The rate of change of the amount of substance in the container is given by $$\\dfrac{\\mathrm{d}Q}{\\mathrm{d}t} = Q'_\\text{in} - Q'_\\text{out},$$ where:\n\n- $Q'_\\text{in}$ is the rate at which the substance *enters* the container. A solution containing $b\\,\\textrm{lb}/\\textrm{gal}$ of the substance enters the container at a rate of $e\\,\\textrm{gal}/\\textrm{min}.$ So, we have $$\\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\\text{in}}^{'} & =(b\\,\\frac{\\text{lb}}{\\text{gal}})\\cdot (e\\,\\frac{\\text{gal}}{\\text{min}}) \\\\ & =(b\\,\\frac{\\text{lb}}{\\cancel{\\text{gal}}})\\cdot (e\\,\\frac{\\cancel{\\text{gal}}}{\\text{min}}) \\\\ & =be\\,\\frac{\\text{lb}}{\\text{min}}.\\end{aligned}$$\n- $Q'_\\text{out}$ is the rate at which the substance *leaves* the container. 17592186116428 :tutorial/content "So far, we have seen that if a container initially holds $V_0\\,\\textrm{gal}$ of solution containing $a\\,\\textrm{lb}$ of a substance, and\n\n- a solution with concentration $b\\,\\textrm{lb}/\\textrm{gal}$ flows into the container at the rate $e\\,\\textrm{gal}/\\textrm{min},$ while\n- the completely mixed solution flows out at the rate $f\\,\\textrm{gal}/\\text{min},$\n\nthen the amount $Q(t)$ of the substance in the container satisfies the differential equation\n\n$$\\dfrac{\\mathrm{d}Q}{\\mathrm{d}t} + f\\left(\\dfrac{Q}{V_0 + (e-f)t}\\right) = be.$$\n\nFor the rest of this lesson, we'll focus on the special case where the input solution contains *no substance*, that is, where $b=0.$ In this case, the right-hand side vanishes, and the differential equation becomes *separable*:\n\n$$\\dfrac{\\mathrm{d}Q}{\\mathrm{d}t} + f\\left(\\dfrac{Q}{V_0 + (e-f)t}\\right) = 0 \\quad\\Longrightarrow\\quad \\dfrac1Q\\cdot\\dfrac{\\mathrm{d}Q}{\\mathrm{d}t} = - \\dfrac{f}{V_0 + (e-f)t}$$\n\nNotice that the right-hand side is negative, meaning the amount of substance in the container decreases over time. We can now solve the differential equation directly by separation of variables.\n\nTo demonstrate, consider our previous example: a tank initially holds $450\\,\\textrm{L}$ of water containing $6\\,\\textrm{kg}$ of dissolved contaminant, and a solution containing no contaminant is pumped into the tank at a rate of $8\\,\\textrm{L/min},$ while the completely mixed solution leaves the tank at a rate of $8\\,\\textrm{L/min}.$\n\nWe found that the amount of dissolved contaminant $Q(t),$ in kilograms, in the tank after $t$ minutes is modeled by the differential equation\n\n$$\\dfrac{\\mathrm{d}Q}{\\mathrm{d}t} + \\dfrac{4}{225}Q = 0 \\qquad\\Longrightarrow\\qquad \\dfrac{1}{Q} \\cdot \\dfrac{\\mathrm{d}Q}{\\mathrm{d}t} = -\\dfrac{4}{225}.$$\n\nWe solve this equation by integrating both sides with respect to $t{:}$\n\n$$\\begin{aligned}\\int \\frac{1}{Q}\\cdot \\frac{dQ}{dt}\\,dt & =\\int (-\\frac{4}{225})\\,dt \\\\ \\int \\frac{1}{Q}\\,dQ & =-\\frac{4}{225}\\int dt \\\\ \\operatorname{ln}|Q| & =-\\frac{4t}{225}+C \\\\ Q & ={e}^{-4t/225+C} \\\\ Q(t) & =A{e}^{-4t/225}\\end{aligned}$$\n\nNote that $A = \\pm e^C$ is a constant of integration.\n\nFinally, since the tank initially contains $6\\,\\textrm{kg}$ of dissolved contaminant, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=6,$ and solve for $A{:}$\n\n$$\\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =6 \\\\ A{e}^{-4(0)/225} & =6 \\\\ A & =6\\end{aligned}$$\n\nTherefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t){:}$\n\n$$\\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{Q(t) = 6e^{-4t/225}}$$" :tutorial/id :step/math-academy-id 593295 :step/next {:db/id 17592186116341}} {:db/id 17592186116341 :step/content {:db/id 17592186116427 :tutorial/content "Previously, we saw that the volume $V$ of solution at time $t$ in a container with initial volume $V_0,$ input rate $e,$ and output rate $f$ is given by\n\n$$V(t) = V_0 + (e - f)t.$$\n\nThere are three possible behaviors for the volume depending on the rates:\n\n- The volume *remains constant* when the input rate equals the output rate, $e=f.$ In this case, $$V(t) = V_0.$$\n- The volume *decreases* when the output rate is greater than the input rate, $f > e > 0,$ and the container begins to empty. Let $t_e$ be the time when the container empties: $V(t_e) = 0.$ Solving for $t_e,$ we get $$\\begin{aligned}V({t}_{e}) & ={V}_{0}+(e-f){t}_{e} \\\\ 0 & ={V}_{0}+(e-f){t}_{e}.\\end{aligned}$$ Solving this equation, we find that the container empties at time $\\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid #d3d3d3]{t_e = \\dfrac{V_0}{f - e}}.$\n\n- The volume *increases* when the input rate is greater than the output rate, $e > f > 0,$ and the container begins filling until it reaches its capacity $V_\\text{cap}.$ Let $t_o$ be the time when the container reaches capacity: $V(t_o) = V_\\text{cap}.$ Solving for $t_o,$ we get $$\\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & ={V}_{\\text{cap}} \\\\ {V}_{0}+(e-f){t}_{o} & ={V}_{\\text{cap}}.\\end{aligned}$$ Solving this equation, we find that the container overflows at time $\\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid #d3d3d3]{t_o = \\dfrac{V_\\text{cap} -
