17592186116339}} {:db/id 17592186116339 :step/content {:db/id 17592186116428 :tutorial/content "So far, we have seen that if a container initially holds $V_0\\,\\textrm{gal}$ of solution containing $a\\,\\textrm{lb}$ of a substance, and\n\n- a solution with concentration $b\\,\\textrm{lb}/\\textrm{gal}$ flows into the container at the rate $e\\,\\textrm{gal}/\\textrm{min},$ while\n- the completely mixed solution flows out at the rate $f\\,\\textrm{gal}/\\text{min},$\n\nthen the amount $Q(t)$ of the substance in the container satisfies the differential equation\n\n$$\\dfrac{\\mathrm{d}Q}{\\mathrm{d}t} + f\\left(\\dfrac{Q}{V_0 + (e-f)t}\\right) = be.$$\n\nFor the rest of this lesson, we'll focus on the special case where the input solution contains *no substance*, that is, where $b=0.$ In this case, the right-hand side vanishes, and the differential equation becomes *separable*:\n\n$$\\dfrac{\\mathrm{d}Q}{\\mathrm{d}t} + f\\left(\\dfrac{Q}{V_0 + (e-f)t}\\right) = 0 \\quad\\Longrightarrow\\quad \\dfrac1Q\\cdot\\dfrac{\\mathrm{d}Q}{\\mathrm{d}t} = - \\dfrac{f}{V_0 + (e-f)t}$$\n\nNotice that the right-hand side is negative, meaning the amount of substance in the container decreases over time. We can now solve the differential equation directly by separation of variables.\n\nTo demonstrate, consider our previous example: a tank initially holds $450\\,\\textrm{L}$ of water containing $6\\,\\textrm{kg}$ of dissolved contaminant, and a solution containing no contaminant is pumped into the tank at a rate of $8\\,\\textrm{L/min},$ while the completely mixed solution leaves the tank at a rate of $8\\,\\textrm{L/min}.$\n\nWe found that the amount of dissolved contaminant $Q(t),$ in kilograms, in the tank after $t$ minutes is modeled by the differential equation\n\n$$\\dfrac{\\mathrm{d}Q}{\\mathrm{d}t} + \\dfrac{4}{225}Q = 0 \\qquad\\Longrightarrow\\qquad \\dfrac{1}{Q} \\cdot \\dfrac{\\mathrm{d}Q}{\\mathrm{d}t} = -\\dfrac{4}{225}.$$\n\nWe solve this equation by integrating both sides with respect to $t{:}$\n\n$$\\begin{aligned}\\int \\frac{1}{Q}\\cdot \\frac{dQ}{dt}\\,dt & =\\int (-\\frac{4}{225})\\,dt \\\\ \\int \\frac{1}{Q}\\,dQ & =-\\frac{4}{225}\\int dt \\\\ \\operatorname{ln}|Q| & =-\\frac{4t}{225}+C \\\\ Q & ={e}^{-4t/225+C} \\\\ Q(t) & =A{e}^{-4t/225}\\end{aligned}$$\n\nNote that $A = \\pm e^C$ is a constant of integration.\n\nFinally, since the tank initially contains $6\\,\\textrm{kg}$ of dissolved contaminant, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=6,$ and solve for $A{:}$\n\n$$\\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =6 \\\\ A{e}^{-4(0)/225} & =6 \\\\ A & =6\\end{aligned}$$\n\nTherefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t){:}$\n\n$$\\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{Q(t) = 6e^{-4t/225}}$$" :tutorial/id :tutorial/content "Previously, we saw that the volume $V$ of solution at time $t$ in a container with initial volume $V_0,$ input rate $e,$ and output rate $f$ is given by\n\n$$V(t) = V_0 + (e - f)t.$$\n\nThere are three possible behaviors for the volume depending on the rates:\n\n- The volume *remains constant* when the input rate equals the output rate, $e=f.$ In this case, $$V(t) = V_0.$$\n- The volume *decreases* when the output rate is greater than the input rate, $f > e > 0,$ and the container begins to empty. Let $t_e$ be the time when the container empties: $V(t_e) = 0.$ Solving for $t_e,$ we get $$\\begin{aligned}V({t}_{e}) & ={V}_{0}+(e-f){t}_{e} \\\\ 0 & ={V}_{0}+(e-f){t}_{e}.\\end{aligned}$$ Solving this equation, we find that the container empties at time $\\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid #d3d3d3]{t_e = \\dfrac{V_0}{f - e}}.$\n\n- The volume *increases* when the input rate is greater than the output rate, $e > f > 0,$ and the container begins filling until it reaches its capacity $V_\\text{cap}.$ Let $t_o$ be the time when the container reaches capacity: $V(t_o) = V_\\text{cap}.$ Solving for $t_o,$ we get $$\\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & ={V}_{\\text{cap}} \\\\ {V}_{0}+(e-f){t}_{o} & ={V}_{\\text{cap}}.\\end{aligned}$$ Solving this equation, we find that the container overflows at time $\\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid #d3d3d3]{t_o = \\dfrac{V_\\text{cap} - V_0}{e - f}}.$\n\nNow, let's apply one of these formulas in a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "3c551e08-3014-52f3-83f1-73ec27aa2e82" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14564 :tutorial/title "Points of Overflow and Emptying"} :step/id #uuid "259727bc-a70f-53ae-9206-f6024bda6e30" :step/math-academy-id 593299 :step/next {:db/id 17592186116342}} {:db/id 17592186116427 :tutorial/content "Previously, we saw that the volume $V$ of solution at time $t$ in a container with initial volume $V_0,$ input rate $e,$ and output rate $f$ is given by\n\n$$V(t) = V_0 + (e - f)t.$$\n\nThere are three possible behaviors for the volume depending on the rates:\n\n- The volume *remains constant* when the input rate equals the output rate, $e=f.$ In this case, $$V(t) = V_0.$$\n- The volume *decreases* when the output rate is greater than the input rate, $f > e > 0,$ and the container begins to empty. :tutorial/content "Let's consider the following matrix:\n\n![](images/ea/ea31a54b90a066b34d28d1af82ee31515f06622a873d5790b2dd73cb2bbd8bb8.svg)\n\nThis is a $3\\times 3$ matrix, yet it has only *two* distinct eigenvalues, namely $\\lambda_1 = 0$ and $\\lambda_2 = 1.$ Note that $\\lambda_1$ is a simple root of the  characteristic polynomial and $\\lambda_2$ is a double root.\n\nTo diagonalize a $3\\times 3$ matrix, we need to find a basis of $\\mathbb R^3$ consisting of linearly independent eigenvectors of $A.$ So the question is, can we diagonalize this matrix even though it does not have three distinct eigenvalues?\n\nLet's start by computing the eigenvectors of $A\\mathbin{:}$\n\n- First, we consider the simple root $\\lambda_1 = 0.$ Solving the equation $A \\mathbf x = \\lambda_1 \\mathbf x$ in the usual way, we obtain a single linearly independent eigenvector:\n\n$$\n[\\begin{aligned}1 \\\\ 1 \\\\ -1\\end{aligned}]\n$$\n\n- Next, we consider the double root $\\lambda_2 = 1.$ Let's solve the equation $A \\mathbf x = \\lambda_2 \\mathbf x$ by reducing $(A - \\lambda_2 I)$ to row-echelon form:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}A-{\\lambda }_{2}I & =[\\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\\\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\\\ 0 & 0 & 0\\end{aligned}]-[\\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 0 & 1\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 1 \\\\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\\\ 0 & 0 & -1\\end{aligned}] &  & \\begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\\\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{1}\\end{aligned} \\\\  & ∼[\\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 1 \\\\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 0 & 0\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThere is one pivot column in the reduced matrix above (the $3$rd one). Thus, $x_1$ and $x_2$ are free variables. From the first equation, we obtain the solution $x_3 = 0.$ Therefore, the general solution is\n![](images/1b/1bfc4a70075d48f926789a8a1d531b20b060172f2eebe862ee5e1a34ed315688.svg)\nwhere $x_1, x_2\\in \\mathbb R.$ Thus, we have obtained *two* linearly independent eigenvectors:\n![](images/a5/a513d529bf797d62ca4df57b37adc3c57e719db4773165b744c70b5a8e071dda.svg)\n\nSo $A$ has three linearly independent eigenvectors that form a basis of $\\mathbb R^3.$ Therefore, $A$ is diagonalizable! \n\nIn terms of eigenspaces, $A$ is diagonalizable because the sum of the dimensions of the eigenspaces equals the number of rows/columns of $A.$ The eigenspaces corresponding to $\\lambda_1 = 0$ and $\\lambda_2 = 1$ are given by\n\n![](images/6e/6e0e00d51cd3eaf3ad0f5d2f7d07d4bd0c00e80d9fc66ccebc690671e98850b8.svg) \n\nIf we sum the dimensions of $V_0$ and $V_1,$ we get precisely $3\\mathbin{:}$\n\n$$\n\\dim(V_{0}) + \\dim(V_{1}) = 1 + 2 = 3 \\quad {\\color{green}\\checkmark}\n$$\n\nwhich means that $A$ is diagonalizable.\n\nIt's important to realize that not all matrices are diagonalizable! Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "10637b3f-57b1-5542-b802-95ed60bc127e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3579 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "7203c46b-0f37-5a6e-85bc-dc8132e299ee" :tutorial/content "Let's now consider the following matrix:\n\n![](images/db/dba80d814848486260c88ce625464f75a18e09963dfd7e16603462cb857b302c.svg)\n\nIts eigenvalues are $\\lambda_1=1$ (simple root) and $\\lambda_2=2$ (double root).\n\nLet's see how many linearly independent eigenvectors we can find for this matrix.\n\n- First, we consider the simple root $\\lambda_1 = 1.$ Solving the equation $A \\mathbf x = \\lambda_1 \\mathbf x$ in the usual way, we obtain a single linearly independent eigenvector:\n\n$$\n[\\begin{aligned}1 \\\\ 1 \\\\ 2\\end{aligned}]\n$$\n\n- Next, we consider the double root $\\lambda_2 = 2.$ Let's solve the equation $A \\mathbf x = \\lambda_2 \\mathbf x$ by reducing $(A - \\lambda_2 I)$ to row-echelon form:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}A-{\\lambda }_{2}I & =[\\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\\\ -3 & 2 & 1 \\\\ -2 & 0 & 2\\end{aligned}]-2[\\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 0 & 1\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\\\ -3 & 0 & 1 \\\\ -2 & 0 & 0\\end{aligned}] &  & \\begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\\\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1}\\end{aligned} \\\\  & ∼[\\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\\\ 0 & 0 & 0\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nIn the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $3$rd). Thus, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first and second equations, we have\n\n$$\nx_1 = x_3 = 0.\n$$\n\nTherefore, the general solution is\n![](images/f1/f1b718cdc6cbb49c9cad5faada737abddccadc83f6f1e94ae64d096863a304ef.svg)\nwhere $x_2\\in\\mathbb R.$ Thus, we have obtained *only one* linearly independent eigenvector:\n\n$$\n[\\begin{aligned}0 \\\\ 1 \\\\ 0\\end{aligned}]\n$$\n\nSo $A$ has *only two* linearly independent eigenvectors, and these cannot form a basis of $\\mathbb R^3.$ Therefore, $A$ is *not* diagonalizable.\n\nIn terms of eigenspaces, the matrix $A$ is not diagonalizable because the sum of the dimensions of the eigenspaces is *smaller* than the number of rows/columns of $A.$ The eigenspaces corresponding to $\\lambda_1 = 1$ and $\\lambda_2 = 2$ are given by\n\n![](images/93/93a38c26711366b4a091900bd410648137a5fede4a155b411038dc3a82a19e23.svg) \n\nIf we sum the dimensions of $V_1$ and $V_2,$ we get\n\n$$\n\\dim(V_{1}) + \\dim(V_{2}) = 1 + 1 = 2 \\neq 3 \\quad {\\color{red}{\\boldsymbol\\times}}\n$$\n\nwhich means that $A$ is *not* diagonalizable." :tutorial/id #uuid "c685cb77-5f99-589a-abac-5ff2154edb7d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6190 :tutorial/title "An Example of a Non-Diagonalizable 3x3 Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "d2466c9e-46cb-5a71-ace7-8154518e92f3" :step/math-academy-id 37526 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125602}} {:db/id 17592186125594 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125857 :tutorial/content "A square matrix $A$ is diagonalizable if there exists a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that\n\n$$\nA = PDP^{-1}.\n$$\n\nSo, diagonalizing $A$ means finding matrices $D$ and $P$ that satisfy this equation. \n\nFor example, let's diagonalize the matrix $A,$ given by\n\n![](images/da/da4b2dd12205b20515a36d06bc5de5b577bec362c5eb9f7942e795fe1511acfb.svg)\n\nTo diagonalize a $3 \\times 3$ matrix, we follow a three-step **diagonalization algorithm.**\n\n**Step 1:** Find the eigenvalues of the matrix.\n\nWe solve the characteristic equation $\\vert A - \\lambda I \\vert = 0.$ For the given matrix, the eigenvalues are \n\n$$\n{\\color{red}{\\lambda_1}} = {\\color{red}{\\lambda_2}} = {\\color{red}2}\\qquad \\textrm{and} \\qquad{\\color{blue}\\lambda_3 =1}.\n$$\n\n**Step 2:** Find a basis (if it exists) consisting of eigenvectors of the matrix.\n\nFollowing the usual method for computing eigenvectors, we get \n\n![](images/57/572a2da243557642332de657b41ee28237385eeaa59ebcef747dd73f9d8e4c36.svg)\n\ncorresponding to the eigenvalues ${\\color{red}{\\lambda_1}} = {\\color{red}{\\lambda_2}} = {\\color{red}2}$ and ${\\color{blue}\\lambda_3 =1},$ respectively.\n\n**Watch out!** In this example, the total number of linearly independent eigenvectors equals the number of rows/columns of the matrix. If we obtain fewer eigenvectors at this step, then the matrix is *not* diagonalizable.\n\n**Step 3: ** Construct the matrices $D$ and $P.$\n\nNow that we have our eigenvalues and corresponding eigenvectors, we can construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and invertible matrix $P.$\n\nThe matrix $D$ has the eigenvalues of the matrix as its entries on the main diagonal. We can write them in any order, so we let\n\n![](images/45/45b4df46c058d00fd8186b2f9dc83ba9772bbe88b17866e6d188ba340e890d6d.svg)\n\nThen, the columns of $P$ are the corresponding eigenvectors. We must write each eigenvector in the *same* column as its respective eigenvalue in the matrix $D.$ So, we get\n\n![](images/c6/c64a8e7a572d5b6dce58390644d5f79d905fcf22c8427487dcc375bc851f7b12.svg)\n\nFinally, we obtain\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}A=PD{P}^{-1} & =[\\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 3 \\\\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\\\ 1 & 0 & 1\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 0 & 1\\end{aligned}]{[\\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 3 \\\\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\\\ 1 & 0 & 1\\end{aligned}]}^{-1}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n**Note:** When diagonalizing a diagonalizable matrix, we can place the eigenvalues into the matrix $P$ in any order. We just need to be sure that the diagonal entries in the matrix $D$ correspond to the columns of $P.$\n\nFor example:\n\n- Swapping the columns $\\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\\mathbf{v}_2,$ we get another valid diagonalization: \n![](images/60/6026d7be0662360726a109c6c665d59a10b805303b2b71934352688c2f17b357.svg)\n\n- Swapping the columns $\\mathbf{v}_2$ and $\\mathbf{v}_3$ above gives another valid diagonalization: \n![](images/22/223f68ef8ba143f1766224972d11e1b899afb64bd8828ec95d7b1c5a2d95519e.svg)" :tutorial/id #uuid "5d7a1ece-ba11-5a1b-9775-8396ebb35e65" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6191 :tutorial/title "The Diagonalization Algorithm"} :step/id #uuid "bd809b96-88bc-52f1-aa25-a46de9be7037" :step/math-academy-id 37527 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125428}} {:db/id 17592186125602 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125862 :tutorial/content "To check whether diagonalization is possible, we can use the following theorem:\n\n*An $n \\times n$ matrix is diagonalizable if and only if the sum of the dimensions of the eigenspaces equals $n$.*\n\nThat is, if \n\n$$\n\\lambda_1, \\: \\lambda_2, \\: \\ldots, \\: \\lambda_k\n$$\n\nare the distinct eigenvalues of an $n \\times n$ matrix, and the corresponding eigenspaces are \n\n$$\nV_{\\lambda_1}, \\: V_{\\lambda_2}, \\: \\ldots, \\: V_{\\lambda_k}\n$$\n\nthen the matrix is diagonalizable if and only if\n\n$$\n\\dim(V_{\\lambda_1}) + \\dim(V_{\\lambda_2}) + \\cdots + \\dim(V_{\\lambda_k}) = n.\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "9b1d1c74-27ca-5336-8e15-c998929c5bd0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6259 :tutorial/title "Determining Whether an NxN matrix, we follow a three-step **diagonalization algorithm.**\n\n**Step 1:** Find the eigenvalues of the matrix.\n\nWe solve the characteristic equation $\\vert A - \\lambda I \\vert = 0.$ For the $\\widehat{\\,p}$ be approximated as\n$\\widehat{\\,p} \\sim N\\left(p,\\dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}\\right)$,\nwhere $p$ is the population proportion?\n\n1. A sample of $120$ apricots from a population of $20\\,000$, where $75\\%$ of the apricots weigh more than $50$ g.\n2. A sample of $25$ gym members from a population containing $200$ members, where $80\\%$ of the gym's members work out for more than $100$ minutes each visit.\n3. A sample of $45$ flights in an airport, given that $90\\%$ of flights arrive on time. You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size." :question/worked-solution "Given a population in which a proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion $\\widehat{\\,p}$ can be approximated as\n\n$$\n\\widehat{\\,p} \\sim N\\left(p, \\dfrac{p(1-p)}{n} \\right)\n$$\n\nwhere\n\n- $n\\leq 5\\% \\cdot N$ (the sample size is less than (or equal to) $5\\%$ of the population size),\n- $np > 5$ (more than $5$ sample elements have the characteristic), and\n- $n(1-p) > 5$ (more than $5$ sample elements do not have the characteristic).\n\nLet's now examine each situation.\n\n- In situation I, we have\n$n|= 120; \\le 5% \\cdot N; = 0.05 \\cdot 20000; = 1000✓; np|= 120(0.75); = 90; > 5✓; n(1 - p)|= 120(1 - 0.75); = 30; > 5.✓$\nTherefore, we can approximate the distribution of $\\widehat{\\,p}$ using the given model.\n- In situation II, we have\n$n|= 25,; 5% \\cdot N|= 0.05 \\cdot 200; = 10; < 25.\\cdot$\nSince the sample size is more than $5\\%$ of the population size, we *cannot* approximate the distribution of $\\widehat{\\,p}$ using the given model.\n- In situation III, we're given that the population is significantly larger than the sample size in each case. Therefore, we may assume that the first condition is satisfied. For the other conditions, we have\n$np|= 45(0.9); = 40.5; > 5✓; n(1 - p)|= 45(1 - 0.9); = 4.5; ≯5.\\cdot$\nSince $n(1-p) \\ngtr 5$, we *cannot* approximate the distribution of $\\widehat{\\,p}$ using the given model.\n\nTherefore, the correct answer is \"I only.\""} {:db/id 17592186048589} {:db/id 17592186188678 :question/id #uuid "90fadc79-6d06-5385-8518-5436dbdfb1f7" :question/math-academy-id "q-146152"} {:db/id 17592186188685 :question/id #uuid "4f6270c9-4286-526b-a383-94a2b499f6f3" :question/math-academy-id "q-146169" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186188258 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "41537c58-9c96-5e6c-b0e6-778ebecb212c" :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Situations When the CLT for Proportions is Appropriate"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "d3601da7-a7c3-52cd-8f70-f617dbff7130" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186186391} {:answer/id #uuid "dccc85bb-7f5c-57a0-98aa-12945003cf5b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186186392} {:answer/id #uuid "f1d07aea-24ea-5f53-9672-04c6dad6b1f4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186186393} {:answer/id #uuid "68126574-febc-56bd-96e3-be660cd1d396" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I and III only" :db/id 17592186186394} {:answer/id #uuid "6f8c475d-4fb2-5d19-8a64-6b6d5fd924f9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186186395}] :answer-field/id #uuid "0083b82a-9efc-51d0-860f-723f4347222c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186186390}] :question/problem "For which of the following situations can the distribution of the sample proportion $p^(^)$ be approximated as\n\n$p^(^)∼N(p, (p(1 - Find a normal approximation for the probability that more than $50\\%$ of the sample has the characteristic. You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.\n\n*Hint: A table of values of $\\Phi(z)$ for different values of $z$ are given below, where $\\Phi(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.*\n\n| $z$ | $\\, 0.07 \\,$ | $\\, 0.08 \\,$ | $\\, 0.09 \\,$ |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| $\\, 1.4 \\,$ | $\\, 0.9292 \\,$ | $\\, 0.9306 \\,$ | $\\, 0.9319 \\,$ |\n| $\\, 1.5 \\,$ | $\\, 0.9418 \\,$ | $\\, 0.9429 \\,$ | $\\, 0.9441 \\,$ |\n| $\\, 1.6 \\,$ | $\\, 0.9525 \\,$ | $\\, 0.9535 \\,$ | $\\, 0.9545 \\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Given a population in which a proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion $\\widehat{\\,p}$ can be approximated as\n\n$$\n\\widehat{\\,p} \\sim N\\left(p, \\dfrac{p(1-p)}{n} \\right)\n$$\n\nwhere the sample size $n$ is much smaller than the population size, $np > 5$, and $n(1-p) > 5$.\n\nIn our case\n\n- the sample size is $n = 84$, and\n- the population proportion is $p = 0.42$.\n\nNow, since\n\n$$\nnp = 84(0.42) = 35.28 > 5\n$$\n\nand\n\n$$\nn(1-p) = 84(1-0.42) = 48.72 > 5\n$$\n\nand $n=84$ is much smaller than the population size, we can apply the above approximation.\n\nThe sampling distribution of the sample proportion, in this case, can be approximated as\n\n$$\np^(^) \\mid ∼N(p, (p(1 - p))/(n)); ∼N(0.42, (0.42(1 - 0.42))/(84)); ∼N(0.42, 0.0029)\n$$\n\nThe probability we wish to find is\n$P(\\widehat{\\,p} > 0.5)$.\nSo, we convert $\\widehat{\\,p}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nP(p^(^) > 0.5) &= P(Z > \\frac{0.5 - 0.42}{\\sqrt{0.0029}}) \\\\\n&\\approx P(Z > 1.49) \\\\\n&= 1 - P(Z < 1.49) \\\\\n&= 1 - Φ(1.49)\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFrom the table, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nΦ(1.49) &= 0.9319\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore,\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nP(p^(^) > 0.5) &= 1 - Φ(1.49) \\\\\n&= 1 - 0.9319 \\\\\n&= 0.0681\n\\end{aligned}\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186188683 :question/id #uuid "8b040f12-bfb6-5271-9a10-66bca5c20f49" :question/math-academy-id "q-146163"} {:db/id 17592186188684 :question/id #uuid "dbed22eb-e3d1-5c23-b166-31d76c217f5d" :question/math-academy-id "q-146165"} {:db/id 17592186188260 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186188195 :question/id #uuid "dac77d50-5617-55c6-9824-37afb60cf639" :question/math-academy-id "e-15153"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "dcbec092-32b6-5e0d-be59-3f0ec18b8c6a" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186188679 :question/id #uuid "0faf39ad-2709-5ec7-94d0-99312772d48f" :question/math-academy-id "q-146155"} {:db/id 17592186188681 :question/id #uuid "da01a854-bda8-5ccb-8dc9-1deaf2392385" :question/math-academy-id "q-146160"}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding an Approximate Probability Using the CLT for Proportions: Applications"} {:db/id 17592186188195 :question/id #uuid "dac77d50-5617-55c6-9824-37afb60cf639" :question/math-academy-id "e-15153" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186188260 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "dcbec092-32b6-5e0d-be59-3f0ec18b8c6a" :knowledge-point/title "Finding an Approximate Probability Using the CLT for Proportions: Applications"}] :question/problem "A popular streaming service has a database of $100$ million songs, of which $64$ million have a duration of less than $3$ minutes. If a user randomly creates a playlist with $128$ songs, find a normal approximation for the probability that between $64$ and $96$ (inclusive) songs in the sample have a duration of less than $3$ minutes. You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.\n\n*Hint: Two tables of values of $\\Phi(z)$ for different values of $z$ are given below, where $\\Phi(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.*\n\n| $z$$\\, 0.00 \\,$$\\, 0.01 \\,$$\\, 0.02 \\,$$\\, -3.4 \\,$ $\\, 0.0003 \\,$ $\\, 0.0003 \\,$ $\\, 0.0003 \\,$ $\\, -3.3 \\,$ $\\, 0.0005 \\,$ $\\, 0.0005 \\,$ $\\, 0.0005 \\,$ $\\, -3.2 \\,$ $\\, 0.0007 \\,$ $\\, 0.0007 \\,$ $\\, 0.0006 \\,$ |  | $z$$\\, 0.07 \\,$$\\, 0.08 \\,$$\\, 0.09 \\,$$\\, 2.5 \\,$ $\\, 0.9949 \\,$ $\\, 0.9951 \\,$ $\\, 0.9952 \\,$ $\\, 2.6 \\,$ $\\, 0.9962 \\,$ $\\, 0.9963 \\,$ $\\, 0.9964 \\,$ $\\, 2.7 \\,$ $\\, 0.9972 \\,$ $\\, 0.9973 \\,$ $\\, 0.9974 \\,$ |\n| --- | ---: | ---: |" :question/worked-solution "Given a population in which a proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion $\\widehat{\\,p}$ can be approximated as\n\n$$\n\\widehat{\\,p} \\sim N\\left(p, \\dfrac{p(1-p)}{n} \\right)\n$$\n\nwhere the sample size $n$ is much smaller than the population size, $np > 5$, and $n(1-p) > 5$.\n\nIn our case\n\n- the sample size is $n = 128$, and\n- the population proportion is $p = \\dfrac{64\\,000\\,000}{100\\,000\\,000} = 0.64$.\n\nNow, since\n\n$$\nnp = 128(0.64) = 81.92 > 5\n$$\n\nand\n\n$$\nn(1-p) = 128(1-0.64) = 46.08 > 5\n$$\n\nand the $n=128$ is much smaller than the population size, we can apply the above approximation.\n\nThe sampling distribution of the sample proportion, in this case, can be approximated as\n\n$$\np^(^) \\mid ∼N(p, (p(1 - p))/(n)); ∼N(0.64, (0.64(1 - 0.64))/(128)); ∼N(0.64, 0.0018)\n$$\n\nNext, we determine the probability we wish to find. If between $64$ and $96$ of the songs in the playlist last less than $3$ minutes, then\n\n$$\n\\begin{bmatrix}\\frac{64}{128} \\le p^(^) & \\le \\frac{96}{128} \\\\ 0.5 \\le p^(^) & \\le 0.75\\end{bmatrix}\n$$\n\nHence, the probability we wish to find is\n\n$$\nP(0.5 \\leq \\widehat{\\,p} \\leq 0.75)\n$$\n\nSo, we convert $\\widehat{\\,p}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nP(0.5 \\le p^(^) \\le 0.75) &= P(\\frac{0.5 - 0.64}{\\sqrt{0.0018}} \\le Z \\le \\frac{0.75 - 0.64}{\\sqrt{0.0018}}) \\\\\n&\\approx P(-3.30 \\le Z \\le 2.59) \\\\\n&= P(Z \\le 2.59) - P(Z \\le - 3.30) \\\\\n&= Φ(2.59) - Φ(-3.30)\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFrom the table, we have\n\n$$\nΦ(2.59) = 0.9952, Φ(-3.30) = 0.0005\n$$\n\nTherefore,\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nP(0.5 \\le p^(^) \\le 0.75) &= Φ(2.59) - Φ(-3.30) \\\\\n&= 0.9952 - 0.0005 \\\\\n&= 0.9947\n\\end{aligned}\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186188679 :question/id #uuid "0faf39ad-2709-5ec7-94d0-99312772d48f" :question/math-academy-id "q-146155"} {:db/id 17592186188681 :question/id #uuid "da01a854-bda8-5ccb-8dc9-1deaf2392385" :question/math-academy-id "q-146160" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186188260 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "dcbec092-32b6-5e0d-be59-3f0ec18b8c6a" :knowledge-point/title "Finding an Approximate Probability Using the CLT for Proportions: Applications"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c2dfdd82-65a5-5171-bc01-7821fbf0698e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.1118" :db/id 17592186186367} {:answer/id #uuid "c39133e9-a888-5d29-b93c-9e5408b6d72f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.3853" :db/id 17592186186368} {:answer/id #uuid "1356a3ec-56fc-5170-816e-abe9552e7e84" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.2605" :db/id 17592186186369} {:answer/id #uuid "2abc7d34-8251-5017-899a-0156b06b5501" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.1846" :db/id 17592186186370} {:answer/id #uuid "7e69b089-b6f5-5b27-9c28-5a5089665d1c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.0835" :db/id 17592186186371}] :answer-field/id #uuid "fd8ca12c-8970-56fc-9321-068eac62971b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186186366}] :question/problem "In a school of $900$ students, $432$ of the students are male. [{:db/id 17592186189055 :step/content {:db/id 17592186189500 :tutorial/content "Suppose we conduct a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N$ where some proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic. Let's denote the random variable $X_i$ as follows:\n\n$$\n{1, [math]i[/math]th member of the sample has the characteristic; 0, otherwise\n$$\n\nIn other words,\n\n$$\nX_i \\sim \\textrm{Bernoulli}(p)\n$$\n\nLet's assume the sample size is less than (or equal to) $5\\%$ of the population size. Under this condition, we've seen that $X_1,X_2,\\ldots,X_n$ can be considered to be (approximately) independent and identically distributed, which means that\n\n$$\nX = \\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i \\approx B(n,p)\n$$\n\nwhere $B(n,p)$ denotes a binomial distribution, and\n\n$$\n\\textrm{E}[X] = np, \\qquad \\textrm{Var}[X] = np(1-p)\n$$\n\nRemember that $X$ represents the number of sample members with the characteristic.\n\nNow, let's assume that $np > 5$ and $n(1-p) > 5$ so we can apply the normal approximation of the binomial distribution (i.e., the central limit theorem). Then,\n\n$$\nX \\approx N\\big(np,np(1-p)\\big)\n$$\n\nFurthermore, we've also seen that we can construct an estimator $\\widehat{\\,p}$ as\n\n$$\n\\widehat{\\,p} = \\dfrac{X}{n}\n$$\n\nwhere\n\n$$\n\\textrm{E}[\\widehat{\\,p}] = p, \\qquad \\textrm{Var}[\\widehat{\\,p}] = \\dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}\n$$\n\nSince $X$ is approximately normally distributed, $\\widehat{\\,p}$ is also normally distributed. Therefore, the sampling distribution of $\\widehat{\\,p}$ is given by\n\n$$\n\\widehat{\\,p}\\approx N\\bigg(p, \\dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}\\bigg)\n$$\n\nFinally, since we usually don't know $p$, we can use a particular estimate to approximate $\\textrm{E}[{\\widehat{\\,p}}]$ and $\\textrm{Var}[\\widehat{\\,p}]$.\n\n**Watch out!** In this lesson, $N$ denotes the size of a population, while $N(\\cdot,\\cdot)$ denotes the normal distribution." :tutorial/id #uuid "d4cf166b-07f1-5e2e-9b9a-8147d42ce348" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9526 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "5ce0e2df-ecaa-5cb0-b322-b2b78e5030ce" :step/math-academy-id 187404 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189056}} {:db/id 17592186189056 :step/content {:db/id 17592186189501 :tutorial/content "Let's summarize everything we know about the sampling distribution of $\\widehat{\\,p}$:\n\n> *Suppose we have a population of size $N$ in which a proportion $p$ has a particular characteristic. Consider a sample of size $n$ drawn from the population, where*\n> - $n \\leq 5\\%\\cdot N$ (the sample size is smaller than (or equal to) $5\\%$ of the population size),\n> - $np > 5$, *and*\n> - $n(1-p) > 5$.\n> *Then, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion $\\widehat{\\,p}$ can be approximated as the normally distributed random variable $\\widehat{\\,p} \\sim N\\left(p, 17592186189500 :tutorial/content "Suppose we conduct a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N$ where some proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic. Let's denote the random variable $X_i$ as follows:\n\n$$\n{1, [math]i[/math]th member of the sample has the characteristic; 0, otherwise\n$$\n\nIn other words,\n\n$$\nX_i \\sim \\textrm{Bernoulli}(p)\n$$\n\nLet's assume the sample size is less than (or equal to) $5\\%$ of the population size. Under this condition, we've seen that $X_1,X_2,\\ldots,X_n$ can be considered to be (approximately) independent and identically distributed, which means that\n\n$$\nX = \\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i \\approx B(n,p)\n$$\n\nwhere $B(n,p)$ denotes a binomial distribution, and\n\n$$\n\\textrm{E}[X] = np, \\qquad \\textrm{Var}[X] = np(1-p)\n$$\n\nRemember that $X$ represents the number of sample members with the characteristic.\n\nNow, let's assume that $np > 5$ and $n(1-p) > 5$ so we can apply the normal approximation of the binomial distribution (i.e., the central limit theorem). Then,\n\n$$\nX \\approx N\\big(np,np(1-p)\\big)\n$$\n\nFurthermore, we've also seen that we can construct an estimator $\\widehat{\\,p}$ as\n\n$$\n\\widehat{\\,p} = \\dfrac{X}{n}\n$$\n\nwhere\n\n$$\n\\textrm{E}[\\widehat{\\,p}] = p, \\qquad \\textrm{Var}[\\widehat{\\,p}] = \\dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}\n$$\n\nSince $X$ is approximately normally distributed, $\\widehat{\\,p}$ is also normally distributed. Therefore, the sampling distribution of $\\widehat{\\,p}$ is given by\n\n$$\n\\widehat{\\,p}\\approx N\\bigg(p, \\dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}\\bigg)\n$$\n\nFinally, since we usually don't know $p$, we can use a particular estimate to approximate $\\textrm{E}[{\\widehat{\\,p}}]$ and $\\textrm{Var}[\\widehat{\\,p}]$.\n\n**Watch out!** In this lesson, $N$ denotes the size of a population, while $N(\\cdot,\\cdot)$ denotes the normal distribution." :tutorial/id #uuid "d4cf166b-07f1-5e2e-9b9a-8147d42ce348" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9526 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "5ce0e2df-ecaa-5cb0-b322-b2b78e5030ce" :step/math-academy-id 187404 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189056}} {:db/id 17592186189500 :tutorial/content "Suppose we conduct a random sample of size $n$ from a population of size $N$ where some proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic. :question/math-academy-id "e-21770" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186119965 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "cedd027b-bceb-5728-9d11-42c9a3c4c015" :knowledge-point/title "Constructing the ODE Solved by the Orthogonal Trajectories of a One-Parameter Family"}] :question/problem "Determine the differential equation satisfied by the orthogonal trajectories of the family of curves $y^2 = 9C^2\\tan(x),$ where $C\\neq0$ is a parameter, in terms of $x$ and $y$ only." :question/worked-solution "Orthogonal trajectories are families of curves that intersect another given family of curves at right angles. In other words, the tangent lines of curves from each family are perpendicular at every intersection point.\n\nLet's determine the slope of the family of curves given by $y^2 = 9C^2\\tan(x).$ First, we implicitly differentiate with respect to $x$ and solve for the derivative of $y{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{d}{dx}({y}^{2}) & =\\frac{d}{dx}\\,(9{C}^{2}\\operatorname{tan}⁡(x)) \\\\ 2y{y}^{′} & =9{C}^{2}{sec}^{2}⁡(x) \\\\ {y}^{′} & =\\frac{9{C}^{2}{sec}^{2}⁡(x)}{2y}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, we must eliminate $C.$ From the original family of curves equation, we have\n\n$$\ny^2 = 9C^2\\tan(x)\n\\quad\\Longrightarrow\\quad\nC^2 = \\dfrac{y^2}{9\\tan(x)}.\n$$\n\nSubstituting this into our slope equation, we get\n\n$$\ny' = \\dfrac{9\\left(\\dfrac{y^2}{9\\tan(x)}\\right)\\sec^2(x)}{2y}\n= \\dfrac{y\\sec^2(x)}{2\\tan(x)}.\n$$\n\nFor a curve to intersect this family orthogonally, its slope $y'_\\perp$ must be the negative reciprocal of the slope $y'$ above. Hence,\n\n$$\ny'_\\perp = -\\dfrac{1}{y'} = -\\dfrac{1}{\\left(\\dfrac{y\\sec^2(x)}{2\\tan(x)}\\right)}\n= -\\dfrac{2\\tan(x)}{y\\sec^2(x)}.\n$$\n\nTherefore, the orthogonal trajectories must satisfy\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{\\mathrm{d}y}{\\mathrm{d}x}= -\\dfrac{2\\tan(x)}{y\\sec^2(x)}.\n$$\n\n**Note**: Since we divide by $y$ when forming the orthogonal slope, the orthogonal-trajectory ODE is only valid where $y\\neq 0$ (and where $\\tan(x)$ is defined). In particular, the original family forces $y=0$ whenever $\\tan(x)=0$."} {:db/id 17592186048357} {:db/id 17592186049470} {:db/id 17592186120265 :question/id #uuid :question/worked-solution "Orthogonal trajectories are families of curves that intersect another given family of curves at right angles. In other words, the tangent lines of curves from each family are perpendicular at every intersection point.\n\nLet's determine the slope of the family of curves given by ${y}^{2}=-\\frac{4{C}^{2}}{x}.$ First, we implicitly differentiate with respect to $x$ and solve for the derivative of $y:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{d}{dx}({y}^{2}) & =\\frac{d}{dx}\\,(-\\frac{4{C}^{2}}{x}) \\\\ 2y{y}^{′} & =\\frac{4{C}^{2}}{{x}^{2}} \\\\ {y}^{′} & =\\frac{2{C}^{2}}{{x}^{2}y}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, we must eliminate $C.$ From the original family of curves equation, we have\n\n$$\n{y}^{2}=-\\frac{4{C}^{2}}{x}\\,⟹\\,{C}^{2}=-\\frac{x{y}^{2}}{4}.\n$$\n\nSubstituting this into our slope equation, we get\n\n$$\n{y}^{′}=\\frac{2(-\\frac{x{y}^{2}}{4})}{{x}^{2}y}=-\\frac{y}{2x}.\n$$\n\nFor a curve to intersect this family orthogonally, its slope ${y}_{⊥}^{′}$ must be the negative reciprocal of the slope ${y}^{′}$ above. Hence,\n\n$$\n{y}_{⊥}^{′}=-\\frac{1}{{y}^{′}}=-\\frac{1}{(-\\frac{y}{2x})}=\\frac{2x}{y}.\n$$\n\nTherefore, the orthogonal trajectories must satisfy\n\n$$\n\\frac{dy}{dx}=\\frac{2x}{y}.\n$$\n\n**Note**: For the original family, since $C\\ne 0,$ we have $y\\ne 0$ whenever $x\\ne 0,$ hence, the slopes are well-defined. Otherwise, when $x=0,$ the curve is not defined."} {:db/id 17592186374896 :question/id #uuid "8d4d5768-937a-5096-afaf-5a1645a9f0c8" :question/math-academy-id "q-337325"} {:db/id 17592186119966 trajectories are families of curves that intersect another given family of curves at right angles. In other words, the tangent lines of curves from each family are perpendicular at every intersection point.\n\nLet's determine the slope of the family of curves given by $y = \\dfrac{C}{x^2}.$ First, we implicitly differentiate with respect to $x$ and solve for the derivative of $y{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{d}{dx}(y) & =\\frac{d}{dx}\\,(\\frac{C}{{x}^{2}}) \\\\ {y}^{′} & =-\\frac{2C}{{x}^{3}}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, we must eliminate $C.$ From the original family of curves equation, we have\n\n$$\ny = \\dfrac{C}{x^2}\n\\quad\\Longrightarrow\\quad\nC = x^2y.\n$$\n\nSubstituting this into our slope equation, we get\n\n$$\ny' = -\\dfrac{2C}{x^3} = -\\dfrac{2x^2y}{x^3}\n= -\\dfrac{2y}{x}.\n$$\n\nFor a curve to intersect this family orthogonally, its slope $y'_\\perp$ must be the negative reciprocal of the slope $y'$ above. Hence,\n\n$$\ny'_\\perp = -\\dfrac{1}{y'} = -\\dfrac{1}{\\left(-\\dfrac{2y}{x}\\right)}\n= \\dfrac{x}{2y}.\n$$\n\nHence, the orthogonal trajectories must satisfy\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{\\mathrm{d}y}{\\mathrm{d}x}= \\dfrac{x}{2y}.\n$$\n\nTo find the general solution, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}2y\\cdot \\frac{dy}{dx} & =x \\\\ \\int 2y\\cdot \\frac{dy}{dx}\\,dx & =\\int x\\,dx \\\\ \\int 2y\\,dy & =\\int x\\,dx \\\\ {y}^{2} & =\\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+K \\\\ 2{y}^{2}-{x}^{2} & =K\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNote that $K$ is a constant of integration.\n\nTherefore, the orthogonal trajectories of the family of curves $y = \\dfrac{C}{x^2},$ where $C$ is a parameter, are given by\n\n$$\n2y^2 - x^2 = K,\n$$\n\nwhere $K$ is a parameter. 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Find the orthogonal trajectories of the family of curves ${y}^{2}=Cx,$ where $C\\ne 0$ and $K$ are parameters." :question/worked-solution "Orthogonal trajectories are families of curves that intersect another given family of curves at right angles. In other words, the tangent lines of curves from each family are perpendicular at every intersection point.\n\nLet's determine the slope of the family of curves given by ${y}^{2}=Cx.$ First, we implicitly differentiate with respect to $x$ and solve for the derivative of $y:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{d}{dx}({y}^{2}) & =\\frac{d}{dx}(Cx) \\\\ 2y{y}^{′} & =C \\\\ {y}^{′} & =\\frac{C}{2y}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, we must eliminate $C.$ From the original family of curves equation, we have\n\n$$\n{y}^{2}=Cx\\,⟹\\,C=\\frac{{y}^{2}}{x}.\n$$\n\nSubstituting this into our slope equation, we get\n\n$$\n{y}^{′}=\\frac{(\\frac{{y}^{2}}{x})}{2y}=\\frac{y}{2x}.\n$$\n\nFor a curve to intersect this family orthogonally, its slope ${y}_{⊥}^{′}$ must be the negative reciprocal of the slope ${y}^{′}$ above. Hence,\n\n$$\n{y}_{⊥}^{′}=-\\frac{1}{{y}^{′}}=-\\frac{1}{(\\frac{y}{2x})}=-\\frac{2x}{y}.\n$$\n\nHence, the orthogonal trajectories must satisfy\n\n$$\n\\frac{dy}{dx}=-\\frac{2x}{y}.\n$$\n\nTo find the general solution, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}y\\cdot \\frac{dy}{dx} & =-2x \\\\ \\int y\\cdot \\frac{dy}{dx}\\,dx & =\\int (-2x)\\,dx \\\\ \\int y\\,dy & =-2\\int x\\,dx \\\\ \\frac{{y}^{2}}{2} & =-{x}^{2}+K \\\\ {y}^{2}+2{x}^{2} & =K\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNote that $K$ is a constant of integration.\n\nTherefore, the orthogonal trajectories of the family of curves ${y}^{2}=Cx,$ where $C$ is a parameter, are given by\n\n$$\n{y}^{2}+2{x}^{2}=K,\n$$\n\nwhere $K$ is a parameter. Some curves from each family for specific parameter values are given in the diagram below.\n\n![](images/03/039a42b728cad07b3e8f5dfd2f1607b36819e586f40e54e06d942679bb4ededa.png)\n\n**Note**: Since $C\\ne 0,$ we have $y\\ne 0$ on every curve in the family (except possibly at $x=0$), so slopes ${y}^{′}$ and ${}_{⊥}^{′}$ are well-defined away from $y=0.$"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186120949 :step/content {:db/id 17592186120982 :tutorial/content "Recall that a *one-parameter family* of curves in the $xy$-plane is defined by $$F(x,y,C) = 0,$$ where $C$ denotes the parameter.\n\nThe **orthogonal trajectories** of a one-parameter family of curves form another one-parameter family of curves such that every curve in one family intersects at right angles every curve in the other.\n\nFor example, circles $x^2+y^2=C^2$ (with parameter $C$) and lines through the origin $y=Kx$ (with parameter $K$) are orthogonal trajectories.\n\n![](images/ca/ca980af3c5db940a9ab95567dfaa1a69ea8afb9f4f42f772bb446df67df129b8.png)\n\nNow, let $F(x,y,C) = 0$ be a family of curves with parameter $C.$ Suppose we can\n\n- implicitly differentiate it with respect to $x,$ and\n- eliminate $C$ using the derived and defining equations,\n\nto get an equation in terms of $x,$ $y,$ and $\\dfrac{\\mathrm{d}y}{\\mathrm{d}x}.$ Next, assume we can solve for the derivative and obtain a differential equation of the form $$\\dfrac{\\mathrm{d}y}{\\mathrm{d}x} = f(x,y)$$ that explicitly gives the slopes of the curves satisfying this ODE (at least locally, where the slope is defined).\n\nFor a curve to intersect at right angles with every curve in the family, its slope must be the negative reciprocal of the slope of curves in the family. "Calculate $\\textrm{Cov}(x,y)$ for the following data sets:\n\n$$\nx = \\big\\{ 6, \\: -2, \\: 7, \\: 1 \\big\\},\\qquad\ny = \\big\\{ 5, \\: -1, \\: 4, \\: 0 \\big\\}\n$$" :question/worked-solution "The (population) covariance of the data sets $x=\\big\\{ x_1,x_2, \\ldots, x_n \\big\\}$ and $y=\\big\\{ y_1,y_2, \\ldots, y_n \\big\\}$ is given by \n\n$$\n\\textrm{Cov}(x,y) =  \\dfrac{1}{n} \\sum\\limits_{i=1}^n (x_i - \\overline{x})(y_i - \\overline{y}),\n$$\n\nwhere $\\overline{x} = \\dfrac{1}{n} \\displaystyle \\sum_{i=1}^n x_i$ and $\\overline{y} = \\dfrac{1}{n} \\displaystyle \\sum_{i=1}^n y_i$ are the means of the data sets.\n\nFirst, we need to compute the means:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\overset{―}{x} & =\\frac{1}{n}{\\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{4}\\cdot (6+(-2)+7+1) \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{4}\\cdot 12 \\\\  & =3 \\\\ \\overset{―}{y} & =\\frac{1}{n}{\\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{y}_{i} \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{4}\\cdot (5+(-1)+4+0) \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{4}\\cdot 8 \\\\  & =2\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the covariance of our data sets is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\text{Cov}(x,y) & =\\frac{1}{n}{\\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\\overset{―}{y}) \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{4}[(6-3)(5-2)+(-2-3)(-1-2)+(7-3)(4-2)+(1-3)(0-2)] \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{4}[(3)(3)+(-5)(-3)+(4)(2)+(-2)(-2)] \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{4}[9+15+8+4] \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{4}\\cdot 36 \\\\  & =9.\\end{aligned}\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186050862} {:db/id 17592186176333 :question/id #uuid "9b3a2205-203a-5056-a951-45e86cc0afea" :question/math-academy-id "q-134066" :knowledge-point/_questions 3591} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186176655 :step/content {:db/id 17592186176950 :tutorial/content "Given two finite data sets of equal length, say,\n\n$$\nx=\\big\\{ x_1,x_2, \\ldots, x_n \\big\\}, \\qquad \ny=\\big\\{ y_1,y_2, \\ldots, y_n \\big\\},\n$$\n\nthe **covariance** between $x$ and $y,$ denoted by $\\textrm{Cov}(x,y),$ is a measure that evaluates the extent to which $x$ and $y$ change together.\n\n- A positive covariance means that if $x$ increases, then $y$ is also likely to increase:\n\n![](images/bb/bbfae3f0fb38bc8652cd26716e4b0b128cf1f2039350267034d97161d7f5dac4.png)\n\n- A negative covariance means that if $x$ increases, then $y$ is likely to decrease:\n\n![](images/fd/fd45053fdc39f070e3438c3b8c61fe01613201595cfe00bd4cc6c6e481bf73ab.png)\n\n- A covariance of zero (or close to zero) indicates that there is no *linear* relationship between $x$ and $y.$\n\n![](images/a5/a58fa4d40d77af23df86b5bd8eaca3119b93bc9ea97cc435eb4e53ba2777b071.png)\n\n**Watch Out!** A covariance of zero does *not* mean that $x$ and $y$ are not related. It simply means the relationship between them is not linear. To illustrate, consider the image below.\n\n![](images/a4/a4bdbf92e691174644dda9b9a84acb1b896c0436afb221501dc10b4635841539.png)\n\nThe (nonlinear) relationship shown above is $y=x^2.$ However, it can be shown that $\\textrm{Cov}(x,y) = 0$ for this data set.\n\nTo calculate $\\textrm{Cov}(x,y),$ we use the following formula: \n\n$$\n\\textrm{Cov}(x,y) =  \\dfrac{1}{n} \\sum\\limits_{i=1}^n (x_i - \\overline{x})(y_i - \\overline{y}),\n$$\n\nwhere $\\overline{x}$  and $\\overline{y}$ denote the means of $x$ and $y$ respectively.\n\n**Note**: This formula for the covariance assumes that $x$ and $y$ are drawn from a *population*. There is a slightly different formula for covariance when $x$ and $y$ are sample data. However, we won't worry about the difference for now." :tutorial/id #uuid "da03b3e7-b452-59b9-b81e-5dd75cea02a2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 10301 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid other hand, covariance measures the relationship between *two* data sets $x$ and $y.$\n\nThe (population) covariance of the data sets\n\n$$\nx=\\big\\{ x_1,x_2, \\ldots, x_n \\big\\}, \\qquad  \ny=\\big\\{ y_1,y_2, \\ldots, y_n \\big\\}\n$$\n\n \n\nis given by \n\n$$\n\\textrm{Cov}(x,y) =  \\dfrac{1}{n} \\sum\\limits_{i=1}^n (x_i - \\overline{x})(y_i - \\overline{y}).\n$$\n\nIf we compare a single data set, say $x$, against itself using our formula for covariance, we obtain\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\text{Cov}(x,x) & =\\frac{1}{n}{\\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\\overset{―}{x})({x}_{i}-\\overset{―}{x}) \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{n}{\\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\\overset{―}{x})^{2} \\\\  & ={\\sigma }^{2},\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwhere $\\sigma^2$ denotes the variance of $x.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "42b9ca98-be0b-50e0-9b90-f3e38732fcd0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 10305 :tutorial/title "The Connection Between Variance and Covariance"} :step/id #uuid 17592186176655 :step/content {:db/id 17592186176950 :tutorial/content "Given two finite data sets of equal length, say,\n\n$$\nx=\\big\\{ x_1,x_2, \\ldots, x_n \\big\\}, \\qquad \ny=\\big\\{ y_1,y_2, \\ldots, y_n \\big\\},\n$$\n\nthe **covariance** between $x$ and $y,$ denoted by $\\textrm{Cov}(x,y),$ is a measure that evaluates the extent to which $x$ and $y$ change together.\n\n- A positive covariance means that if $x$ increases, then $y$ is also likely to increase:\n\n![](images/bb/bbfae3f0fb38bc8652cd26716e4b0b128cf1f2039350267034d97161d7f5dac4.png)\n\n- A negative covariance means that if $x$ increases, then $y$ is likely to decrease:\n\n![](images/fd/fd45053fdc39f070e3438c3b8c61fe01613201595cfe00bd4cc6c6e481bf73ab.png)\n\n- A covariance of zero (or close to zero) indicates that there is no *linear* relationship between $x$ and $y.$\n\n![](images/a5/a58fa4d40d77af23df86b5bd8eaca3119b93bc9ea97cc435eb4e53ba2777b071.png)\n\n**Watch Out!** A covariance of zero does *not* mean that $x$ and $y$ are not related. It simply means the relationship between them is not linear. To illustrate, consider the image below.\n\n![](images/a4/a4bdbf92e691174644dda9b9a84acb1b896c0436afb221501dc10b4635841539.png)\n\nThe (nonlinear) relationship shown above is $y=x^2.$ However, it can be shown that $\\textrm{Cov}(x,y) = 0$ for this data set.\n\nTo calculate $\\textrm{Cov}(x,y),$ we use the following formula: \n\n$$\n\\textrm{Cov}(x,y) =  \\dfrac{1}{n} \\sum\\limits_{i=1}^n (x_i - \\overline{x})(y_i - \\overline{y}),\n$$\n\nwhere $\\overline{x}$  and $\\overline{y}$ denote the means of $x$ and $y$ respectively.\n\n**Note**: This formula for the covariance assumes that $x$ and $y$ are drawn from a *population*. There is a slightly different formula for covariance when $x$ and $y$ are sample data. [{:db/id 17592186069563 :step/content {:db/id 17592186070020 :tutorial/content "The **point-slope form** of a line that passes through any point $(x_1,y_1)$ with slope $m$ is given by \n\n$$\ny - y_1 = m(x-x_1).\n$$\n\n \n\nFor example, consider the straight line graph which passes through the points $(3,1)$ and $(5,5)$, as shown below.\n\n![](images/e7/e7838ffcb8f56ebffd384763ff761990e15031bdc5cdf3f0cc1f964ed69a4806.png)\n\nWe know that the line passes through the point $(3,1),$ so we can use $(x_1,y_1) = (3,1)$ in our point-slope formula. All that remains is to compute $m,$ and we can do this using the given points.\n\nFirst, calculate the slope $m$ using the given points:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}m=\\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}}=\\frac{5-1}{5-3}=\\frac{4}{2}=2\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThen, we substitute $m=2$ and the point $(x_1,y_1) = (3,1)$ into the point-slope formula:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\\\ y-1 & =2(x-3)\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n**Note:** If we simplify this point-slope formula, we obtain the slope-intercept form of the line:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}y-1 & =2(x-3) \\\\ y-1 & =2x-6 \\\\ y & =2x-5\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n**Watch out!** We could put $(x_1,y_1)=(5,5).$ In this case, the point-slope form will be different:\n\n$$\ny-5=2(x-5)\n$$\n\n \nBut the resulting simplified slope-intercept form will be the same:\n\n$$\ny = 2x-5\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "43f9e39e-fc27-549d-8ec4-b2bf4f375a33" :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation $T,$ where $T$ is defined as\n\n$$\nT:[\\begin{aligned}u \\\\ v\\end{aligned}]⟶[\\begin{aligned}{u}^{2}+{v}^{2} \\\\ uv\\end{aligned}].\n$$" :question/worked-solution "Given a transformation \n\n$$\nT:[\\begin{aligned}u \\\\ v\\end{aligned}]\\to [\\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\\\ y(u,v)\\end{aligned}],\n$$\n\nthe Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \\frac{∂x}{∂v} \\\\ \\frac{∂y}{∂u} & \\frac{∂y}{∂v}\\end{aligned}|.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTo find the locations of the critical points of $T,$ we need to solve \n\n$$\n\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.\n$$\n\nHere, we have $x(u,v)={u}^{2}+{v}^{2}$ and $y(u,v)=uv.$\n\nFirst, we find the partial derivatives:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2u & \\,\\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =2v \\\\ \\frac{∂y}{∂u} & =v & \\,\\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =v\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \\frac{∂x}{∂v} \\\\ \\frac{∂y}{∂u} & \\frac{∂y}{∂v}\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =|\\begin{aligned}2u & 2v \\\\ v & u\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =2u\\cdot u-2v\\cdot v \\\\  & =2{u}^{2}-2{v}^{2}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThe function has critical points when $\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.$ So, we obtain\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =0 \\\\ 2{u}^{2}-2{v}^{2} & =0 \\\\ {v}^{2} & ={u}^{2}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThe equation ${v}^{2}={u}^{2}$ defines a pair of intersecting lines $v=u$ and $v=-u$ in the $uv$-plane."} {:db/id 17592186199001 :question/id #uuid given by\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \\frac{∂x}{∂v} \\\\ \\frac{∂y}{∂u} & \\frac{∂y}{∂v}\\end{aligned}|.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nIn this case, we're derivatives:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =2 & \\,\\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =-1 \\\\ \\frac{∂v}{∂x} & =1 & \\,\\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =2\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the Jacobian determinant of \\\\ 1 & 2\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =2\\cdot 2-(-1)\\cdot 1 \\\\  & =5.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, we take the reciprocal:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & 17592186045485} :question/problem "![](images/0a/0a79260df29825684d6bdf6197df8581adf5a5a2d1d89938c299f18b3f33bf7c.png)\n\nThe function $f(x),$ whose graph is shown above, has a stationary point at $x=2$ and is continuously differentiable everywhere except at $x=3.$  By considering the points indicated in the diagram, determine which of the following statements **must** be true according to the inverse function theorem.\n\n- $f$ is invertible in some neighborhood of $x=1$\n- ${f}^{-1}(y)$ is continuously differentiable in a neighborhood of $y=-2$\n- The derivative of ${f}^{-1}(y)$ at $y=2.91$ equals $\\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(3)}$\n\nSelect all that apply.\n\nIf none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "The inverse function theorem for single-variable functions states the following:\n\n*If $f:U\\to R$ is continuously differentiable on an open set $U⊆R,$ $f(a)=b$ and ${f}^{′}(a)\\ne 0$ for $a\\in U,$ then*\n\n- *$f$ is invertible in some neighborhood of $a,$*\n\n- *${f}^{-1},$ the inverse of $f,$ is continuously differentiable in a neighborhood of $b,$ and*\n\n- *the derivative of ${f}^{-1}$ is given by* \n\n$$\n{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(b)=\\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(a)}=\\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(b))}\\,.\n$$\n\nWith that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.\n\n- Statement I is true. The function $f$ satisfies the conditions for the inverse function theorem at $x=1.$ Indeed,\n\n- $f$ is continuously differentiable on an open set containing $x=1,$ for example, $(0,2),$ and\n\n- the derivative of $f$ is nonzero at $x=1,$ i.e., ${f}^{′}(1)\\ne 0.$\n\nTherefore, by the inverse function theorem, $f$ is invertible in *some* neighborhood of $x=1.$\n\n- Statement II is false. Notice that $y=-2=f(2).$  However, the function $f$ does *not* satisfy the conditions for the inverse function theorem at $x=2$ since ${f}^{′}(2)=0.$ So, the theorem can't be applied in this situation.\n\n- Statement III is false. Notice that $y=2.91=f(3),$ but $f$ is not continuous at $x=3.$ So, the theorem can't be applied in this situation.\n\nTherefore, the correct answer is \"I only.\""} {:db/id 17592186281362 :question/id transformation $\\mathbf T,$ given by\n\n![](images/fe/fefb7b82a6da1421bb96798fe6377e66199b50b8630dc396518927a0f3fe204b.svg)\n\nThe points in the $(u,v)$ plane where $\\mathbf T$ is *locally* non-invertible are known as **critical points**. \n\nWe've already seen that $\\mathbf T$ is locally non-invertible when the Jacobian determinant is zero. Therefore, the critical points of $\\mathbf T$ are the solutions to the equation\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{\\partial (x, y)}{\\partial (u, v)}=0.\n$$\n\n  \n\nLet's compute the critical points of the following transformation:\n\n![](images/8e/8e55b2da9a0c1fcf1ab901d361c50b652c906b92f0fcd4b158793f7782cfe5f4.svg)\n\nFirst, we find the partial derivatives: \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =4u & \\,\\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-6v \\\\ \\frac{∂y}{∂u} & =-1 & \\,\\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \\frac{∂x}{∂v} \\\\ \\frac{∂y}{∂u} & \\frac{∂y}{∂v}\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =|\\begin{aligned}4u & -6v \\\\ -1 & 1\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =4u\\cdot 1-(-6v)\\cdot (-1) \\\\  & =4u-6v.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThe function has critical points when the Jacobian equals zero. So, we obtain\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =0 \\\\ 4u-6v & =0 \\\\ 2u-3v & =0.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the critical points of $\\mathbf{T}$ consist of those points that lie on the line $2u-3v=0$  in the $uv$-plane, shown below. \n\n![](images/5c/5c544e3d3ecbdeaf7dc372b40ee0f37cb14e3ba292b8180a263c91103a9efe61.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "5f47e688-774b-5c89-a90d-ead52a871598" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4312 :tutorial/title "Critical Points of Transformations"} :step/id #uuid "16b2c818-03e6-5801-97b2-0ce8d225c3d5" :step/math-academy-id 26206 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199248}} {:db/id 17592186199266 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199460 :tutorial/content "Let's now state the so-called **inverse function theorem** for single-variable functions:\n\n*If $f: U \\to \\Bbb R$ is continuously differentiable on an open set $U\\subseteq \\mathbb R,$ $f(a) = b$ and $f'(a)\\neq 0$ for $a\\in U,$ then*\n\n- *$f$ is invertible in some neighborhood of $a,$*\n\n- *$f^{-1},$ the inverse of $f,$ is continuously differentiable in a neighborhood of $b,$ and*\n\n- *the derivative of $f^{-1}$ is given by* \n\n$$\n\\left(f^{-1}\\right)'(b) = \\dfrac{1}{f'(a)} =\\dfrac{1}{f'(f^{-1}(b))}\\,.\n$$\n\nTo explain this concretely, consider the graph below:\n\n![](images/4d/4dfd8b142b594a2ca4f0e39f9b8ca1e04018bf0efd63f9dc2235bd61e9f9d70e.png)\n\nIn this example, the function $f$ is continuously differentiable at $x=a$ and has a nonzero derivative. As a result, $f^{-1}$ exists in a neighborhood of $x=b$ and is continuously differentiable at this point.\n\nOn the other hand, if $f$ is continuously differentiable at $x=a$ but $f'(a) = 0,$ then one of two things can happen:\n\n- **Case 1**: The function $f$ does not have a local inverse at $a.$\n\n![](images/04/04ee310e6068e517aec42a67fa83837986f8807e1250b89b52e7a62e3975bb38.png)\n\nIn the example above, $f$ is not one-to-one in a neighborhood of $a,$ so it's not invertible there.\n\n- **Case 2**: The function $f$ has a local inverse at $a,$ but its inverse is not continuously differentiable at $b.$\n\n![](images/3e/3e2738a16f999d503fb295f4fd6535a854884468a4d190ffa537a4ec9295490c.png)\n\nIn the example above, $f$ is invertible in a neighborhood of $a,$ but $f^{-1}$ is not differentiable at $x=b$ since it has a vertical tangent at this point." :tutorial/id #uuid "c45037f7-31c7-5911-a00d-edaa4c5b86e4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7036 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "54cb06ef-1ffc-5b15-9147-a1baf70b985c" :step/math-academy-id 42404 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199315}} {:db/id 17592186199268 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198370 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198012 :question/id #uuid "f794d50a-cb44-5a6f-a922-8438a6192d46" :question/math-academy-id "e-11157"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "2fe16334-8f63-56ed-bd58-95e095993b9f" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186199002} {:db/id 17592186199003} {:db/id 17592186278312} {:db/id 17592186278313} {:db/id 17592186278314} {:db/id 17592186278315} {:db/id 17592186278316} {:db/id 17592186351292} {:db/id 17592186351297} {:db/id 17592186479853} {:db/id 17592186486385}] :knowledge-point/title "Jacobian Determinants of Inverse Transformations"} :step/id #uuid "1b07afe2-9993-5d3c-bfe7-b98917224b3b" :step/math-academy-id 42423} {:db/id 17592186199314 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199477 :tutorial/content "The inverse function theorem can be generalized to transformations too. *\n![](images/82/829c083606df36014d5b5b078b80c1c0ff1edb72f981880b4a1a6a16affb32dc.svg)\n\n*Further, suppose that $(u_0,v_0)$ is **not** a critical point of $\\mathbf T.$* Then,\n\n- *$\\mathbf T$ is So, we obtain\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =0 \\\\ 4u-6v & =0 \\\\ 2u-3v & =0.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the critical points of $\\mathbf{T}$ consist of those points that lie on the line $2u-3v=0$  in the $uv$-plane, shown below. \n\n![](images/5c/5c544e3d3ecbdeaf7dc372b40ee0f37cb14e3ba292b8180a263c91103a9efe61.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "5f47e688-774b-5c89-a90d-ead52a871598" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4312 :tutorial/title "Critical Points of Transformations"} :step/id #uuid "16b2c818-03e6-5801-97b2-0ce8d225c3d5" :step/math-academy-id 26206 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199248}} {:db/id 17592186199450 :tutorial/content "Consider a transformation $\\mathbf T,$ given by\n\n![](images/fe/fefb7b82a6da1421bb96798fe6377e66199b50b8630dc396518927a0f3fe204b.svg)\n\nThe points in the $(u,v)$ plane where $\\mathbf T$ is *locally* non-invertible are known as **critical points**. \n\nWe've already seen that $\\mathbf T$ is locally non-invertible when the Jacobian determinant is zero. example above, $f$ is not one-to-one in a neighborhood of $a,$ so it's not invertible there.\n\n- **Case 2**: The function $f$ has a local inverse at $a,$ but its inverse is not continuously differentiable at $b.$\n\n![](images/3e/3e2738a16f999d503fb295f4fd6535a854884468a4d190ffa537a4ec9295490c.png)\n\nIn the example above, $f$ is invertible in a neighborhood of $a,$ but $f^{-1}$ is not transformation \n\n$$\nT:[\\begin{aligned}u \\\\ v\\end{aligned}]\\to [\\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\\\ y(u,v)\\end{aligned}],\n$$\n\nthe Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \\frac{∂x}{∂v} \\\\ \\frac{∂y}{∂u} & \\frac{∂y}{∂v}\\end{aligned}|.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTo find the derivatives:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =6u & \\,\\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =4v \\\\ \\frac{∂y}{∂u} & =1 & \\,\\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \\frac{∂x}{∂v} \\\\ \\frac{∂y}{∂u} & \\frac{∂y}{∂v}\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =|\\begin{aligned}6u & 4v obtain\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =0 \\\\ 6u-4v & =0 \\\\ v & =\\frac{3}{2}u.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThe equation $v=\\frac{3}{2}u$ defines a line in the $uv$-plane."} :step/id stationary point at $x=2$ and is continuously differentiable everywhere except at $x=3.$  By considering the points indicated in the diagram, determine which of the following statements **must** be true according to the inverse function theorem.\n\n- $f$ is invertible in some neighborhood of $x=1$\n- ${f}^{-1}(y)$ is continuously differentiable in a neighborhood of $y=-2$\n- The derivative of ${f}^{-1}(y)$ at $y=2.91$ equals $\\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(3)}$\n\nSelect all that apply.\n\nIf none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "The inverse function theorem for single-variable functions states the following:\n\n*If $f:U\\to R$ is continuously differentiable on an open set $U⊆R,$ $f(a)=b$ and ${f}^{′}(a)\\ne 0$ for $a\\in U,$ then*\n\n- *$f$ is invertible in some neighborhood of $a,$*\n\n- *${f}^{-1},$ the inverse of $f,$ is continuously differentiable in a neighborhood of $b,$ and*\n\n- *the derivative of ${f}^{-1}$ is given by* \n\n$$\n{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(b)=\\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(a)}=\\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(b))}\\,.\n$$\n\nWith that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.\n\n- Statement I is true. The function $f$ satisfies the conditions for the inverse function theorem at $x=1.$ Indeed,\n\n- $f$ is continuously differentiable on an open set containing $x=1,$ for example, $(0,2),$ and\n\n- the derivative of $f$ is nonzero at $x=1,$ i.e., ${f}^{′}(1)\\ne 0.$\n\nTherefore, by the inverse function theorem, $f$ is invertible in *some* neighborhood of $x=1.$\n\n- Statement II is false. Notice that $y=-2=f(2).$  However, the function $f$ does *not* satisfy the conditions for the inverse function theorem at $x=2$ since ${f}^{′}(2)=0.$ So, the theorem can't be applied in this situation.\n\n- Statement III is false. Notice that $y=2.91=f(3),$ but $f$ is not continuous at $x=3.$ So, the theorem can't be applied in this situation.\n\nTherefore, the correct answer is \"I only.\""} :step/id #uuid "Given a transformation \n\n$$\nT:[\\begin{aligned}u \\\\ v\\end{aligned}]\\to [\\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\\\ y(u,v)\\end{aligned}],\n$$\n\nthe Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \\frac{∂x}{∂v} \\\\ \\frac{∂y}{∂u} & \\frac{∂y}{∂v}\\end{aligned}|.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTo find the locations of the critical points of $T,$ we need to solve \n\n$$\n\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.\n$$\n\nHere, we have $x(u,v)={u}^{2}+{v}^{2}$ and $y(u,v)=uv.$\n\nFirst, we find the partial derivatives:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2u & \\,\\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =2v \\\\ \\frac{∂y}{∂u} & =v & \\,\\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =v\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \\frac{∂x}{∂v} \\\\ \\frac{∂y}{∂u} & \\frac{∂y}{∂v}\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =|\\begin{aligned}2u & 2v \\\\ v & u\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =2u\\cdot u-2v\\cdot v \\\\  & =2{u}^{2}-2{v}^{2}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThe function has critical points when $\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.$ So, we obtain\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =0 \\\\ 2{u}^{2}-2{v}^{2} & =0 \\\\ {v}^{2} & ={u}^{2}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThe equation ${v}^{2}={u}^{2}$ defines a pair of intersecting lines $v=u$ and $v=-u$ in the $uv$-plane."} :step/id #uuid "4da312bf-59b4-5062-8ec0-dbcdcb029a0e" :step/next {:db/id 17592186486481}} {:db/id 2 & 1\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =2\\cdot 1-3\\cdot 2 \\\\  & =-4.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, we take the reciprocal:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & ={(\\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1} \\frac{∂y}{∂v}\\end{aligned}|.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTo find the locations of the critical points of $T,$ we need to solve \n\n$$\n\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.\n$$\n\nHere, we have $x(u,v)={u}^{2}+{v}^{2}$ and $y(u,v)=uv.$\n\nFirst, we find the partial derivatives:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2u & \\,\\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =2v \\\\ \\frac{∂y}{∂u} & =v & \\,\\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =v\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \\frac{∂x}{∂v} \\\\ \\frac{∂y}{∂u} & \\frac{∂y}{∂v}\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =|\\begin{aligned}2u & 2v \\\\ v & u\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =2u\\cdot u-2v\\cdot v \\\\  & =2{u}^{2}-2{v}^{2}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThe function has critical points when $\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}=0.$ So, we obtain\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =0 \\\\ 2{u}^{2}-2{v}^{2} & =0 \\\\ {v}^{2} & ={u}^{2}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThe equation ${v}^{2}={u}^{2}$ defines a pair of intersecting lines $v=u$ and $v=-u$ in the $uv$-plane."} :step/id #uuid "4da312bf-59b4-5062-8ec0-dbcdcb029a0e" :step/next {:db/id 17592186486481}} {:db/id and is continuously differentiable everywhere except at $x=3.$  By considering the points indicated in the diagram, determine which of the following statements **must** be true according to the inverse function theorem.\n\n- $f$ is invertible in some neighborhood of $x=1$\n- ${f}^{-1}(y)$ is continuously differentiable in a neighborhood of $y=-2$\n- The derivative of ${f}^{-1}(y)$ at $y=2.91$ equals $\\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(3)}$\n\nSelect all that apply.\n\nIf none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "The inverse function theorem for single-variable functions states the following:\n\n*If $f:U\\to R$ is continuously differentiable on an open set $U⊆R,$ $f(a)=b$ and ${f}^{′}(a)\\ne 0$ for $a\\in U,$ then*\n\n- *$f$ is invertible in some neighborhood of $a,$*\n\n- *${f}^{-1},$ the inverse of $f,$ is continuously differentiable in a neighborhood of $b,$ and*\n\n- *the derivative of ${f}^{-1}$ is given by* \n\n$$\n{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(b)=\\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(a)}=\\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(b))}\\,.\n$$\n\nWith that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.\n\n- Statement I is true. The function $f$ satisfies the conditions for the inverse function theorem at $x=1.$ Indeed,\n\n- $f$ is continuously differentiable on an open set containing $x=1,$ for example, $(0,2),$ and\n\n- the derivative of $f$ is nonzero at $x=1,$ i.e., ${f}^{′}(1)\\ne 0.$\n\nTherefore, by the inverse function theorem, $f$ is invertible in *some* neighborhood of $x=1.$\n\n- Statement II is false. Notice that $y=-2=f(2).$  However, the function $f$ does *not* satisfy the conditions for the inverse function theorem at $x=2$ since ${f}^{′}(2)=0.$ So, the theorem can't be applied in this situation.\n\n- Statement III is false. Notice that $y=2.91=f(3),$ but $f$ is not continuous at $x=3.$ So, the theorem can't be applied in this situation.\n\nTherefore, the correct answer is \"I only.\""} :step/id #uuid (u(x,y),v(x,y))$ is given by\n\n$$\n{T}^{-1}:[\\begin{aligned}x \\\\ y\\end{aligned}]⟶[\\begin{aligned}\\frac{x}{{y}^{2}} \\\\ 3xy\\end{aligned}].\n$$\n\nFind the Jacobian determinant of $T$ in terms of $u$ and $v.$" :question/worked-solution "Given a transformation \n\n$$\nT:[\\begin{aligned}u \\\\ v\\end{aligned}]\\to [\\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\\\ y(u,v)\\end{aligned}],\n$$\n\nthe Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \\frac{∂x}{∂v} \\\\ \\frac{∂y}{∂u} & \\frac{∂y}{∂v}\\end{aligned}|.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nIn this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:\n\n- First, we compute $\\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$\n\n- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation\n\n$$\n\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}.\n$$\n\nHere, we have $u(x,y)=\\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}$ and $v(x,y)=3xy.$ \n\nFirst, we compute the partial derivatives:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =\\frac{1}{{y}^{2}} & \\,\\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =-\\frac{2x}{{y}^{3}} \\\\ \\frac{∂v}{∂x} & =3y & \\,\\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =3x\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \\frac{∂u}{∂y} \\\\ \\frac{∂v}{∂x} & \\frac{∂v}{∂y}\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =|\\begin{aligned}\\frac{1}{{y}^{2}} & -\\frac{2x}{{y}^{3}} \\\\ 3y & 3x\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\\cdot 3x-(-\\frac{2x}{{y}^{3}})\\cdot 3y \\\\  & =\\frac{9x}{{y}^{2}} \\\\  & =9\\cdot \\frac{x}{{y}^{2}} \\\\  & =9u.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, we take the reciprocal:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & ={(\\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1} \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{9u}\\end{aligned}\n$$"} :step/id #uuid "8799c879-5fd1-5dbd-8c44-d6fe6d0c6a5b" :step/next {:db/id 17592186486477}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "Let $Q$ be the amount of nutrient in the tank at time $t,$ in minutes. Then, the derivative \n\n$$\n\\dfrac{\\mathrm{d}Q}{\\mathrm{d}t}\n$$\n\ndescribes how this amount changes with respect to time $t.$ This is equal to the rate at which nutrient enters the tank minus the rate at which nutrient leaves the tank.\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{\\mathrm{d}Q}{\\mathrm{d}t} = Q'_{\\textrm{in}} - Q'_{\\textrm{out}}\n$$\n\nNote that the units of $\\dfrac{\\mathrm{d}Q}{\\mathrm{d}t}, Q'_{\\textrm{in}}$ and $Q'_{\\textrm{out}}$ are $\\textrm{kg}/\\textrm{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.\n\n**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which additives enter the tank.\n\nNote that a feed solution containing $0.01\\,\\textrm{kg/L}$ of the nutrient enters the tank at a rate of $40\\,\\textrm{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *nutrient* enters the tank is \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.01\\,\\frac{\\text{kg}}{\\text{L}})\\cdot (40\\,\\frac{\\text{L}}{\\text{min}}) \\\\  & =(0.01\\,\\frac{\\text{kg}}{\\cancel{\\text{L}}})\\cdot (40\\,\\frac{\\cancel{\\text{L}}}{\\text{min}}) \\\\  & =0.4\\,\\frac{\\text{kg}}{\\text{min}}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which additives exit the tank.\n\nNext, note that the rate of flow in equals the rate of flow out, so the volume in the tank remains $800\\,\\textrm{L}.$ Then, since $Q$ is the amount of nutrient in the tank, the *concentration* of the solution at time $t$ is\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{Q}{800}\\,\\textrm{kg/L}.\n$$\n\nTherefore, as the completely mixed liquid leaves at a rate of $40\\,\\textrm{L/min},$ *nutrient* leaves at a rate of\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\\text{out}}^{′} & =(40\\,\\frac{\\text{L}}{\\text{min}})\\cdot (\\frac{Q}{800}\\,\\frac{\\text{kg}}{\\text{L}}) \\\\  & =(40\\,\\frac{\\cancel{\\text{L}}}{\\text{min}})\\cdot (\\frac{Q}{800}\\,\\frac{\\text{kg}}{\\cancel{\\text{L}}}) \\\\  & =\\frac{40Q}{800}\\,\\frac{\\text{kg}}{\\text{min}} \\\\  & =\\frac{Q}{20}\\,\\frac{\\text{kg}}{\\text{min}}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.\n\nThe rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\\text{out}}^{′} \\\\  & =0.4-\\frac{Q}{20}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwhich gives the equation\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{\\mathrm{d}Q}{\\mathrm{d}t} + \\dfrac{1}{20}Q = 0.4.\n$$\n\n**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.\n\nThis is a first-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.\n\n- To find the complementary solution $Q_c,$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{\\mathrm{d}Q_c}{\\mathrm{d}t} + \\dfrac{1}{20}Q_c = 0.\n$$\n\nSolving using an integration technique, such as separation of variables, we obtain the complementary solution\n\n$$\nQ_c(t) = Ae^{-t/20},\n$$\n\nwhere $A$ is a constant of integration.\n\n- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $0.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $0,$ i.e.,\n\n$$\nQ_p(t) = \\alpha.\n$$\n\nTo find the value of $\\alpha,$ we substitute $Q_p = \\alpha$ and $\\dfrac{\\mathrm{d}Q_p}{\\mathrm{d}t} = (\\alpha)' = 0$ into the inhomogeneous equation:\n\n$$\n0 + \\dfrac{1}{20}\\alpha = 0.4\n  \\quad\\Longrightarrow\\quad\n  \\alpha = 8.\n$$\n\nTherefore, the particular solution is $Q_p(t) = 8.$\n\nNow, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is\n\n$$\nQ(t) = Q_c(t) + Q_p(t) = Ae^{-t/20} + 8.\n$$\n\nWe're told that the tank initially contains $7\\,\\textrm{kg}$ of dissolved nutrient. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0) = 7,$ and solve for $A{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =7 \\\\ A{e}^{-0/20}+8 & =7 \\\\ A & =-1\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t){:}$\n\n$$\nQ(t) = 8 - e^{-t/20}.\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186048569} {:db/id 17592186049370} {:db/id 17592186229724 :question/id #uuid "872cac41-3a52-503a-bac8-64cc582ee5f1" :question/math-academy-id "q-339385" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186229181 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "1403309b-bb10-5ce3-bd8f-97915bb837ca" :knowledge-point/title "Constructing and Solving a Dilution Model: Inflow Equals Outflow"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "99808cf8-bbc9-54ff-a1ba-83f2a5fdeb6b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "Q(t) = 22.5 -  & =0.6\\,\\frac{\\text{kg}}{\\text{min}}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which additives exit the tank.\n\nNext, note that the rate of flow in equals the rate of flow out, Then, the derivative \n\n$$\n\\dfrac{\\mathrm{d}Q}{\\mathrm{d}t}\n$$\n\ndescribes how this amount changes with respect to time $t.$ This is equal to the rate at which coagulant enters the tank minus the rate at which coagulant leaves the tank.\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{\\mathrm{d}Q}{\\mathrm{d}t} = Q'_{\\textrm{in}} - Q'_{\\textrm{out}}\n$$\n\nNote that the units of $\\dfrac{\\mathrm{d}Q}{\\mathrm{d}t}, Q'_{\\textrm{in}}$ and $Q'_{\\textrm{out}}$ are $\\textrm{kg}/\\textrm{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.\n\n**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which coagulant enters the tank.\n\nNote that a feed solution containing $0.05\\,\\textrm{kg/L}$ of the coagulant enters the tank at a rate of $30\\,\\textrm{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *coagulant* enters the tank is \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.05\\,\\frac{\\text{kg}}{\\text{L}})\\cdot (30\\,\\frac{\\text{L}}{\\text{min}}) \\\\  & =(0.05\\,\\frac{\\text{kg}}{\\cancel{\\text{L}}})\\cdot (30\\,\\frac{\\cancel{\\text{L}}}{\\text{min}}) \\\\  & =1.5\\,\\frac{\\text{kg}}{\\text{min}}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which coagulant exits the tank.\n\nTo find the rate at which coagulant leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of liquid in the tank at time $t.$\n\nThe tank initially contains $700\\,\\textrm{L}$ of liquid; a solution enters at $30\\,\\textrm{L/min}$ and leaves at $20\\,\\textrm{L/min}.$\nAs a result, the volume of liquid in the tank after $t$ minutes is \n\n$$\n700 + 30t - 20t = (700+10t)\\,\\textrm{L}.\n$$\n\nSince $Q$ is the amount of coagulant in the tank, the *concentration* of the mixed solution at time $t$ is\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{Q}{700+10t}\\,\\textrm{kg/L}.\n$$\n\nTherefore, as the completely mixed liquid leaves at a rate of $20\\,\\textrm{L/min},$ *coagulant* leaves at a rate of\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\\text{out}}^{′} & =(20\\,\\frac{\\text{L}}{\\text{min}})\\cdot (\\frac{Q}{700+10t}\\,\\frac{\\text{kg}}{\\text{L}}) \\\\  & =(20\\,\\frac{\\cancel{\\text{L}}}{\\text{min}})\\cdot (\\frac{Q}{700+10t}\\,\\frac{\\text{kg}}{\\cancel{\\text{L}}}) \\\\  & =\\frac{20Q}{700+10t}\\,\\frac{\\text{kg}}{\\text{min}} \\\\  & =\\frac{2Q}{70+t}\\,\\frac{\\text{kg}}{\\text{min}}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.\n\nThe rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\\int 2/(70+t)\\,dt} \\\\  & ={e}^{2\\operatorname{ln}⁡|70+t|} \\\\  & ={e}^{\\operatorname{ln}⁡(70+t)^{2}} \\\\  & =(70+t)^{2}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nMultiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t) = (70+t)^2$ yields\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}(70+t)^{2}\\cdot (\\frac{dQ}{dt}+\\frac{2}{70+t}Q) & =(70+t)^{2}\\cdot 1.5 \\\\ (70+t)^{2}\\frac{dQ}{dt}+2(70+t)Q & =1.5(70+t)^{2} \\\\ \\frac{d}{dt}(Q(70+t)^{2}) & =1.5(70+t)^{2}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, we integrate with respect to $t{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\int \\frac{d}{dt}(Q(70+t)^{2})\\,dt & =\\int 1.5(70+t)^{2}\\,dt \\\\ Q(70+t)^{2} & =1.5\\cdot \\frac{1}{3}(70+t)^{3}+C \\\\ Q(t) & =0.5(70+t)+\\frac{C}{(70+t)^{2}}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNote that $C$ is a constant of integration.\n\nWe're told that the tank initially contains $12\\,\\textrm{kg}$ of coagulant. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0) = 12,$ and solve for $C{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =12 \\\\ 0.5(70+0)+\\frac{C}{(70+0)^{2}} & =12 \\\\ 35+\\frac{C}{{70}^{2}} & =12 \\\\ \\frac{C}{{70}^{2}} & =-23 \\\\ C & =-23(70)^{2}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t){:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =0.5(70+t)-\\frac{23(70)^{2}}{(70+t)^{2}} \\\\  & =0.5(70+t)-23{(\\frac{70}{70+t})}^{2}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally,  the amount of coagulant in the tank $8$ minutes after pumping begins is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}Q(8) & =0.5(70+8)-23{(\\frac{70}{70+8})}^{2} \\\\  & =39-23{(\\frac{70}{78})}^{2} \\\\  & ≈20.48\\,\\text{kg},\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nrounded to two decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186229692 :question/id #uuid
