pumping begins." :question/worked-solution "Let $Q$ be the amount of nutrient in the vat at time $t,$ in minutes. Then, the derivative \n\n$$\n\\frac{dQ}{dt}\n$$\n\ndescribes how this amount changes with respect to time $t.$ This is equal to the rate at which nutrient enters the tank minus the rate at which nutrient leaves the tank.\n\n$$\n\\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\\text{out}}^{′}\n$$\n\nNote that the units of $\\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\\text{kg}/\\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.\n\n**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which nutrient enters the vat.\n\nNote that a feed solution containing $0.06\\,\\text{kg/L}$ of the nutrient enters the vat at a rate of $10\\,\\text{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *nutrient* enters the vat is \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.06\\,\\frac{\\text{kg}}{\\text{L}})\\cdot (10\\,\\frac{\\text{L}}{\\text{min}}) \\\\  & =(0.06\\,\\frac{\\text{kg}}{\\cancel{\\text{L}}})\\cdot (10\\,\\frac{\\cancel{\\text{L}}}{\\text{min}}) \\\\  & =0.6\\,\\frac{\\text{kg}}{\\text{min}}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which nutrient exits the vat.\n\nTo find the rate at which nutrient leaves the vat, we must first determine the volume of liquid in the vat at time $t.$\n\nThe vat initially contains $500\\,\\text{L}$ of liquid; a solution enters at $10\\,\\text{L/min}$ and leaves at $5\\,\\text{L/min}.$\nAs a result, the volume of liquid in the vat after $t$ minutes is \n\n$$\n500+10t-5t=(500+5t)\\,\\text{L}.\n$$\n\nSince $Q$ is the amount of nutrient in the vat, the *concentration* of the mixed solution at time $t$ is\n\n$$\n\\frac{Q}{500+5t}\\,\\text{kg/L}.\n$$\n\nTherefore, as the completely mixed liquid leaves at a rate of $5\\,\\text{L/min},$ *nutrient* leaves at a rate of\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\\text{out}}^{′} & =(5\\,\\frac{\\text{L}}{\\text{min}})\\cdot (\\frac{Q}{500+5t}\\,\\frac{\\text{kg}}{\\text{L}}) \\\\  & =(5\\,\\frac{\\cancel{\\text{L}}}{\\text{min}})\\cdot (\\frac{Q}{500+5t}\\,\\frac{\\text{kg}}{\\cancel{\\text{L}}}) \\\\  & =\\frac{5Q}{500+5t}\\,\\frac{\\text{kg}}{\\text{min}} \\\\  & =\\frac{Q}{100+t}\\,\\frac{\\text{kg}}{\\text{min}}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.\n\nThe rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\\text{out}}^{′} \\\\  & =0.6-\\frac{Q}{100+t}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwhich gives the equation\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{dQ}{dt}+\\frac{1}{100+t}Q=0.6.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.\n\nThis is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\\int 1/(100+t)\\,dt} \\\\  & ={e}^{\\operatorname{ln}⁡|100+t|} \\\\  & =100+t\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nMultiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=100+t$ yields\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}(100+t)\\cdot (\\frac{dQ}{dt}+\\frac{1}{100+t}Q) & =(100+t)\\cdot 0.6 \\\\ (100+t)\\frac{dQ}{dt}+Q & =0.6(100+t) \\\\ \\frac{d}{dt}(Q(100+t)) & =0.6(100+t).\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, we integrate with respect to $t:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\int \\frac{d}{dt}(Q(100+t))\\,dt & =\\int 0.6(100+t)\\,dt \\\\ Q(100+t) & =0.6\\cdot \\frac{1}{2}(100+t)^{2}+C \\\\ Q(t) & =0.3(100+t)+\\frac{C}{100+t}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNote that $C$ is a constant of integration.\n\nWe're told that the vat initially contains $8\\,\\text{kg}$ of nutrient. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=8,$ and solve for $C:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =8 \\\\ 0.3(100+0)+\\frac{C}{100+0} & =8 \\\\ 30+\\frac{C}{100} & =8 \\\\ \\frac{C}{100} & =-22 \\\\ C & =-2200\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =0.3(100+t)-\\frac{2200}{100+t}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally,  the amount of nutrient in the vat $8$ minutes after pumping begins is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}Q(8) & =0.3(100+8)-\\frac{2200}{100+8} \\\\  & =32.4-\\frac{2200}{108} \\\\  & ≈12.03\\,\\text{kg},\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nrounded to two decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186229183 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186228931 :question/id #uuid Amount at an Overflow Point"}] :question/problem "A syrup mixing tank in a confectionery factory can hold up to $240\\,\\textrm{gal}$ of liquid. Initially, it contains $96\\,\\textrm{gal}$ of syrup solution with $32\\,\\textrm{lb}$ of dissolved sugar. A more concentrated syrup with concentration $1.5\\,\\textrm{lb/gal}$ flows into the tank at a rate of $24\\,\\textrm{gal/min},$ while the completely mixed solution drains out at a rate of $16\\,\\textrm{gal/min}.$ Rounded to one decimal place, find the amount of sugar in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow." :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is the amount of sugar in the tank at time $t,$ the derivative \n\n$$\n\\dfrac{\\mathrm{d}Q}{\\mathrm{d}t}\n$$\n\ndescribes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which sugar enters the tank minus the rate at which sugar leaves the tank.\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{\\mathrm{d}Q}{\\mathrm{d}t} = Q'_{\\textrm{in}} - Q'_{\\textrm{out}}\n$$\n\nNote that the units of $\\dfrac{\\mathrm{d}Q}{\\mathrm{d}t}, Q'_{\\textrm{in}}$ and $Q'_{\\textrm{out}}$ are $\\textrm{lb}/\\textrm{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.\n\n**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which sugar enters the tank.\n\nFirst, note that a solution containing $1.5\\,\\textrm{lb/gal}$ of sugar enters the tank at a rate of $24\\,\\textrm{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *sugar* enters the tank is \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\\text{in}}^{′} & =(1.5\\,\\frac{\\text{lb}}{\\text{gal}})\\cdot (24\\,\\frac{\\text{gal}}{\\text{min}}) \\\\  & =(1.5\\,\\frac{\\text{lb}}{\\cancel{\\text{gal}}})\\cdot (24\\,\\frac{\\cancel{\\text{gal}}}{\\text{min}}) \\\\  & =36\\,\\frac{\\text{lb}}{\\text{min}}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which sugar exits the tank.\n\nTo find the rate at which sugar leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of solution in the tank at time $t.$\n\nThe tank initially contains $96\\,\\textrm{gal}$ of solution; solution enters at $24\\,\\textrm{gal/min}$ and mixed solution leaves at $16\\,\\textrm{gal/min}.$\nAs a result, the amount of solution in the tank after $t$ minutes is \n\n$$\nV(t) = 96 + 24t - 16t = 8(12+t)\\,\\textrm{gal}.\n$$\n\nNote that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the tank is filling.\n\nSince $Q$ is the amount of sugar in the tank, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{Q}{8(12 + t)}\\,\\textrm{lb/gal}.\n$$\n\nTherefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $16\\,\\textrm{gal/min},$ *sugar* leaves at a rate of\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\\text{out}}^{′} & =(16\\,\\frac{\\text{gal}}{\\text{min}})\\cdot (\\frac{Q}{8(12+t)}\\,\\frac{\\text{lb}}{\\text{gal}}) \\\\  & =(16\\,\\frac{\\cancel{\\text{gal}}}{\\text{min}})\\cdot (\\frac{Q}{8(12+t)}\\,\\frac{\\text{lb}}{\\cancel{\\text{gal}}}) \\\\  & =\\frac{16Q}{8(12+t)}\\,\\frac{\\text{lb}}{\\text{min}} \\\\  & =\\frac{2Q}{12+t}\\,\\frac{\\text{lb}}{\\text{min}}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.\n\nThe rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\\text{out}}^{′} \\\\  & =36-\\frac{2Q}{12+t}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwhich gives the equation\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{\\mathrm{d}Q}{\\mathrm{d}t} + \\dfrac{2}{12 + t}\\,Q = 36.\n$$\n\n**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.\n\nThis is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\\int 2/(12+t)\\,dt} \\\\  & ={e}^{2\\operatorname{ln}⁡|12+t|} \\\\  & ={e}^{\\operatorname{ln}⁡(12+t)^{2}} \\\\  & =(12+t)^{2}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nMultiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t) = (12+t)^2$ yields\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}(12+t)^{2}\\cdot (\\frac{dQ}{dt}+\\frac{2}{12+t}\\,Q) & =(12+t)^{2}\\cdot 36 \\\\ (12+t)^{2}\\frac{dQ}{dt}+2(12+t)Q & =36(12+t)^{2} \\\\ \\frac{d}{dt}(Q(12+t)^{2}) & =36(12+t)^{2}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, we integrate with respect to $t{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\int \\frac{d}{dt}(Q(12+t)^{2})\\,dt & =\\int 36(12+t)^{2}\\,dt \\\\ Q(12+t)^{2} & =36\\cdot \\frac{1}{3}(12+t)^{3}+C \\\\ Q(t) & =12(12+t)+\\frac{C}{(12+t)^{2}}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe're told that the tank initially contains $32\\,\\textrm{lb}$ of sugar. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0) = 32,$ and solve for $C{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =32 \\\\ 12(12+0)+\\frac{C}{(12+0)^{2}} & =32 \\\\ 12\\cdot 12+\\frac{C}{(12)^{2}} & =32 \\\\ 144+\\frac{C}{{12}^{2}} & =32 \\\\ \\frac{C}{{12}^{2}} & =-112 \\\\ C & =-112(12)^{2}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t){:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =12(12+t)-\\frac{112(12)^{2}}{(12+t)^{2}} \\\\  & =12(12+t)-112{(\\frac{12}{12+t})}^{2}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, let $t_o$ be the time when the tank begins to overflow. The tank has a capacity of $240\\,\\textrm{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V(t_o) = 240$ to solve for $t_o{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =240 \\\\ 96+24{t}_{o}-16{t}_{o} & =240 \\\\ 96+8{t}_{o} & =240 \\\\ 8{t}_{o} & =144 \\\\ {t}_{o} & =18\\,\\text{min}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, rounded to one decimal place, the amount of sugar in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}Q(18) & =12(12+18)-112{(\\frac{12}{12+18})}^{2} \\\\  & =360-112{(\\frac{12}{30})}^{2} \\\\  & ≈342.1\\,\\text{lb}.\\end{aligned}\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186229693 Initially, it contains $180\\,\\text{gal}$ of brine with $54\\,\\text{lb}$ of dissolved salt. A stronger brine with concentration $0.8\\,\\text{lb/gal}$ flows into the reservoir at a rate of $6\\,\\text{gal/min},$ while the completely mixed brine drains out at a rate of $4\\,\\text{gal/min}.$\nFind the amount of salt in the reservoir at the moment it begins to overflow." :question/requires-calculator true :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is the amount of salt in the tank at time $t,$ the derivative \n\n$$\n\\frac{dQ}{dt}\n$$\n\ndescribes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which minerals enter the tank minus the rate at which minerals leave the tank.\n\n$$\n\\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\\text{out}}^{′}\n$$\n\nNote that the units of $\\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\\text{kg}/\\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.\n\n**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which minerals enter the tank.\n\nFirst, note that a brine solution containing $0.8\\,\\text{lb/gal}$ of salt enters the reservoir at a rate of $6\\,\\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *salt* enters the reservoir is \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.8\\,\\frac{\\text{lb}}{\\text{gal}})\\cdot (6\\,\\frac{\\text{gal}}{\\text{min}}) \\\\  & =(0.8\\,\\frac{\\text{lb}}{\\cancel{\\text{gal}}})\\cdot (6\\,\\frac{\\cancel{\\text{gal}}}{\\text{min}}) \\\\  & =4.8\\,\\frac{\\text{lb}}{\\text{min}}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which minerals exit the tank.\n\nTo find the rate at which salt leaves the reservoir, we must first determine the volume of brine in the reservoir at time $t.$\n\nThe reservoir initially contains $180\\,\\text{gal}$ of brine; brine enters at $6\\,\\text{gal/min}$ and mixed brine leaves at $4\\,\\text{gal/min}.$\nAs a result, the amount of brine in the reservoir after $t$ minutes is \n\n$$\nV(t)=180+6t-4t=2(90+t)\\,\\text{gal}.\n$$\n\nNote that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the reservoir is filling.\n\nSince $Q$ is the amount of salt in the reservoir, the concentration of the brine at time $t$ is\n\n$$\n\\frac{Q}{2(90+t)}\\,\\text{lb/gal}.\n$$\n\nTherefore, as the completely mixed brine leaves at a rate of $4\\,\\text{gal/min},$ *salt* leaves at a rate of\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\\text{out}}^{′} & =(4\\,\\frac{\\text{gal}}{\\text{min}})\\cdot (\\frac{Q}{2(90+t)}\\,\\frac{\\text{lb}}{\\text{gal}}) \\\\  & =(4\\,\\frac{\\cancel{\\text{gal}}}{\\text{min}})\\cdot (\\frac{Q}{2(90+t)}\\,\\frac{\\text{lb}}{\\cancel{\\text{gal}}}) \\\\  & =\\frac{4Q}{2(90+t)}\\,\\frac{\\text{lb}}{\\text{min}} \\\\  & =\\frac{2Q}{90+t}\\,\\frac{\\text{lb}}{\\text{min}}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.\n\nThe rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\\text{out}}^{′} \\\\  & =4.8-\\frac{2Q}{90+t}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwhich gives the equation\n\n$$\n\\frac{dQ}{dt}+\\frac{2}{90+t}\\,Q=4.8.\n$$\n\n**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.\n\nThis is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\\int 2/(90+t)\\,dt} \\\\  & ={e}^{2\\operatorname{ln}⁡|90+t|} \\\\  & ={e}^{\\operatorname{ln}⁡(90+t)^{2}} \\\\  & =(90+t)^{2}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nMultiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(90+t)^{2}$ yields\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}(90+t)^{2}\\cdot (\\frac{dQ}{dt}+\\frac{2}{90+t}\\,Q) & =(90+t)^{2}\\cdot 4.8 \\\\ (90+t)^{2}\\frac{dQ}{dt}+2(90+t)Q & =4.8(90+t)^{2} \\\\ \\frac{d}{dt}(Q(90+t)^{2}) & =4.8(90+t)^{2}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, we integrate with respect to $t:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\int \\frac{d}{dt}(Q(90+t)^{2})\\,dt & =\\int 4.8(90+t)^{2}\\,dt \\\\ Q(90+t)^{2} & =4.8\\cdot \\frac{1}{3}(90+t)^{3}+C \\\\ Q(t) & =1.6(90+t)+\\frac{C}{(90+t)^{2}}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe're told that the reservoir initially contains $54\\,\\text{lb}$ of salt. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=54,$ and solve for $C:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =54 \\\\ 1.6(90+0)+\\frac{C}{(90+0)^{2}} & =54 \\\\ 144+\\frac{C}{(90)^{2}} & =54 \\\\ C & =-90(90)^{2}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =1.6(90+t)-\\frac{90(90)^{2}}{(90+t)^{2}} \\\\  & =1.6(90+t)-90{(\\frac{90}{90+t})}^{2}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the reservoir begins to overflow. The reservoir has a capacity of $300\\,\\text{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=300$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =300 \\\\ 2(90+{t}_{o}) & =300 \\\\ 90+{t}_{o} & =150 \\\\ {t}_{o} & =60\\,\\text{min}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, the amount of salt in the reservoir at the moment it begins to overflow is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}Q(60) & =1.6(90+60)-90{(\\frac{90}{90+60})}^{2} \\\\  & =240-90{(\\frac{9}{15})}^{2} \\\\  & =207.6\\,\\text{lb}.\\end{aligned}\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186229694 :question/id #uuid 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "A flavoring tank at a beverage factory can hold up to $150\\,\\text{gal}$ of liquid. Initially, it contains $75\\,\\text{gal}$ of flavoring solution with $25\\,\\text{lb}$ of dissolved flavoring. A more concentrated solution with concentration $\\frac{2}{3}\\,\\text{lb/gal}$ flows into the tank at a rate of $9\\,\\text{gal/min},$ while the completely mixed solution drains out at a rate of $6\\,\\text{gal/min}.$ Rounded to one decimal place, find the amount of flavoring in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow." :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is the amount of flavoring in the tank at time $t,$ the derivative \n\n$$\n\\frac{dQ}{dt}\n$$\n\ndescribes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which flavoring enters the tank minus the rate at which flavoring leaves the tank.\n\n$$\n\\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\\text{out}}^{′}\n$$\n\nNote that the units of $\\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\\text{lb}/\\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.\n\n**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which flavoring enters the tank.\n\nFirst, note that a solution containing $\\frac{2}{3}\\,\\text{lb/gal}$ of flavoring enters the tank at a rate of $9\\,\\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *flavoring* enters the tank is \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\\text{in}}^{′} & =(\\frac{2}{3}\\,\\frac{\\text{lb}}{\\text{gal}})\\cdot (9\\,\\frac{\\text{gal}}{\\text{min}}) \\\\  & =(\\frac{2}{3}\\,\\frac{\\text{lb}}{\\cancel{\\text{gal}}})\\cdot (9\\,\\frac{\\cancel{\\text{gal}}}{\\text{min}}) \\\\  & =6\\,\\frac{\\text{lb}}{\\text{min}}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which flavoring exits the tank.\n\nTo find the rate at which flavoring leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of solution in the tank at time $t.$\n\nThe tank initially contains $75\\,\\text{gal}$ of solution; solution enters at $9\\,\\text{gal/min}$ and mixed solution leaves at $6\\,\\text{gal/min}.$\nAs a result, the amount of solution in the tank after $t$ minutes is \n\n$$\nV(t)=75+9t-6t=3(25+t)\\,\\text{gal}.\n$$\n\nNote that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the tank is filling.\n\nSince $Q$ is the amount of flavoring in the tank, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is\n\n$$\n\\frac{Q}{3(25+t)}\\,\\text{lb/gal}.\n$$\n\nTherefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $6\\,\\text{gal/min},$ *flavoring* leaves at a rate of\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\\text{out}}^{′} & =(6\\,\\frac{\\text{gal}}{\\text{min}})\\cdot (\\frac{Q}{3(25+t)}\\,\\frac{\\text{lb}}{\\text{gal}}) \\\\  & =(6\\,\\frac{\\cancel{\\text{gal}}}{\\text{min}})\\cdot (\\frac{Q}{3(25+t)}\\,\\frac{\\text{lb}}{\\cancel{\\text{gal}}}) \\\\  & =\\frac{6Q}{3(25+t)}\\,\\frac{\\text{lb}}{\\text{min}} \\\\  & =\\frac{2Q}{25+t}\\,\\frac{\\text{lb}}{\\text{min}}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.\n\nThe rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\\text{out}}^{′} \\\\  & =6-\\frac{2Q}{25+t}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwhich gives the equation\n\n$$\n\\frac{dQ}{dt}+\\frac{2}{25+t}\\,Q=6.\n$$\n\n**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.\n\nThis is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\\int 2/(25+t)\\,dt} \\\\  & ={e}^{2\\operatorname{ln}⁡|25+t|} \\\\  & ={e}^{\\operatorname{ln}⁡(25+t)^{2}} \\\\  & =(25+t)^{2}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nMultiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(25+t)^{2}$ yields\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}(25+t)^{2}\\cdot (\\frac{dQ}{dt}+\\frac{2}{25+t}\\,Q) & =(25+t)^{2}\\cdot 6 \\\\ (25+t)^{2}\\frac{dQ}{dt}+2(25+t)Q & =6(25+t)^{2} \\\\ \\frac{d}{dt}(Q(25+t)^{2}) & =6(25+t)^{2}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, we integrate with respect to $t:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\int \\frac{d}{dt}(Q(25+t)^{2})\\,dt & =\\int 6(25+t)^{2}\\,dt \\\\ Q(25+t)^{2} & =6\\cdot \\frac{1}{3}(25+t)^{3}+C \\\\ Q(t) & =2(25+t)+\\frac{C}{(25+t)^{2}}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe're told that the tank initially contains $25\\,\\text{lb}$ of flavoring. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=25,$ and solve for $C:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =25 \\\\ 2(25+0)+\\frac{C}{(25+0)^{2}} & =25 \\\\ 50+\\frac{C}{(25)^{2}} & =25 \\\\ \\frac{C}{{25}^{2}} & =-25 \\\\ C & =-25(25)^{2}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =2(25+t)-\\frac{25(25)^{2}}{(25+t)^{2}} \\\\  & =2(25+t)-25{(\\frac{25}{25+t})}^{2}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the tank begins to overflow. The tank has a capacity of $150\\,\\text{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=150$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =150 \\\\ 75+9{t}_{o}-6{t}_{o} & =150 \\\\ 75+3{t}_{o} & =150 \\\\ 3{t}_{o} & =75 \\\\ {t}_{o} & =25\\,\\text{min}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, rounded to one decimal place, the amount of flavoring in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}Q(25) & =2(25+25)-25{(\\frac{25}{25+25})}^{2} \\\\  & =100-25{(\\frac{25}{50})}^{2} \\\\  & ≈93.8\\,\\text{lb}.\\end{aligned}\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186377212 :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186230082 :step/content {:db/id 17592186230205 :tutorial/content "In the previous lesson, we focused on dilution problems in which the incoming solution contained none of the substance being modeled. In those cases, the rate at which the substance entered the container was zero.\n\nIn many practical situations, however, the incoming solution *does* contain some amount of the substance. When this happens,\n\n- the rate of entry is no longer zero, and\n- the resulting differential equation takes the form of a first-order linear differential equation.\n\nFor example, suppose a storage tank initially holds $650\\,\\textrm{L}$ of water containing $1\\,300\\,\\textrm{g}$ of dissolved chlorine.\n\n- A solution containing $20\\,\\textrm{g/L}$ of dissolved chlorine is pumped into the tank at a rate of $5\\,\\textrm{L/min}.$\n- At the same time, the completely mixed water is drained out at a rate of $5\\,\\textrm{L/min}.$\n\nTo construct the model for the amount of chlorine $Q$ in the tank, we compare the rates of chlorine entering and leaving. The derivative $\\dfrac{\\mathrm{d}Q}{\\mathrm{d}t}$ describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t.$ This is equal to the rate at which chlorine enters the tank minus the rate at which chlorine leaves the tank.\n\n$$\\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\\dfrac{\\mathrm{d}Q}{\\mathrm{d}t} = Q'_{\\textrm{in}} - Q'_{\\textrm{out}}}$$\n\nWe compute the required rates of change in steps.\n\n**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which chlorine enters the tank.\n\nThe rate of chlorine entering is the concentration times the flow rate: $$\\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\\text{in}}^{'} & =(20\\,\\frac{\\text{g}}{\\text{L}})\\cdot (5\\,\\frac{\\text{L}}{\\text{min}}) \\\\ & =(20\\,\\frac{\\text{g}}{\\cancel{\\text{L}}})\\cdot (5\\,\\frac{\\cancel{\\text{L}}}{\\text{min}}) \\\\ & =100\\,\\frac{\\text{g}}{\\text{min}}\\end{aligned}$$\n\n**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which chlorine exits the tank.\n\nSince the volume remains constant at $650\\,\\textrm{L},$ the concentration in the tank is $\\dfrac{Q}{650}\\,\\dfrac{\\textrm{g}}{\\textrm{L}}.$ So, the rate of chlorine exiting is $$\\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\\text{out}}^{'} & =(5\\,\\frac{\\text{L}}{\\text{min}})\\cdot (\\frac{Q}{650}\\,\\frac{\\text{g}}{\\text{L}}) \\\\ & =(5\\,\\frac{\\cancel{\\text{L}}}{\\text{min}})\\cdot (\\frac{Q}{650}\\,\\frac{\\text{g}}{\\cancel{\\text{L}}}) \\\\ & =\\frac{Q}{130}\\,\\frac{\\text{g}}{\\text{min}}.\\end{aligned}$$\n\n**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.\n\nThe net rate of change $\\dfrac{\\mathrm{d}Q}{\\mathrm{d}t} = Q'_\\text{in} - Q'_\\text{out}$ is the difference between the rate in and the rate out. Combining this with the initial condition $Q(0) = 1\\,300\\,\\textrm{g},$ we can state the complete initial value problem: $$\\dfrac{\\mathrm{d}Q}{\\mathrm{d}t} = 100 - \\dfrac{1}{130}Q \\quad\\Longrightarrow\\quad \\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\\dfrac{\\mathrm{d}Q}{\\mathrm{d}t} + \\dfrac{1}{130}Q = 100, \\quad Q(0) = 1\\,300\\,\\textrm{g}}$$" :tutorial/id #uuid :step/content {:db/id 17592186230205 :tutorial/content "In the previous lesson, we focused on dilution problems in which the incoming solution contained none of the substance being modeled. In those cases, the rate at which the substance entered the container was zero.\n\nIn many practical situations, however, the incoming solution *does* contain some amount of the substance. When this happens,\n\n- the rate of entry is no longer zero, and\n- the resulting differential equation takes the form of a first-order linear differential equation.\n\nFor example, suppose a storage tank initially holds $650\\,\\textrm{L}$ of water containing $1\\,300\\,\\textrm{g}$ of dissolved chlorine.\n\n- A solution containing $20\\,\\textrm{g/L}$ of dissolved chlorine is pumped into the tank at a rate of $5\\,\\textrm{L/min}.$\n- At the same time, the completely mixed water is drained out at a rate of $5\\,\\textrm{L/min}.$\n\nTo construct the model for the amount of chlorine $Q$ in the tank, we compare the rates of chlorine entering and leaving. The derivative $\\dfrac{\\mathrm{d}Q}{\\mathrm{d}t}$ describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t.$ This is equal to the rate at which chlorine enters the tank minus the rate at which chlorine leaves the tank.\n\n$$\\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\\dfrac{\\mathrm{d}Q}{\\mathrm{d}t} = Q'_{\\textrm{in}} - Q'_{\\textrm{out}}}$$\n\nWe compute the required rates of change in steps.\n\n**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which chlorine enters the tank.\n\nThe rate of chlorine entering is the concentration times the flow rate: $$\\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\\text{in}}^{'} & =(20\\,\\frac{\\text{g}}{\\text{L}})\\cdot (5\\,\\frac{\\text{L}}{\\text{min}}) \\\\ & =(20\\,\\frac{\\text{g}}{\\cancel{\\text{L}}})\\cdot (5\\,\\frac{\\cancel{\\text{L}}}{\\text{min}}) \\\\ & =100\\,\\frac{\\text{g}}{\\text{min}}\\end{aligned}$$\n\n**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which chlorine exits the tank.\n\nSince the volume remains constant at $650\\,\\textrm{L},$ the concentration in the tank is $\\dfrac{Q}{650}\\,\\dfrac{\\textrm{g}}{\\textrm{L}}.$ So, the rate of chlorine exiting is $$\\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\\text{out}}^{'} & =(5\\,\\frac{\\text{L}}{\\text{min}})\\cdot (\\frac{Q}{650}\\,\\frac{\\text{g}}{\\text{L}}) \\\\ & =(5\\,\\frac{\\cancel{\\text{L}}}{\\text{min}})\\cdot (\\frac{Q}{650}\\,\\frac{\\text{g}}{\\cancel{\\text{L}}}) \\\\ & =\\frac{Q}{130}\\,\\frac{\\text{g}}{\\text{min}}.\\end{aligned}$$\n\n**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.\n\nThe net rate of change $\\dfrac{\\mathrm{d}Q}{\\mathrm{d}t} = Q'_\\text{in} - Q'_\\text{out}$ is the difference between the rate in and the rate out. Combining this with the initial condition $Q(0) = 1\\,300\\,\\textrm{g},$ we can state the complete initial value problem: $$\\dfrac{\\mathrm{d}Q}{\\mathrm{d}t} = 100 - \\dfrac{1}{130}Q \\quad\\Longrightarrow\\quad \\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\\dfrac{\\mathrm{d}Q}{\\mathrm{d}t} + \\dfrac{1}{130}Q = 100, \\quad Q(0) = 1\\,300\\,\\textrm{g}}$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "fc8b0fc6-c25c-50f5-adbd-028adf7c6698" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14578 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "70852def-fb14-50cc-b88d-6fe2af2343bf" :step/math-academy-id 601750 :step/next {:db/id 17592186230083}} {:db/id 17592186230205 :tutorial/content "In the previous lesson, we focused on dilution problems in which the incoming solution contained none of the substance being modeled. ={1}_{A}(x)+{1}_{B}(x)-{1}_{A}(x)\\cdot {1}_{B}(x).\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe can prove these results by splitting them into cases." :tutorial/id #uuid "a111c445-39e3-5ddd-8272-48ef3795a3b0" to $\\textrm{Span}\\{\\mathbf{v}_1\\}$ as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\\frac{{a}_{2}\\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1} \\\\  & ={a}_{2}-\\frac{4\\cdot 1+6\\cdot machine learning.\nThis course is divided into three main categories: linear algebra, multivariable calculus, and probability & statistics. The linear algebra section covers crucial machine learning fundamentals such as matrices, vector spaces, diagonalization, projections, singular value decomposition, and regression, as well as dimensionality reduction techniques such as principal component analysis. The multivariable calculus section develops the tools needed for optimization and learning algorithms, including vector and matrix calculus. Finally, the probability and statistics section covers random variables, point estimation, maximum likelihood estimation, and confidence intervals.\nOn completing this course, students will be well-prepared for a university-level machine learning course that tackles concepts such as gradient descent, neural networks, backpropagation, support vector machines, naive Bayes classifiers, and Gaussian mixture models." 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1009 "The course begins with foundational topics in set theory and logic. Students develop a precise mathematical language for describing sets, functions, and predicates, and are introduced to key ideas such as supremum and infimum, as well as argmax and argmin notation. Logical reasoning and Boolean functions are also studied, providing important conceptual motivation for understanding the expressive limitations of some simple machine learning models, such as why certain functions (e.g. XOR) cannot be represented by a single-layer neural network.\nStudents then explore matrices in-depth. They study Gaussian elimination, solve systems of equations, learn about determinants and their properties, and compute inverse matrices. These tools form the computational backbone of many machine learning algorithms.\nAs part of this course, students perform a deep dive into vector spaces, exploring linear independence, subspaces, bases, dimension, rank, and nullity. They also study operations such as the Hadamard product, which appears naturally in element-wise computations in neural networks. Students generalize key concepts to abstract vector spaces and inner product spaces, and study orthogonality, projections, and the Gram–Schmidt process.\nStudents will learn how to find eigenvectors of a matrix, compute matrix diagonalizations, and extend these ideas to orthogonal diagonalization of symmetric matrices. These techniques underpin dimensionality reduction methods and are central to understanding the structure of data.\nThe course then develops key applications of linear algebra in machine learning. Students study singular value decomposition and its relationship to principal component analysis, and learn how these tools are used for dimensionality reduction, feature extraction, and identifying structure in high-dimensional datasets. Linear least-squares problems and regression techniques are also studied as foundational methods for fitting models to data.\nA solid grasp of multivariable calculus is essential for understanding modern machine learning algorithms. In this course, students become well-versed in partial derivatives and gradient vectors (used in gradient-based optimization), the multivariable chain rule (essential for backpropagation), and vector-valued functions. Students extend differentiation to maps between multi-dimensional vector spaces and develop the tools of vector and matrix calculus used to compute gradients of loss functions in neural networks.\nStudents also study optimization of multivariable functions, including critical points, second derivative tests, and constrained optimization using Lagrange multipliers. These techniques form the mathematical foundation of algorithms such as support vector machines and constrained optimization problems in machine learning.\nStudents work with standard multivariable surfaces to build intuition for loss surfaces, and study double integrals as a tool for understanding continuous probability distributions.\nOn the probability and statistics side, students study discrete and continuous random variables, including probability density functions, cumulative distribution functions, transformations, expectation, moments, variance, and Bayes' theorem. Important probability distributions are explored in detail.\nStudents extend their understanding to joint, marginal, and conditional distributions, as well as sums and products of random variables. Topics such as covariance, correlation, and multivariate normal distributions are introduced, which are essential in probabilistic modeling.\nThe course concludes with parametric inference, focusing on point estimation, maximum likelihood estimation, and confidence intervals, which form the statistical foundation for many machine learning methods." 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1012 145 Building on calculus and introductory linear algebra, the course introduces vector geometry, multivariable analysis, and differential equations in a unified framework designed for modeling physical systems.\nStudents learn how mathematical concepts such as vector spaces, linear transformations, multivariable functions, and differential equations provide the language and computational techniques used to describe motion, fields, and dynamical processes. The course emphasizes connections between abstract mathematical ideas and the physical principles they support, preparing students for advanced study in classical mechanics, electromagnetism, and related areas of physics." 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1009 "The course begins with foundational topics that support later mathematical modeling in physics. Students study vector geometry in three-dimensional space, including equations of lines and planes and geometric relationships between them. These tools appear naturally in the description of trajectories, rays, and intersections of physical surfaces. Introductory set theory provides a precise language for describing mathematical structures and regions in space, supporting later work in multivariable analysis and probability.\nStudents then develop computational tools from linear algebra. Methods such as Gaussian elimination, matrix inverses, determinants, and LU factorization are used to analyze and solve systems of linear equations. These techniques arise when solving coupled equations in physical models, such as electrical circuits, mechanical systems with multiple interacting components, and discretized approximations of physical fields.\nThe course next develops the structure of vector spaces and linear transformations. Students study spans, bases, dimension, rank, and null spaces, and extend these ideas to abstract vector spaces. Linear maps and their matrix representations are examined, establishing the connection between geometric transformations and matrix algebra. These ideas culminate in the study of eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and matrix diagonalization, which are central tools for solving differential equations describing oscillations, normal modes of vibration, and stability of dynamical systems.\nThe course then turns to multivariable calculus and vector analysis. Students analyze functions of several variables, quadric surfaces, and coordinate transformations. Partial derivatives, gradients, and the multivariable chain rule are developed along with linear approximations and higher-order derivatives. These concepts describe how physical quantities such as temperature, pressure, or electric potential vary in space. Vector-valued functions and vector fields are studied together with curvature, divergence, and curl, providing the mathematical language used to describe velocity fields in fluid flow and electric and magnetic fields in electromagnetism.\nStudents then study multiple integration, focusing on double integrals and coordinate transformations such as polar coordinates. These techniques allow the computation of physical quantities distributed over regions, such as mass, charge, or probability density.\nThe final portion of the course introduces differential equations as models of dynamical systems. Students study first-order equations and qualitative behavior of solutions through phase-line analysis. Applications include motion under drag, gravitational attraction, electrical circuits, and population dynamics. The course concludes with second-order linear differential equations and oscillatory systems, including harmonic motion, damped oscillators, and resonance—fundamental mathematical models for vibrating In such cases, a rectangle in the $uv$-plane collapses to either a line segment or point in the $xy$-plane.\n\n![](images/9a/9a038c5de0e9f3205194fd7941a4b371c695c51c294f2ad5ac0b8fc1015811d1.png)\n\n![](images/98/9813ba294a0242abbfb885ebd3e82505d05a2f8a1cfa3975c7859f9530cac8b1.png)\n\nAffine transformations are special because these properties are *global*. In other words, they apply *everywhere* in the plane. So, for example, if $\\textrm{det}(T) = 2$, then the image of *every* rectangle in the $uv$-plane is a parallelogram with double the area of its preimage." 17592186045417] [17592186130461 1065 7672 17592186045417] [17592186130461 1066 #uuid "4dcb1ce1-bfad-524c-a89a-a589532a1067" 17592186045417] [17592186130461 1067 "A Review of Affine Transformations" 17592186045417] [17592186130462 1064 "The Jacobian determinant gives information about nonlinear transformations similar to that described by the determinant properties of affine transformations.\n\nThe critical difference is that, in general, the Jacobian describes *local* effects, not global ones. \n\nTo understand what this means, suppose that $\\mathbf{T}: U \\to \\mathbb{R}^2$ is a transformation, where\n![](images/d0/d0149013f12e5cdad31611d4c64489c0aaf6049707e9eed22202ae70d2d8a38a.svg) \n\nand we assume that $x(u,v)$ and $y(u,v)$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives on $U.$\n\nFor ease of notation, let's introduce $J(u_0,v_0)$ to denote the Jacobian determinant of $\\mathbf T$ evaluated at $(u_0, v_0){:}$\n\n$$\nJ(u_0,v_0) = \\left.\\dfrac{\\partial(x,y)}{\\partial(u,v)}\\right|_{(u_0,v_0)}\n$$\n\nLet's describe $\\mathbf T$'s effect on a *tiny* rectangle in the $uv$-plane whose bottom-left corner is the point $(u_0,v_0).$\n\n![](images/dc/dc084ec02cd0c4fac71379590e8dc4973354cacc898e267a0eb15a6e8500f31f.png)\n\nIt's important to note that the image of our rectangle in the $xy$-plane is typically *not* a parallelogram! However, provided that our rectangle is very small, its image can be *approximated* by a parallelogram (we'll justify this in a future lesson). \n\nThe Jacobian determinant of $\\mathbf T$ evaluated at $(u_0,v_0)$ describes the following key features between our tiny rectangle and its (approximate) image:\n\n- The *local* area scale factor of $\\mathbf T$. \n\nSuppose the length and width of our rectangle are $\\delta u$ and $\\delta v,$ so its area is $\\delta A = \\delta u\\delta v.$ Then, it can be shown that the parallelogram in the $xy$-plane has an area equal to $\\left|J(u_0,v_0)\\right| \\cdot \\delta A.$\n\n![](images/be/be1771ebb041c418c58d7d5615510e2fcacfeaf3677fbace739498ef1998ef11.png)\n\nNote the similarity of this formula with that of affine transformations described earlier (we've simply replaced $\\det(T)$ with the Jacobian).\n\n- Whether the transformation is *locally* orientation-preserving or *locally* orientation-reversing.\n\nIf $J(u_0,v_0)> 0,$ the transformation is (locally) orientation-preserving.\n\n![](images/8c/8c649fdd526a831fb990393b292fb4582dad14c2391d129e9ed59792ebb8ac31.png)\n\nIf $J(u_0,v_0)<  0,$ the transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing.\n\n![](images/ae/ae5a3d0a42e1c4b9f692994b89815382a30cdf3e676bbd9844258ad2a6961608.png)\n\n- Whether the transformation is *locally* invertible or *locally* non-invertible.\n\nIf $J(u_0,v_0)\\neq 0,$ the transformation is (locally) invertible.\n\n![](images/33/33ca98206a347e13aa8ec179a52dd755008d9a7d74882391e0c3f2344f6f6641.png)\n\nIf $J(u_0,v_0)= 0,$ the transformation is (locally) non-invertible.\n\n![](images/3d/3d4534c263a9a5bb26ba35ce8f879cf01db741441d948c023acaa9407d58e6e0.png)\n\n![](images/65/659f26ac6aba808d66a760d5683f265fd7c54431d894b2eabdc255b46368fc24.png)\n\nPoints $(u_0,v_0)$ such that $J(u_0,v_0)=0$ are called **critical points.** Critical points are very important. Building on the analytical framework established in the first course, students study orthogonality, multivariable integration, vector calculus theorems, and advanced methods for differential equations.\nThe course emphasizes mathematical structures that arise naturally in physics, including inner product spaces, orthogonal projections, integral theorems of vector calculus, and transform methods for solving differential equations. These tools provide the mathematical foundation for analyzing electromagnetic fields, wave phenomena, dynamical systems, and statistical models encountered in advanced physics courses." 17592186045417] [17592186046660 1009 "The course begins with the theory of projections in inner product spaces. Students study norms, inner products, orthogonality, and orthogonal complements in vector spaces over the real and complex numbers. Techniques such as orthogonal projections, the Gram–Schmidt process, and QR factorization allow vectors to be decomposed into orthogonal components. These ideas play a role in Fourier analysis, signal decomposition, and numerical methods used in physical simulations.\nStudents then explore quadratic forms and the diagonalization of symmetric matrices. The spectral theorem provides a geometric interpretation of symmetric transformations and leads to techniques for analyzing energy functions and stability in physical systems. Singular value decomposition is also introduced as a powerful matrix factorization with applications in numerical modeling and data analysis.\nApplications of linear algebra follow, including least-squares methods for solving overdetermined systems. These methods arise when fitting theoretical models to experimental data and when approximating solutions to physical equations.\nThe course then develops multivariable integration in three dimensions. Students compute triple integrals over general regions and apply coordinate transformations such as cylindrical and spherical coordinates. These techniques allow physicists to compute quantities such as mass distributions, charge densities, and gravitational or electric potentials.\nStudents next study line integrals and surface integrals of scalar and vector fields. Concepts such as circulation, flux, and path independence lead to the fundamental theorems of vector calculus, including Green’s theorem, the divergence theorem, and Stokes’ theorem. These results form the mathematical framework underlying conservation laws and the differential and integral formulations of electromagnetic theory.\nApplications of multivariable calculus follow, including vector mechanics and optimization. Students analyze motion using vector-valued functions, apply Newton’s second law to systems in the plane, and study work–energy relationships. Multiple integrals are used to compute mass, centers of mass, moments of inertia, and other physical quantities.\nThe course then returns to differential equations, extending earlier techniques to systems of linear differential equations. Students analyze dynamical systems using eigenvalues, phase portraits, and matrix methods, which appear in models of interacting systems such as coupled oscillators or predator–prey dynamics.\nLaplace transforms are introduced as a powerful tool for solving linear differential equations with discontinuous inputs or initial conditions. Boundary value problems and Fourier series are then developed, providing mathematical techniques used to solve differential equations describing heat flow, vibrating strings, wave propagation, and other physical phenomena.\nThe course concludes with numerical methods for differential equations and advanced probability topics. Students analyze the accuracy and stability of numerical schemes used in computational physics and study multivariate probability distributions and the central limit theorem, which appear in statistical physics and experimental analysis." 17592186045417] [17592186046660 1012 155 17592186045417] [17592186046660 1013 "PS2" 17592186045417] [17592186046660 1014 #uuid
